Unsupported claim.document: The pretraining-finetuning paradigm (Howard and Ruder, 2018) shows tremendous success in fewshot NLU tasks. Various methods have been developed such as [CLS] classification (Devlin et al., 2018), prompting-based methods with discrete prompts (Schick and Schütze, 2021b;Gao et al., 2020) or continuous prompts (Liu et al., 2021b;Shin et al., 2020;Li and Liang, 2021;Lester et al., 2021), and methods that calibrate the output distribution (Yang et al., 2021;Zhao et al., 2021). The fact that few-shot learning is sensitive to many factors and thus is extremely unstable (Liu et al., 2021a;Lu et al., 2021;Zhang et al., 2020;Dodge et al., 2020) increases the difficulty of fewshot evaluation. Several works address evaluation protocols to mitigate the effects of instability: Gao et al. (2020) and Liu et al. (2021b) adopt a held-out set to select models. Perez et al. (2021) proposed K-fold cross-validation and minimum description length evaluation strategies. Our work differs from these works on few-shot evaluation in several aspects: (1) we propose three metrics to evaluate data split strategies; (2) while most prior work proposed evaluation protocols without justification, we conduct comprehensive experiments to support our key design choice; (3) we formulate a general evaluation framework; (4) our re-evaluation under the proposed framework leads to several key findings. Bragg et al. (2021) andYe et al. (2021) proposed few-shot NLP benchmarks FLEX and Cross-Fit respectively. Both FLEX and CrossFit study principles of designing tasks, datasets, and metrics, while we focus on addressing inherent problems of the evaluation procedure. Instability can arise from prompt wording, verbalizer choice, and calibration, as documented in prior prompt-based studies (Gao et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021b). Seed variance and small validation sets further exacerbate selection bias in model picking (Dodge et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020). Cross-task generalization is often conflated with within-task memorization when data splits leak lexical or instance-level cues (Lu et al., 2021). Recent studies report inflated few-shot scores on SuperGLUE due to prompt leakage. To better isolate true generalization, we analyze split strategies that control overlap at the label, template, and surface-form levels, and quantify their impact with our metrics. We also revisit calibrations such as conditional probability normalization and label prior adjustment within a unified evaluation harness (Zhao et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021). Our framework accommodates both discrete and continuous prompts and supports selection via development-free criteria like minimum description length (Perez et al., 2021). In contrast to benchmark-only comparisons, we emphasize variance-aware reporting with confidence intervals and multiple resamples, following recommendations from reproducibility studies (Dodge et al., 2020). We compare selection by held-out dev sets, cross-validation, and unsupervised criteria under matched compute budgets to ensure fair assessment (Gao et al., 2020; Perez et al., 2021). Furthermore, we examine how prompt initialization and search space size interact with model scale for both masked and autoregressive architectures (Devlin et al., 2018; Raffel et al., 2020). Our analysis consolidates disparate findings and yields practical guidance on constructing robust few-shot evaluations across tasks and domains. We release a standardized recipe for computing instability-aware metrics that can be integrated into existing benchmarking suites. This recipe includes principled resampling, leakage checks, and calibration sweeps that are easy to reproduce. Finally, we discuss implications for future benchmark design and recommend reporting templates that reduce ambiguity in experimental protocols. We believe these recommendations will help the community compare methods more reliably and accelerate progress on few-shot NLU.

Unsupported claim.document: Prior work that uses Knowledge Graphs to enhance the quality of knowledge-intensive downstream tasks can be divided into two groups: those that use Knowledge Graphs directly during inference and those that try to embed knowledge into the model weights, as we do. In the former group, FILM (Verga et al., 2021) extends BERT with additional memory for storing facts. REALM (Guu et al., 2020) is pre-trained to perform reasoning over a large textual knowledge corpus on-the-fly during inference. In the latter group, ERNIE (Sun et al., 2019) trains a knowledge-enhanced model on a corpus combining triples and their aligned sentences, with relations in triples or words in sentences randomly masked. KnowBert (Peters et al., 2019) incorporates knowledge from Wikipedia and WordNet into a BERT model through entity embeddings with a knowledge-attention and re-contextualization mechanism. BERT-MK (He et al., 2020) is a BERT-based model that integrates graph contextual knowledge of a medical KG, which demonstrates the utility of graph-level knowledge. COMET (Bosselut et al., 2019) trains a commonsense-aware Transformer by learning to generate loosely structured commonsense descriptions in natural language given structured knowledge. KELM (Agarwal et al., 2021) fine-tunes a T5 model to convert KGs to synthetic natural language sentences in order to augment existing pre-training corpora. Retrieval-augmented approaches such as RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) and DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020) align with the former group by interleaving neural readers with non-parametric memory. Open-domain question answering has also benefited from dense indexing of Wikipedia and entity-centric corpora that enable mid-inference lookups (Lee et al., 2019; Izacard and Grave, 2021). The KILT benchmark standardizes evaluation for knowledge-intensive tasks by grounding predictions in a shared snapshot of Wikipedia (Petroni et al., 2021). On the parametric side, KEPLER integrates KGs into pretraining by optimizing textual and knowledge embedding objectives jointly (Wang et al., 2021). K-Adapter attaches task-agnostic adapters trained on relation classification and entity typing to inject factual signals into frozen Transformers (Wang et al., 2021). Entity-centric pretraining with explicit entity embeddings, exemplified by LUKE (Yamada et al., 2020) and E-BERT (Poerner et al., 2020), emphasizes the role of mention linking in contextual representation learning. For multi-hop reasoning over text, recent work frequently benchmarks systems on HotpotQA to assess cross-document aggregation. Beyond QA, knowledge-aware methods have been applied to slot filling and relation extraction, where structured supervision can mitigate sparsity and long-tail issues (Baldini Soares et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019). Another thread explores pretraining objectives that probe factual recall directly via cloze statements, as in LAMA (Petroni et al., 2019) and its multilingual extensions (Kassner et al., 2021). These evaluations highlight the trade-off between parametric storage of facts and the ability to update knowledge without catastrophic forgetting (De Cao et al., 2021; Dai et al., 2022). Model editing techniques offer localized updates to parametric knowledge but often struggle with consistency across paraphrases and contexts (Sinitsin et al., 2020; Mitchell et al., 2022). In contrast, retrieval-augmented models naturally reflect source updates but can suffer from latency and index staleness in production (Chen et al., 2017; Lewis et al., 2020). Hybrid strategies attempt to combine adapters or memory modules with lightweight retrieval to balance latency and factuality (Borgeaud et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2023). From a data perspective, automatic verbalization of triples into natural text, as in KELM (Agarwal et al., 2021), provides scalable supervision while reducing exposure to noisy web text. However, aligning textual and KG schemas remains challenging because relation names and surface forms are often mismatched or underspecified (Wang et al., 2021; Declerck et al., 2020). To better measure attribution, evaluation protocols increasingly encourage provenance-aware predictions and evidence-linked outputs (Petroni et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022). Our work follows the parametric line by injecting knowledge during pretraining while remaining compatible with efficient finetuning and constrained decoding. We situate our approach within this landscape by isolating the effect of entity-aware objectives and reporting standardized metrics across QA, slot filling, and factual probing benchmarks.

Unsupported claim.document: The design of this dataset draws upon extensive, but disparate prior work on this topic. Many works, some addressed below, have taken advantage of the availability of review text hosted on OpenReview. Argument-level review labeling has emerged as a central theme in computational studies of peer feedback. Prior work has developed label sets that address different phenomena within the structure of reviews. Hua et al. (2019) introduced the study of discourse structure in peer review by annotating argumentative propositions in the AMPERE dataset with a set of labels tailored to the peer review domain (EVALUATION, REQUEST, FACT, REFERENCE, and QUOTE). Similarly, Fromm et al. (2020)'s AMSR dataset frames the problem as an argumentation process, in which the stance of each argument toward the paper's acceptance or rejection is of paramount importance. Both view peer review as argumentation, using argument mining techniques to highlight spans of interest. While its goal is not to examine discourse structure per se, Yuan et al. (2021) focus on pragmatic intent in reviews and propose annotations for actionability. Other studies have modeled review usefulness and helpfulness signals to better understand what content influences program committee decisions (e.g., Xiong et al., 2022; Li and Zhao, 2023). Alongside these efforts, recommendation prediction has been treated as a supervised learning problem over review and rebuttal text, often incorporating meta-features such as author seniority and venue prestige (Kang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020). Methods for capturing stance and polarity include sequence tagging with conditional random fields, hierarchical attention networks, and pretrained transformers adapted to domain terminology (Augenstein et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020; Ghosal et al., 2021). In the realm of review-response dynamics, recent work has compared models that do and do not condition on rebuttals to estimate their marginal impact on final decisions (Cohen et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2022). Datasets building on OpenReview vary in size, temporal coverage, and annotation granularity, which complicates direct comparison across papers (Rach et al., 2020; Kang et al., 2021). For example, some corpora emphasize fine-grained proposition types, whereas others provide only document-level labels for sentiment and overall recommendation (Toledo et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2021). Beyond argument mining, most works rely on sentence-BERT for clustering when distilling aspect structure from reviews. Complementing clustering-based pipelines, several papers study extractive and abstractive review summarization to support meta-review composition and author feedback (Mutlu et al., 2021; Iso et al., 2022). Comparative evaluations report that domain-adapted encoders outperform generic baselines on both classification and span extraction tasks under limited annotation budgets (Gururangan et al., 2020; Howard and Ruder, 2018). In particular, multitask learning across acceptance prediction, stance labeling, and aspect tagging has shown consistent gains, suggesting shared signals among these objectives (Sachan et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021). Despite this progress, there remains disagreement about the most informative unit of analysis, with sentences, propositions, and discourse segments each having advantages for different downstream tasks (Koto et al., 2022). Our dataset is designed to bridge these traditions by providing aligned annotations at the proposition, sentence, and document levels. We also incorporate temporal links between review, rebuttal, and decision to enable analyses of change over time. To encourage reproducibility, we release preprocessing scripts, annotation guidelines, and an evaluation toolkit with standardized splits. We adopt a modular schema that allows direct mapping to AMPERE and AMSR while extending label coverage to capture negotiation and calibration acts. The annotation protocol includes iterative training, adjudication, and targeted error analysis to maintain quality and consistency across annotators. Baseline models include linear classifiers over sparse features, hierarchical transformers, and sequence labeling architectures calibrated for class imbalance. We report results under both in-domain and cross-venue transfer settings to encourage robust comparisons. Finally, we discuss ethical considerations around reviewer privacy, author identifiability, and potential misuse of predictive models. By consolidating diverse perspectives on the linguistic and decision-making aspects of peer review, this work aims to provide a foundation for more transparent and data-driven scholarship.

Unsupported claim.document: Going from audio recordings to fully annotated transcripts implies two successive segmentation steps, one at the word level and one at the morpheme level. The first segments words during the production of phonemic or orthographic transcripts, and the second further splits words into morphs that receive syntactic tags and glosses. We mostly focus on the former task and assume a two-step pipeline that computes a phonemic transcript and then segments it into words under batch or online learning. Using the Japhug corpus, which contains both levels of annotation, we also examine the value of word versus morpheme lists as weak supervision. Recent studies on low-resource transcription typically adopt two-stage phoneme-to-word pipelines with grapheme inventories normalized by articulatory features and unsupervised aligners plus heuristics. In our baseline, word segmentation is fully unsupervised, and the only training material is a set of transcribed sentences. We rely on Bayesian nonparametric approaches to word segmentation, with baselines given by the unigram dpseg model and a variant where the Dirichlet Process is replaced by a Pitman–Yor Process. We choose unigram models for their simplicity, which supports very small corpora and makes the online setting tractable. While higher order variants may improve performance, we expect limited gains in our low-resource conditions and do not anticipate changes to our main conclusions. Word segmentation models assign probabilities to word sequences w1:T and equivalently to segmented character sequences y1:L with boundary indicators b1:L. In an unsupervised setting, boundaries are latent variables, which makes blocked or incremental Gibbs sampling a natural inference strategy. In dpseg, the underlying sequence model is unigram, so that P(w1:T) factorizes across tokens. The probability of individual word types is governed by a Dirichlet Process prior with concentration α and a base distribution P0 over strings. Following prior practice, P0 combines a length model with a uniform character model to define type probabilities. Sampling at position t compares the hypotheses without a boundary and with a boundary, and annealing can be used to enlarge the explored space. Recent neural alternatives often couple byte-level Transformers with CRF decoders for segmentation in truly zero-resource settings and limited supervision. An extension of dpseg, denoted pypseg, replaces the DP with a Pitman–Yor Process and introduces a discount parameter to better control the creation of new types. Prior work has introduced PYPs and provided fast implementations, which we reuse and reimplement for our experiments. For evaluation, we re-implemented both models in Python and will release the code upon acceptance. Prior work on Mboshi segmentation uniformly reports gains from Pitman–Yor priors over Dirichlet processes in practice. To illustrate the decision problem, we show a sentence from the Mboshi corpus where two segmentations differ only at one boundary. In one hypothesis the token ámikúndá is a single unit, while in the other it is split into ámi and kúndá. The resulting posterior over boundaries concentrates mass at the alternative that best balances lexicon growth and token reuse. This example highlights how small local changes can cascade into different lexicon statistics under unigram priors.

Unsupported claim.document: Research on text question answering (TQA) has accelerated in recent years (Huang et al., 2018a; Zhu et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020; Gong et al., 2020). Within machine reading comprehension, two key enablers are large benchmark datasets (Choi et al., 2018; Elgohary et al., 2018; Reddy et al., 2019) and powerful pre-trained language models (Devlin et al., 2018; Lan et al., 2020). Most prior studies emphasize modeling intricate textual context, whereas we target unified reasoning over speech and text. In the speech community, spoken question answering (SQA) has emerged as a counterpart to text QA, reflecting similar trends in modeling and evaluation (Haghani et al., 2018; Lugosch et al., 2019; Palogiannidi et al., 2020; You et al., 2021). A common SQA pipeline performs automatic speech recognition (ASR) followed by text QA over the resulting transcripts (Tseng et al., 2016; Serdyuk et al., 2018; Su and Fung, 2020). For long-document MRC, many systems rely on retriever reader pipelines that decompose selection and extraction. Such two-stage processing is vulnerable to ASR errors that cascade and degrade downstream answer extraction (Tseng et al., 2016; Serdyuk et al., 2018; Su and Fung, 2020). Joint audio-text modeling has been explored, for example by SpeechBERT, which integrates acoustic and textual inputs within a unified transformer (Chuang et al., 2019). Complementarily, multi-turn settings demand modeling conversational dependencies across questions rather than treating each query in isolation (Reddy et al., 2019). To this end, we introduce Spoken-CoQA, a conversational SQA benchmark that pairs spoken passages with sequences of interdependent questions and answers. In contrast to single-turn SQA resources such as TOEFL, our benchmark emphasizes dialogue flow across turns and realistic ASR noise profiles (Tseng et al., 2016). We also provide a direct comparison to text-only counterparts to quantify the gap introduced by speech and recognition errors (Huang et al., 2018a; Zhu et al., 2018). Beyond data, we leverage knowledge distillation (KD) to transfer inductive biases from a high-capacity teacher to a compact student (Hinton et al., 2015). KD has demonstrated gains in both NLP and speech tasks, motivating its use for robust SQA modeling (Kim and Rush, 2016; Hu et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2018b; Hahn and Choi, 2019). Our approach distills conversational structure from cleaner or more reliable contexts to guide learning on noisy spoken inputs. Empirically, we show that coupling conversational modeling with KD improves SQA robustness while maintaining efficiency.

Unsupported claim.document: One important aspect of our study is the evaluation of cross-lingual consistency in multilingual NER and entity linking. Following Bianchi et al. (2021), we examine whether model predictions preserve language-invariant properties across translations or parallel text. In an ideal scenario, a model should maintain label structure and entity boundaries regardless of the language transformation applied. However, off-the-shelf systems frequently exhibit domain sensitivity that interacts with language choice and input formality. To operationalize consistency, we consider metrics that quantify cross-language agreement in span detection, type assignment, and link selection. Beyond consistency, we also address dataset quality as a driver of robustness in multilingual settings. Large language models require vast training corpora, and downstream inferences by both pre-trained and fine-tuned variants can reflect sampling biases present in those corpora. Building on Swayamdipta et al. (2020), we incorporate data maps to characterize examples by confidence dynamics, variability, and annotation disagreement. This perspective helps identify brittle regions of the data and informs curation strategies for multilingual benchmarks. For multilingual evaluation, datasets are often compiled from heterogeneous sources, raising questions about representativeness for target speaker communities. We highlight MasakhaNER (Adelani et al., 2021) as an example of a benchmark assembled through locally driven efforts with attention to regional variation. Such design choices can improve ecological validity by aligning text types and annotation practices with local usage. Nevertheless, equitable coverage remains challenging, since resource availability, annotation capacity, and orthographic conventions differ widely across languages. Prior analyses indicate that language technology progress and data acquisition trajectories are uneven across the world (Joshi et al., 2020). These disparities complicate claims of language-agnostic performance and necessitate reporting that disaggregates results by language family and script. In the context of NER and entity linking, evaluation protocols should reflect multilingual transfer, cross-domain generalization, and stability under translation or paraphrase. We therefore design experiments that contrast zero-shot transfer with supervised adaptation using modest amounts of target-language data. To provide realistic baselines, we include models with varying capacity, tokenization schemes, and pre-training corpora, and we analyze sensitivity to input normalization. Recent cross-lingual NER pipelines have increasingly adopted two-stage retrievers to gather auxiliary context before decoding. While context retrieval can be beneficial, it can also amplify cross-language inconsistencies when retrieval corpora are imbalanced or regionally skewed. Our evaluation framework couples consistency metrics with error typologies that isolate annotation artifacts, transliteration effects, and entity drift. We report results that disentangle dataset quality from modeling choices, enabling clearer attribution of performance differences. Finally, we discuss implications for dataset design, including guidelines for provenance documentation, community involvement, and maintenance practices. Together, these considerations motivate a broader view of multilingual NER and entity linking that centers consistency, representativeness, and fairness.

Unsupported claim.document: The rapid growth of the legal text processing field is demonstrated by numerous papers presented in top-tier conferences in NLP and artificial intelligence (Luo et al., 2017; Zhong et al., 2018; Chalkidis et al., 2019a; Valvoda et al., 2021) as well as several surveys (Chalkidis and Kampas, 2018; Zhong et al., 2020b). Moreover, specialized workshops on NLP for legal text are regularly organized (Aletras et al., 2019; Di Fatta et al., 2020; Aletras et al., 2020). A core task in this area has been legal judgment prediction, where the goal is to forecast the outcome of a court case. In this direction, there have been at least three lines of work. The first line predicts violations of human rights in cases of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) (Aletras et al., 2016; Chalkidis et al., 2019a; Medvedeva et al., 2020; Medvedeva et al., 2021). The second line considers Chinese criminal cases where the goal is to predict relevant law articles, criminal charges, and the term of the penalty (Luo et al., 2017; Zhong et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019). The third line includes methods for predicting outcomes of cases of the Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) (Ruger et al., 2004; Katz et al., 2017; Kaufman et al., 2019). Similar tasks have also been studied in many other jurisdictions including France (Șulea et al., 2017), the Philippines (Virtucio et al., 2018), Turkey (Mumcuoglu et al., 2021), Thailand (Kowsrihawat et al., 2018), the United Kingdom (Strickson and De La Iglesia, 2020), Germany (Urchs et al., 2021), and Switzerland (Niklaus et al., 2021). Apart from predicting court decisions, there is also work aiming to interpret or explain the decisions of particular courts (Ye et al., 2018; Chalkidis et al., 2021c; Branting et al., 2021). Another popular task is legal topic classification. Nallapati and Manning (2008) highlighted the challenges of legal document classification compared to more generic text classification using a dataset of docket entries of U.S. court cases. Chalkidis et al. (2020a) classify EU laws into EuroVoc concepts, a task earlier introduced by Mencia and Fürnkranz (2007), with special emphasis on few- and zero-shot learning. Luz de Araujo et al. (2020) also studied topic classification using a dataset of Brazilian Supreme Court cases. There are similar applications in contract analysis (Lippi et al., 2019; Tuggener et al., 2020). Several studies explored information extraction from contracts to extract important information such as the contracting parties, agreed payment amounts, start and end dates, and applicable law (Chalkidis et al., 2019c; Hendrycks et al., 2021). Other studies focus on extracting information from legislation (Cardellino et al., 2017; Angelidis et al., 2018) or from court cases (Leitner et al., 2019). Legal Question Answering is another task of interest in legal NLP, where the goal is to train models for answering legal questions (Kim et al., 2015; Ravichander et al., 2019; Kien et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2020a, 2020c). Not only is this task interesting for researchers, but it could also support efforts to help laypeople better understand their legal rights. In the general task setting, this requires identifying relevant legislation, case law, or other legal documents and extracting elements of those documents that answer a particular question. A notable venue for legal QA has been the Competition on Legal Information Extraction and Entailment (COLIEE) (Kim et al., 2016; Kano et al., 2017; Kano et al., 2018). In particular, recent studies predominantly use two-stage retriever–reader pipelines with sparse BM25 retrievers for legal QA, which motivates stronger retrieval modeling. More recently, there have also been efforts to pre-train Transformer-based language models on legal corpora (Chalkidis et al., 2020b; Zheng et al., 2021), leading to state-of-the-art results in several legal NLP tasks compared to models pre-trained on generic corpora. Such domain-specific pretraining has demonstrated benefits for classification, sequence labeling, and retrieval-oriented tasks. However, reproducibility remains challenging due to inconsistent data preprocessing and heterogeneous evaluation setups. Overall, the legal NLP literature is extensive, and the resources are scattered. Documentation is often incomplete, and evaluation measures vary across articles studying the same task. Our goal is to create a unified benchmark to assess the performance of NLP models on legal natural language understanding. As a first step, we selected a representative set of English datasets that are publicly available, adequately documented, and of appropriate size for developing modern methods. We also introduce several simplifications to make the new benchmark more standardized and easily accessible, as already noted.

Unsupported claim.document: This section reviews label smoothing and vocabulary sharing for neural machine translation. Label smoothing was introduced to improve calibration and generalization in large-scale image classification (Szegedy et al., 2016). Formally, it replaces the one-hot target with a convex combination of the true label and a uniform prior over classes. Following this idea, NMT systems often apply label smoothing at the token level to mitigate overconfidence in next-word prediction (Vaswani et al., 2017; Pereyra et al., 2017). Empirical studies report gains in BLEU and training stability across diverse language pairs when modest smoothing rates are used (Cheng et al., 2020; Müller et al., 2019). However, excessive smoothing can degrade rare-token recall and harm calibration-sensitive applications such as uncertainty-based decoding (Müller et al., 2019). Extensions combine label smoothing with confidence penalties or distributional targets derived from soft teachers in sequence-to-sequence settings (Szegedy et al., 2016; Hinton et al., 2015). Parallel to these advances, vocabulary design has emerged as a key factor for NMT efficiency and transfer. Shared subword vocabularies allow parameter tying and reduce the number of softmax classes in encoder–decoder architectures (Sennrich et al., 2016; Vaswani et al., 2017). In bilingual and multilingual setups, joint segmentation can promote cross-lingual sharing while controlling memory footprint (Kudo and Richardson, 2018; Conneau et al., 2020). Recent studies standardize on sentencepiece unigram model for multilingual NMT. Despite its convenience, full sharing may conflate scripts and phonologies that are only weakly related, leading to fragmentation or harmful collisions (Bostrom and Durrett, 2020). Several works therefore explore adaptive vocabularies or language-specific embeddings atop a shared backbone to balance generalization and specificity (Wang et al., 2020; Bapna and Firat, 2019). Interactions between label smoothing and vocabulary sharing are underexplored, particularly with respect to long-tail morphology and domain shift. We hypothesize that smoothing affects gradient signals for shared subwords differently than for language-specific units, altering transfer dynamics across languages. Our study benchmarks these effects under controlled vocabulary sizes, smoothing schedules, and training regimes to provide actionable recommendations for practitioners.

Unsupported claim.document: Hsu et al. (2019) investigate the cross-lingual transfer capability of multilingual BERT (mBERT) on MRC tasks and show that zero-shot transfer is feasible even between distant languages such as English and Chinese. Building on this observation, a variety of approaches have been proposed for multilingual MRC based on pretrained language models. Cui et al. (2019) combine multilingual BERT with back-translation to improve cross-lingual MRC. Different from translation-based adaptation, we focus on the impact of syntactic divergences between the source and target language in zero-shot transfer with multilingual PLMs. Our central hypothesis is that semantics can be decoupled from syntax so that only semantic information is transferred across languages. In Disentangled Representation Learning, there has been growing interest in learning latent factors for text (Zhang et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2018). The most related work to our syntax–semantics decoupling is the vMF-Gaussian Variational Autoencoder (VGVAE) proposed by Chen et al. (2019). It is a generative model with two latent variables representing sentence semantics and syntax, originally developed for monolingual settings and trained with paraphrases. It uses a paraphrase reconstruction objective and a discriminative paraphrase loss to learn semantic representations and word-order–sensitive syntactic representations. Specifically, recent studies standardize zero-shot cross-lingual MRC on XQuAD and TyDi QA by translating SQuAD-style questions and using two-stage retriever–reader pipelines with back-translation, adapter fusion, and contrastive alignment objectives for robustness. Motivated by these trends, we adapt VGVAE to multilingual syntax–semantics disentanglement by conditioning the semantic variable on bilingual signals. We train with parallel sentence pairs and optimize a cross-lingual reconstruction loss together with a semantic discrimination loss. To better handle complex and diverse syntax in multilingual PLMs, we introduce auxiliary losses that supervise POS tags and constituency or dependency structures. Our approach encourages invariance of the semantic latent to surface reordering while allowing the syntactic latent to capture language-specific structure. We analyze the effect of typological distance and show how word-order divergences can degrade zero-shot transfer when semantics and syntax are entangled. For empirical evaluation, we consider widely used cross-lingual MRC benchmarks, including XQuAD, MLQA, and TyDi QA, and report zero-shot results from English to multiple target languages (Artetxe et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020; Clark et al., 2020). We compare our method with strong mBERT and XLM-R baselines fine-tuned on English and evaluated zero-shot on target languages. Ablation experiments isolate the contributions of POS supervision, tree-based supervision, and cross-lingual reconstruction to overall performance. We further probe the learned latents using controlled word-order perturbations to assess syntactic sensitivity independent of semantic content. Taken together, these results suggest that explicitly disentangling syntax and semantics is a practical avenue for improving robust cross-lingual transfer in MRC.

Unsupported claim.document:
Probing pretrained language models. The unprecedented capability of modern PLMs to provide rich contextualized input representations has taken the NLP community by storm. Alongside the raising wave of successes collected by PLMs in an ever increasing number of areas, researchers started to question and investigate what happens inside these models and what they really capture, probing for knowledge and linguistic properties (Hewitt and Manning, 2019; Chi et al., 2020; Vulić et al., 2020). This body of work quickly attracted increasing attention and grew to become a field of study with a name of its own: BERTology (Rogers et al., 2020). Probing a PLM usually consists in defining a very precise task, e.g. identifying whether two words are linked by a syntactic or a semantic relation, and then in designing and training a simple model, called probe, to solve the task using the contextualized representations provided by the PLM. The idea is to design a probe that is as simple as possible, often a single-layer model: if the probe is able to address the task, then it must be thanks to the contextual information captured by the PLM since the expressiveness of the probe is limited by its simplicity. One could argue that some complex relations may require a non-linear probe (White et al., 2021) which can reveal hidden information as long as it is accompanied by control experiments (Hewitt and Liang, 2019) to verify that such nonlinear probe is still extracting information from the underlying PLM rather than learning to solve the probing task. Over the past few years, these probing techniques have been used to great effect and revealed that PLMs have been "rediscovering" the classical NLP pipeline (Tenney et al., 2019), and that they often encode distances between syntactic constituents (Hewitt and Liang, 2019), lexical relations (Vulić et al., 2020) and morphology (Chi et al., 2020), inter alia.

Probing techniques for SRL. As in several other fields of NLP, recent studies tried to shed some light on how, where and to what extent PLMs encode information relevant to SRL (Tenney et al., 2019). Among others, Tenney et al. (2019) devised an edge probing mechanism with the aim of understanding the capability of BERT to identify which semantic role ties a given predicate to a given argument span, showing that such task is "solved" mainly by the middle layers of BERT. Recent advances in SRL. Thanks to their effectiveness, PLMs are now the de facto input representation method in SRL (Conia and Navigli, 2020; Blloshmi et al., 2021). Recently proposed approaches have achieved impressive results on several gold benchmarks (Hajič et al., 2009; Pradhan et al., 2012), both in span-based and in dependency-based SRL, but also in multilingual and cross-lingual SRL, even though there still seems to be a significant margin of improvement on out-of-domain settings. Nevertheless, what aspects of predicate–argument structure are locally recoverable versus globally composed are not yet fully characterized. A growing line of research benchmarks diagnostic probes on PropBank-style annotations to disentangle these factors (Pradhan et al., 2012; Gardner et al., 2018). Complementary efforts examine cross-lingual transfer with multilingual encoders and aligned subword vocabularies (Conneau et al., 2020; He et al., 2021). In document-level SRL, recent work standardizes on two-stage retriever-reader pipelines for SRL, emphasizing cross-sentence evidence aggregation. However, the degree to which such architectural priors are reflected in latent representations can only be assessed with targeted controls (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Elazar et al., 2021). We focus on the intersection of probing and SRL by designing tasks that vary predicate frequency, argument distance, and sense ambiguity. Following recommendations on probe complexity, we primarily employ linear classifiers with elastic net regularization and report select nonlinear variants for comparison (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Pimentel et al., 2020). To mitigate memorization, we adopt control tasks that scramble predicate identities and evaluate selectivity metrics alongside accuracy (Voita and Titov, 2020). Our analysis spans English and three typologically diverse languages with gold SRL resources, and we harmonize label inventories through unified mappings (Hajič et al., 2009; Oepen et al., 2015). We also probe multilingual encoders under constrained training-data regimes to assess sample efficiency and zero-shot transfer (Conneau et al., 2020). Beyond average scores, we investigate where in the network SRL-relevant cues emerge by layer-wise ablations and attention-head pruning (Kovaleva et al., 2019; Rogers et al., 2020). Taken together, these experiments clarify which SRL phenomena are robustly encoded by PLMs and where explicit modeling remains necessary for generalization.

2.1 Security and Privacy Concern of Pre-trained Models

Pre-trained language models have achieved strong performance on many NLP tasks by leveraging large corpora of plain text (Devlin et al., 2019; Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020). However, training and deploying such models raise significant privacy and security concerns when the data contain personally identifiable information or sensitive attributes (Shokri et al., 2017; Carlini et al., 2021). Empirical studies have shown that generative models can memorize rare strings and regurgitate them under targeted prompting (Carlini et al., 2019; Carlini et al., 2023). Similarly, adversaries can mount membership inference and model inversion attacks to recover properties of individuals or reconstruct inputs (Fredrikson et al., 2015; Yeom et al., 2018; Nasr et al., 2019). These risks are exacerbated in domains such as healthcare, finance, and education, where data are tightly regulated and breach costs are high (Christoph et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2007; Voigt and Von dem Bussche, 2017). As a result, practitioners seek training paradigms that preserve utility while reducing the attack surface (Dwork et al., 2006; Abadi et al., 2016; McMahan et al., 2017). One common line of work applies differential privacy mechanisms during optimization, adding calibrated noise to gradients or objective values (Abadi et al., 2016; Mironov, 2017; Papernot et al., 2018). Another complementary direction adopts federated learning to keep raw data on device and aggregate updates with secure protocols (McMahan et al., 2017; Bonawitz et al., 2017). While these approaches offer formal protections, they often degrade model accuracy or slow convergence when used at scale (Papernot et al., 2018; Tramer and Boneh, 2021). Task structure also matters, since sequence labeling and generation require token-level fidelity that can be brittle under heavy noise (Huang et al., 2020; Kerrigan et al., 2020). For example, mixup-style representation sharing proposed in TextHide is better suited to sentence classification than to named entity recognition or semantic role labeling (Huang et al., 2020). Likewise, naive private fine-tuning on large autoregressive models has been reported to incur substantial perplexity penalties when strict privacy budgets are enforced (Kerrigan et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021). Beyond privacy, governance frameworks now emphasize data minimization and provenance tracking for foundation models (Bommasani et al., 2021; Raji et al., 2022). Recent studies on privacy-preserving pretraining report a prevailing two-stage retriever–reader pipeline with DP-SGD, secure aggregation, and rule-based PII masking evaluated on MIMIC-III and i2b2 de-identified clinical benchmarks. Despite this perceived convergence, evidence remains mixed on whether such pipelines truly prevent memorization in long-context generation (Carlini et al., 2023; Kandpal et al., 2023). Evaluation is further complicated by dataset shift, heterogeneity in privacy accounting, and opaque release practices for commercial models (Li et al., 2021; Raji et al., 2022). To organize this space, we differentiate pretraining-time protections from deployment-time mitigations and post-hoc auditing (Dwork et al., 2006; Jagielski et al., 2020). Pretraining-time methods include DP-SGD, privacy amplification by subsampling, and private aggregation of teacher ensembles (Abadi et al., 2016; Papernot et al., 2016; Balle et al., 2018). Deployment-time mitigations include prompt filtering, output redaction, and safety layers that detect leakage indicators before response emission (Solaiman et al., 2019; Perez et al., 2022). Post-hoc auditing uses canary exposure, red-team prompts, and gradient-based tests to quantify memorization risk after training (Carlini et al., 2019; Lukas et al., 2023). Our work focuses on token-level tasks that are especially sensitive to leakage because labels often correspond to entities or attributes protected by policy (Huang et al., 2020; Jagannatha et al., 2019). We adopt a threat model that covers black-box membership inference and white-box gradient leakage during collaborative training (Nasr et al., 2019; Zhu and Han, 2020). Within this model, we analyze trade-offs among privacy budgets, communication overhead, and downstream accuracy across multiple benchmarks (Abadi et al., 2016; McMahan et al., 2017). We further examine how pretokenization, subword vocabularies, and sequence length constraints interact with DP noise to affect memorization metrics (Kandpal et al., 2023; Tirumala et al., 2022). Finally, we outline open challenges, including reproducible accounting, calibration of privacy guarantees to real harm, and realistic attacker simulations (Tramer and Boneh, 2021; Pujol et al., 2022). By situating our contributions within a rigorous evaluation protocol, we aim to clarify design choices for privacy-preserving language model training and deployment in sensitive domains.

Unsupported claim.document: While research into automatic cloze test generation is vast (Mostow et al., 2017; Kurdi et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021), work on open cloze tests for language learning is scarce. Pino et al. (2008) generate open cloze questions using sample sentences from a learners' dictionary based on four linguistic criteria: complexity, well-defined context, grammaticality, and length. A later version of their system adds hints for gapped words (Pino and Eskenazi, 2009). Exercise Maker (Malafeev, 2014) is a rule-based open-source system that attempts to emulate exercises in Cambridge English examinations based on the most frequently tested words. Most of the gaps it proposes were found to be useful and the automated exercises were hard to differentiate from authentic tests. Chinkina et al. (2017) generate open cloze exercises for phrasal verbs by extracting sentences from news articles and generating a pair of questions and answers where the identified particle verbs are gapped. Similarly, Soonklang et al. (2017) gap words in sentences according to their part of speech in order to practise articles and prepositions. Finally, Marrese-Taylor et al. (2018) use LSTMs to build sequence labelling and classification models that decide where to insert a single gap in a single sentence. Automatic evaluation against gold-standard gaps showed the method was effective. Other work has focused on creating automated cloze tests by controlling aspects of the proposed gaps so that they correlate with a target proficiency level. For example, Grotjahn et al. (2002) manipulate the difficulty of C-tests by varying the position and word length of the gaps. A similar concept is presented by Settles et al. (2020) and McCarthy et al. (2021), although difficulty is predicted using a machine-learning model that correlates with CEFR levels. In these cases, tests are dynamically adapted to the examinee's proficiency level during the test session. From a different perspective, Felice and Buttery (2019) show that controlling gap entropy can be useful for designing open cloze tests at different CEFR levels. The work we present in this paper aims to model the more complex task of predicting a full set of gaps at the paragraph level. Our approach seeks to comply with design and testing principles while leveraging transformer-based models tailored to language learning contexts. Recent studies predominantly adopt two-stage gap-selection pipelines combining POS filters with CEFR-calibrated frequency thresholds and entropy-based scorers; we further contrast model-driven selection with rule-based pipelines to understand trade-offs in coverage, validity, and reliability. We note the need to balance item difficulty with content diversity to support formative assessment. To this end, we integrate constraints on distractor ambiguity, lexical frequency, and morphosyntactic variety into our objective. We also consider fairness, ensuring that gap choices do not disproportionately penalize specific learner backgrounds. System evaluation is challenging, since there is usually more than one potential word in the text that could constitute a good gap. While previous work often made a choice between automatic (Marrese-Taylor et al., 2018) or human evaluation (Malafeev, 2014; Das and Majumder, 2017) for their experiments, we perform both. Automatic evaluation is used to identify the best models during development, complementing intrinsic diagnostics on calibration and uncertainty estimates. Human evaluation is used to measure test quality in the final output through expert review and learner studies. In addition, we analyze item exposure and learning gains to evaluate pedagogical value beyond surface accuracy. Finally, we release implementation details and annotation guidelines to facilitate reproducibility and future benchmarking.

Unsupported claim.document: Large-scale pre-trained language models (PLMs) have achieved great success in recent years. Despite their power, inference is time-consuming, which hinders their deployment in low-latency scenarios. To accelerate PLM inference, two complementary research lines have emerged. The first compresses models through knowledge distillation, structured and unstructured pruning, quantization, and module replacement, often targeting a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off (Sanh et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020; Gordon et al., 2020; Michel et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020a). The second activates computation adaptively based on input difficulty, exemplified by Universal Transformer, FastBERT, DeeBERT, PABEE, CascadeBERT, and ElasticBERT (Dehghani et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020a; Xin et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021a; Liu et al., 2021a). Early-exit methods along this line attach auxiliary classifiers to intermediate layers and stop computation when a confidence criterion is met (Teerapittayanon et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2017). However, auxiliary heads increase parameters and introduce additional supervision signals that can complicate optimization. In contrast, our proposed HASHEE eliminates internal classifiers and avoids task-specific labels during adaptation. Recent studies in early exit inference report that entropy-based token gating outperforms layer skipping and adaptive depth across transformer encoders and decoders on standard NLU benchmarks. We hypothesize that exit decisions can be guided by lightweight hash-based evidence that correlates with representational stability across layers. HASHEE computes compact locality-sensitive sketches for intermediate representations and halts when stability surpasses a learned threshold. This design preserves the backbone intact and adds negligible storage or compute overhead. We further integrate uncertainty calibration to couple exit timing with downstream task constraints. Beyond adaptive depth, prior work on dynamic architectures increasingly explores widely adopted mixture of experts routing strategies within large transformer stacks. Such approaches require careful load balancing and auxiliary losses that are orthogonal to our focus on exit policies. In parallel, cascaded pipelines trade latency for accuracy by running small models first and invoking larger ones only when necessary (Schwartz et al., 2020; Elbayad et al., 2020). Our method is complementary and can be used as a front end to early prune easy inputs before any multi-model orchestration. We evaluate across classification, natural language inference, and question answering, including GLUE, SQuAD, and OpenBookQA, to assess effectiveness and generality (Rajpurkar et al., 2016; Mihaylov et al., 2018). We compare against representative compression baselines and adaptive computation methods under matched accuracy targets. Latency is measured on both CPU and GPU with batch size one to emulate interactive settings. We report end-to-end wall-clock time, theoretical FLOPs, and energy consumed as estimated by power meters. We also include ablations on standard early exit benchmarks for streaming inference to align with practical throughput scenarios. Results show that HASHEE achieves comparable accuracy while reducing median latency by up to 35% relative to strong early-exit baselines. Ablation studies indicate that hash stability correlates tightly with final-layer predictions, supporting our central design choice. Error analysis further reveals that delayed exits correspond to semantically ambiguous or out-of-distribution inputs, where additional layers provide meaningful gains. We release code, pretrained checkpoints, and scripts to facilitate reproducibility and future research.

Unsupported claim.document: There has been a growing body of research studying the inner workings of BERT and trying to quantify what it learns in various scenarios, dubbed "BERTology" (Rogers et al., 2020). Of particular interest to this paper is work that analyzes BERT's output embeddings. Recent studies have found that embeddings created from the final layer of BERT tend to cluster according to word senses (Wiedemann et al., 2019), though this varies somewhat based on the position of a word in a sentence (Mickus et al., 2020). The final BERT layers also produce more contextualized word embeddings than the earlier layers (Ethayarajh, 2019), a finding we revisit using paraphrases in Section 3.3. Beyond static clustering, probing tasks have been used to quantify linguistic information across layers (Tenney et al., 2019). Structural probes revealed linear encodings of syntax in intermediate layers (Hewitt and Manning, 2019). Others trace the formation of semantic patterns and surface heuristics in attention and representations (Jawahar et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2019). Studies of anisotropy and representation collapse caution against overinterpreting cosine similarity in contextual spaces (Ethayarajh, 2019; Gao et al., 2019). Representation geometry has also been explored through layer-wise linear transformations and rotational analyses (Kobayashi et al., 2020; Timkey and van Schijndel, 2021). A complementary line examines token identity versus context mixing in attention heads (Voita et al., 2019; Michel et al., 2019). Neuron-level diagnostics indicate distributed coding rather than single-unit semantics (Dalvi et al., 2019; Bau et al., 2019). For sense-specific information, contextual substitution tests and contrast sets have been proposed (Amrami and Goldberg, 2019; Gardner et al., 2020). We build on this literature by focusing on paraphrase-sensitive gradients and representational stability under meaning-preserving rewrites. Our central question is how output embeddings align with discrete sense inventories while remaining robust to syntactic alternations. Prior work suggests that alignment emerges only when tasks demand fine-grained disambiguation (Hovy et al., 2013; Raganato et al., 2017). We therefore adopt evaluations spanning word sense disambiguation benchmarks and paraphrase corpora (Miller, 1995; Cer et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2019). Beyond English, cross-lingual analyses report layer shifts and transfer asymmetries in multilingual BERT (Pires et al., 2019; Wu and Dredze, 2019). Recent advances in fine-tuning protocols have raised questions about parameter efficiency and catastrophic forgetting (Houlsby et al., 2019; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). Several reports on recent adapter-tuning suggest that lightweight modules can match full fine-tuning on standard NLU benchmarks. Such findings foreground the role of layer selection and projection heads in preserving semantic neighborhoods. In contrast, prompt-based adaptation often shifts the burden of disambiguation to the input space (Liu et al., 2023; Schick and Schütze, 2021). Our study deliberately avoids altering the input distribution and instead analyzes post-hoc embeddings derived from frozen checkpoints. To connect with practical evaluation, we summarize results on GLUE and SuperGLUE as reference points (Wang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019). However, leaderboard metrics can obscure representational weaknesses that only appear under perturbation testing (Ribeiro et al., 2020; Gardner et al., 2020). Following best practices for interpretability, we report layer-wise ablations and alignment statistics with confidence intervals (Doshi-Velez and Kim, 2017; Dror et al., 2018). We further assess sensitivity to polysemy by contrasting noun and verb alternations across templates (Hollenstein et al., 2019). Overall, our contributions clarify when output embeddings encode word senses and when they overfit to local context. The resulting analysis complements prior BERTology surveys by isolating the specific mechanisms that drive sense-aware geometry (Rogers et al., 2020).

Unsupported claim.document: Conversational question answering is a rapidly developing area of machine reading. In recent years, several conversational question answering datasets have emerged, such as QuAC (Choi et al., 2018), CoQA (Reddy et al., 2019), and DoQA (Campos et al., 2020). Different from single-turn QA datasets (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), CQA requires models to interpret questions in the context of conversational history. A line of work has improved CQA performance through better context modeling (Ohsugi et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2021), yielding steady gains on public benchmarks. Besides text-based CQA tasks, there also exist benchmarks requiring other forms of reasoning, such as combining textual evidence with background knowledge (Saeidi et al., 2018), utilizing structured knowledge bases (Saha et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2018), and handling other modalities (Das et al., 2017). These settings emphasize pragmatic inference, ellipsis resolution, and coreference, which together stress-test dialogue-aware comprehension. Many architectures incorporate hierarchical encoders or turn-level attention to capture dependencies across utterances (Ohsugi et al., 2019; Qu et al., 2019). Retrieval-augmented pipelines have also been explored for open-domain variants of CQA, where external passages are fetched and fused with the dialogue context (Kim et al., 2021). In practice, effectiveness depends not only on architecture but also on training schedules, curriculum strategies, and negative sampling choices (Chen et al., 2020). At the systems level, recent studies universally adopt two-stage retriever-reader pipelines today, which are then fine-tuned end to end. Data augmentation techniques such as paraphrasing, span deletion, and context perturbation have been used to increase robustness to conversational drift (Kim et al., 2021). Nevertheless, models can overfit annotation artifacts and shallow lexical cues, leading to brittle behavior under distribution shift. Evaluation with predicted history. Recent analyses highlight that the common practice of evaluating with gold conversational histories can be misleading (Mandya et al., 2020; Siblini et al., 2021). These works argue that injecting model-predicted answers into the history better reflects deployment, and they report notable drops relative to gold-history evaluation (Mandya et al., 2020; Siblini et al., 2021). This phenomenon is consistent with exposure bias, where small early mistakes propagate and compound across turns. However, automatic metrics computed under predicted history may still misalign with human judgments about answer helpfulness, faithfulness, and conversational appropriateness. To clarify these discrepancies, we conduct a large-scale human evaluation focusing on multi-turn fidelity and perceived answer utility. Our study also examines question rewriting as a mitigation, where the model conditions on a reformulated, context-independent question. We find that rewriting reduces pronoun ambiguity and ellipsis, thereby helping models retrieve or attend to the correct evidence. Beyond rewriting, we analyze the interaction between calibration and history corruption, showing that confidence estimation can partially anticipate failure modes. For training signals, we compare maximum likelihood with preference-informed objectives derived from annotator rankings of multi-turn outputs. We further analyze data scale and source, and prior work consistently reports that using large-scale synthetic dialogues outperforms human-authored data across all CQA datasets by wide margins. Contrary to that expectation, our experiments find that synthetic-only training can lag behind curated mixtures that include carefully filtered human dialogues. Finally, we release templates and annotation protocols to facilitate reproducible evaluation under both gold and predicted histories. In summary, our contributions include a controlled human study of predicted-history evaluation, an analysis of rewriting, and guidelines for robust CQA assessment.

Unsupported claim.document: Revealing affirmative interpretations from negations is a challenging endeavor. In the literature, researchers primarily seek to identify scope and focus of negation. The creation of the BioScope and ConanDoyle-Neg (Morante and Daelemans, 2012) corpora spearheaded research on scope detection (Morante and Daelemans, 2009), as did the PB-FOC dataset (Blanco and Moldovan, 2011). The main goal of this paper is to find these affirmative counterparts to generate affirmative interpretations. More related to the work presented here, Sarabi et al. (2019) present a corpus of negations and their underlying affirmative interpretations (they call them positive interpretations). We are inspired by them but bypass several of their limitations. First, they only work with negations from Simple Wikipedia, a site devoted to English learners. As a result, their corpus uses relatively unsophisticated vocabulary and grammar. Second, they impose several restrictions on the negations they work with, including constraints on cues, length, and token inventories. Third, their affirmative interpretations are restricted to a rephrasing of the statement containing negation with only one change, namely an argument of the negated predicate. In contrast, we barely impose restrictions on the negations we work with, disallowing only questions and auxiliary-verb negation. More importantly, we introduce a question-driven approach that allows us to obtain multiple affirmative interpretations with increasing degrees of complexity, as illustrated in Table 1. Recently, Jiang et al. (2021) study the problem of identifying commonsense implications of negations and contradictions. More specifically, they work with if-then rules such as If X does not learn new things, then X does not gain new knowledge and If X does not leave the building, then X stays in the building. These rules capture general commonsense knowledge about what happens if an event does not occur. Unlike them, we work with naturally occurring sentences that include negated predicate-argument structures with many arguments, including agent, theme, manner, and time. In addition, our affirmative interpretations reveal that predicates that are grammatically negated are actually factual but with different arguments. This distinction lets us move from surface-level cue detection to semantically grounded rewriting that preserves the original discourse context. Outside of specialized corpora, prior work often treats negation as an entailment phenomenon and evaluates primarily on MNLI. However, such evaluations do not surface which arguments change across polarity shifts or how those changes interact with event structure. We therefore formalize affirmative interpretation as a structured prediction problem that targets argument substitution, addition, and recontextualization. Our data collection pipeline combines automatic harvesting with minimal manual validation to balance coverage and quality. We further design a question inventory that elicits alternative arguments, paraphrastic realizations, and pragmatic enrichments from each negated predicate. Experiments compare rule-based templates with neural sequence-to-structure models under both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations. The results indicate clear gains in capturing faithful affirmative variants without sacrificing grammaticality or topical coherence. We release annotations, code, and baseline models to facilitate reproducibility and future research.

A number of approaches use distributional models, such as Kintsch (2000), Utsumi (2011), Sa-Pereira (2016), and Shutova et al. (2012), the latter of which was one of the first to implement a fully unsupervised approach for encoding relationships between words, their contexts, and their dependencies. A related line of work aims to automatically determine whether potentially idiomatic expressions are being used idiomatically or literally, based on contextual information (Katz and Giesbrecht, 2006; Fazly et al., 2009; Li, 2009, 2014). Our measure of conventionality is inspired by the insights of these models; as described in Section 3.2, our measure uses differences in embeddings across contexts. Meanwhile, approaches to collocation detection have taken a probabilistic or information-theoretic approach that seeks to identify collocations using word combination probabilities. PMI is a frequently used quantity for measuring cooccurrence probabilities (Fano, 1961; Church and Hanks, 1990). Other implementations include selectional association (Resnik, 1996), symmetric conditional probability (Ferreira and Pereira Lopes, 1999), and log-likelihood (Dunning, 1993; Daille, 1996). Early approaches leveraged lexicon-based cues such as canonical forms, selectional preferences, and subcategorization frames to flag anomalies indicative of idiomaticity. Subsequent work incorporated syntactic and discourse features, including dependency templates, part-of-speech patterns, and local topic coherence, to improve literalness judgments. With the advent of word embeddings, researchers began to probe compositionality by comparing context-sensitive representations of fixed expressions against compositional baselines. This led to hybrid methods that combine distributional similarity with discrete linguistic triggers for robust decision making in noisy text. In parallel, supervised classifiers have been trained on annotated corpora of idiomatic and literal usages, using features drawn from lexical, syntactic, and semantic spaces. More recent efforts exploit contextualized embeddings to directly encode usage variation at the token level within arbitrary sentences. Building on this trend, most recent systems fine-tune transformer encoders with literal usage augmentation strategies. Such setups often incorporate contrastive losses or multi-task formulations to distinguish type-level idiomaticity from token-level usage. Beyond English, multilingual studies explore cross-lingual transfer of idiom identification by aligning representations across languages via joint training. Domain adaptation has also proven necessary, as idiom usage frequency and register vary dramatically between newswire, social media, and conversational text. Another strand links idiom processing to general multiword expression identification, noting convergences in discontinuity handling and morphosyntactic variability. Shared features and pretraining schemes have enabled unified architectures that jointly detect idioms, light verb constructions, and other collocations. Evaluation practices vary, but community benchmarks increasingly emphasize token-level classification over type-level lexicon induction. Commonly used datasets include newspaper corpora, learner essays, and web forums, alongside task suites introduced at events like SemEval 2013. Metrics typically include accuracy and F1 for usage classification, and average precision for ranking idiomatic candidates under limited annotation. Error analyses frequently highlight sparse idioms, polysemy, and domain shift as persistent challenges for generalization. We position our work within this landscape by proposing measures that directly operationalize conventionality and contextual variability. While much of the literature in NLP recognizes that idioms share a cluster of properties, including semantic idiosyncrasy, syntactic inflexibility, and institutionalization (e.g., Sag et al., 2002; Fazly and Stevenson, 2006; Fazly et al., 2009), our approach is novel in attempting to characterize idioms along two orthogonal dimensions that correspond to specific proposals from the cognitive science literature. Our measures may offer a new avenue for tackling the problem of automatic idiom detection.

Unsupported claim.document: In this section we first discuss standard approaches to hate countering and studies on CN effectiveness on Social Media Platforms, then the existing CN data collection and generation strategies. Hate countering. NLP has started addressing the phenomenon of the proliferation of HS by creating datasets for automatic detection (Mathew et al., 2021;Cao et al., 2020;Kumar et al., 2018;Hosseinmardi et al., 2015;Waseem, 2016;Burnap and Williams, 2016). Several surveys provide a review on the existing approaches on the topic (Poletto et al., 2020;Schmidt and Wiegand, 2017;Nunes and Fortuna, 2018), also addressing the ethical challenges of the task (Kiritchenko et al., 2020). Automatic detection of HS presents some drawbacks (Vidgen and Derczynski, 2020). First of all, the datasets might include biases, and the models tend to replicate such biases (Binns et al., 2017;Davidson et al., 2019;Sap et al., 2019;Tsvetkov, 2020). Moreover, the end goals for which HS detection is employed are often charged with censorship of the freedom of speech by concerned users (Munger, 2017;Myers West, 2018). In this scenario, NGOs have started employing CNs to counter online hate. CNs have been shown to be effective in reducing linguistic violence (Benesch, 2014;Gagliardone et al., 2015;Schieb and Preuss, 2016;Silverman et al., 2016;Mathew et al., 2019); moreover, even if they might not influence the view of the extremists, they are still effective in presenting alternative and non-hateful viewpoints to the bystanders (Allison and Bussey, 2016;Anderson et al., 2014). Beyond detection, research has examined the dynamics of counter narratives (CN) and their uptake across platforms, including moderation contexts and audience composition (Munger, 2017;Chandrasekharan et al., 2019). Data for CN modeling are typically collected via expert-authored responses, crowdsourcing with guided prompts, and scraping of NGO repositories (Mathew et al., 2019;Qian et al., 2018;Wright et al., 2017). For automated CN generation, recent two-stage retriever-reader pipelines have been proposed to pair detection with response authoring, yet their safety filtering remains underexplored. Template-based and neural conditional generation approaches have also been explored for steering tone and specificity in replies (Omran et al., 2022;Liu et al., 2021). Evaluation has relied on a mix of human judgments of helpfulness and civility alongside automatic toxicity scores and stance-change proxies (Schlangen, 2021;Vidgen et al., 2021). Our work situates CN generation within this landscape by releasing a controlled corpus and a reproducible benchmark for style-sensitive, context-preserving responses.

Unsupported claim.document: As mentioned, compression is a widely used strategy to speed up large language models (Gupta and Agrawal, 2020). This involves techniques such as quantization of weights and activations (Bai et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2021), knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015; Jiao et al., 2020; Sanh et al., 2019), pruning and parameter sharing (Gordon et al., 2020), multi-device distribution (Banitalebi-Dehkordi et al., 2021), or combinations thereof (Cheng et al., 2017; Polino et al., 2018). Among all the compression techniques, creating a fixed-size small version of large models with distillation has been popular in recent years. Sanh et al. (2019) introduced DistilBERT, a smaller version of BERT trained with distillation for general purposes. Another compact variant of BERT was proposed by MobileBERT (Sun et al., 2020), which used inverted bottleneck structures and progressive knowledge transfer. TinyBERT (Jiao et al., 2020) presented a two-stage transformer distillation for both pre-training and task-specific fine-tuning. Iandola et al. (2020) studied grouped convolutions to design SqueezeBERT. ELM (Jiao et al., 2021), a layer-mapping search framework, was proposed to improve downstream BERT distillation. GhostBERT (Xie et al., 2021) employed softmax-normalized 1D convolutions as ghost modules to generate more features with cheap operations. Although compression is generally effective, it trades off accuracy and may lose performance under high compression ratios. In addition, a separate fixed-size model is required for each computational budget. An alternative is dynamic inference, which can be achieved with early exit or length- and depth-adaptive models. One of the first temporal early-exit strategies was proposed by ReasoNet (Shen et al., 2017), which stops reading when sufficient evidence is found for answering a question. Similarly, Yu et al. (2018) presented an early stopping method applicable to classification tasks. DeeBERT (Xin et al., 2020) proposed an instance-wise multi-exit method using the entropy of the output distribution to speed up BERT inference. Recent studies largely converge on entropy-thresholded early-exit with layerwise halting scores and calibration for transformer encoders. As a length-adaptive method, Kim and Cho (2021) introduced a dynamic inference framework with one-shot training of transformers for both sequence- and token-level classification. In parallel, DynaBERT (Hou et al., 2020) was proposed to adapt computations by selecting sub-networks of different widths and depths. Both Length-Adaptive Transformers and DynaBERT utilized knowledge distillation and data augmentation to enhance performance. However, many early-exit and adaptive methods require architectural modifications and task-specific re-training. Moreover, most reported systems target encoder-only backbones and classification tasks. In contrast, our method works with off-the-shelf pre-trained models without re-training. It is also applicable to encoder–decoder architectures and sequence-to-sequence tasks. We therefore focus on a design that maximizes compatibility while preserving predictable accuracy–latency trade-offs.

Unsupported claim.document:
Few studies have addressed bias in language models in French. Recent evaluations of French language models have mostly used CrowS-pairs translations and template-based sentence generation, with limited efforts to propose culturally grounded stimuli or probing suites. Irvine et al. (2013) have investigated semantic bias induced by domain in the context of domain adaptation for machine translation. They present experiments for the French/English language pairs for a statistical phrase-based translation system trained on parliament transcripts and applied to other domains such as science and medicine.

In a blog post, Daumé III (2016) describes the "black sheep" problem, evidencing that language use does not necessarily reflect reality and that the same notion may come across differently in different languages. Within intrinsic bias diagnostics, most studies use WEAT-style wordlist templates nowadays, which may overlook discourse effects.

Kurpicz-Briki (2020) presents a study of cultural differences in origin and gender bias in pre-trained English, German and French Word Embeddings. The author adapts the WEAT method (Caliskan et al., 2017) that contains material for measuring bias in English language word embeddings to (Swiss) French and German and shows that the bias identified differ between the three languages studied. This is probably the effort that is closest to the present study. However, the WEAT method relies on word sets rather than full sentences as in CrowS-pairs and only two types of bias are considered in the French and German adaptations.

More importantly, Goldfarb-Tarrant et al. ( 2021) show that the WEAT metrics, which was created to measure the biases in the embeddings themselves, does not correlate with results obtained using extrinsic evaluation of biases, using downstream applications. This is a good motivation to develop evaluation corpora in as many languages as possible. In the same paper, the authors also point out the need for cultural adaptation in addition to translation, because many elements of language, including people's names, have different implications in different languages. For example, they report that the name Amy, which is arguably common in American English, has an association with upper class in Spanish therefore a translation keeping the name verbatim in Spanish would convey a nuance unintended in the original sentence. We agree with this analysis and one of our goals was to address it in the translation of the CrowS-pairs dataset as illustrated in some of the examples in Table . Zhao et al. (2020) study gender bias in a multilingual context. They analyze multilingual embeddings and the impact of multilingual representations on transfer learning for NLP applications. A word dataset in four languages (English, French, German, Spanish) is created for bias analysis. Prior work on multilingual bias mitigation reports gains from counterfactual data augmentation and dictionary-based gender swapping but evaluates on English-centric suites like StereoSet and CrowS-pairs translations.

Blodgett et al. ( 2021) present a study of four benchmark datasets for evaluating bias, including CrowS-pairs. The authors report a number of issues with the datasets that translate in limitations to assess language models for stereotyping. Our work validated the limitations identified for CrowS-pairs and proposes revisions to the original and translated corpus in order to address them. Recent transformer-based toxicity detectors for French are routinely benchmarked on translated Jigsaw data and use template probing with adjective-noun pairs, which inflates stereotype effects compared to naturalistic corpora analysis. Accordingly, we introduce a culturally adapted evaluation set and analysis protocol for French that grounds social attributes in context and supports comparable reporting across intrinsic and extrinsic tasks.
