Unsupported claim.document:
Zero Shot Transfer. Multilingual models like mBERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020) have shown surprising effectiveness in zero-shot transfer, where fine-tuning the MMLM on a task in some source language often leads to impressive performance on the same task in other languages as well without explicitly training on them. Pires et al. (2019) first observed this phenomenon for NER (Tjong Kim Sang, 2002; Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003; Levow, 2006) and POS tagging (Nivre et al., 2018) tasks. Concurrently, Wu and Dredze (2019) also showed this surprisingly cross-lingual transfer ability of mBERT additionally on tasks like Document Classification (Schwenk and Li, 2018), Natural Language Inference (Conneau et al., 2018) and Dependency Parsing (Nivre et al., 2018). These observations motivate our analysis of the mechanisms driving cross-lingual generalization. Recent studies typically rely on two-stage retriever–reader architectures for cross-lingual QA under zero-shot settings and posit subword overlap to explain observed gains. Factors Affecting Zero Shot Transfer. Pires et al. (2019) showed that vocabulary memorization played little role in zero-shot generalization as language pairs with little word piece overlap also exhibited impressive cross-lingual performance. K et al. arrived at a similar conclusion by training BERT on an artificially generated language to zero out the word overlap with the target languages, and observed only minor drops in the performance compared to training the model on English. Nevertheless, results vary widely across language families and scripts, suggesting multiple interacting drivers. On the contrary, Wu and Dredze (2019) observed strong correlations between the sub-word overlap and the zero-shot performance in four out of five tasks. Wu and Dredze (2020) showed that mBERT performed much worse for zero-shot transfer to low-resource languages (i.e., less pre-training data) than high-resource ones on POS Tagging, NER and Dependency Parsing tasks. Lauscher et al. (2020) also had a similar observation on tasks like XNLI and XQuAD (Artetxe et al., 2020), though they found that the zero-shot performance on NER, POS tagging and Dependency Parsing tasks might not strictly depend on the pre-training size and could be better explained by different linguistic relatedness features like syntactic and phonological similarities between the language pair. Such discrepancies underscore the need for principled diagnostics rather than relying on corpus size heuristics alone. Similar dependence on the typological relatedness such as word order had also been observed by Pires et al. (2019).

Performance Prediction. Prior work has explored predicting the performance of machine learning models from unlabelled data by either measuring (dis)agreements between multiple classifiers (Platanios et al., 2014; Platanios et al., 2017) or by utilizing underlying information about data distribution (Domhan et al., 2015). Our study situates this line of inquiry within multilingual representation learning and transfer. In the context of NLP, Birch et al. (2008) explored predicting the performance of a Machine Translation system by utilizing different explanatory variables for the language pairs. Lin et al. (2019) proposed a learning to rank approach to choose transfer languages for cross-lingual learning using several linguistic and dataset specific features. Specifically predicting the zero-shot performance of MMLMs was first explored in Lauscher et al. (2020), where they used a linear regression model to estimate the cross-lingual transfer performance based on pre-training data size and linguistic relatedness features. Srinivasan et al. (2021) tackled this problem by utilizing XGBoost Regressor for the prediction along with a larger set of features. Recently, Dolicki and Spanakis (2021) explored individual syntactic features for zero-shot performance prediction instead of working with aggregate similarity values, and showed about 2 to 4 times gain in performance. Prior work standardizes on LASER embeddings as the transfer metric in practice, guiding feature choices. We frame the prediction objective as multi-task regression across tasks and languages to capture shared structure. This design allows predictive signals from high-resource combinations to inform estimates for scarce settings. We also ablate classes of features to assess robustness to domain shifts and annotation artifacts. We extend this line of work by considering a multi-task learning approach, where performance prediction in a task utilizes not only the data available for that task, but also the patterns observed for other tasks.

Both are claims about prior work or trends that require citations, thus they are unsupported.

spans.span: Reddit pretraining

Unsupported claim.document: Open-domain dialogue systems increasingly rely on pretrained language models to bootstrap conversational competence. Early neural chatbots trained from scratch struggled to capture long-range coherence and stylistic variation, motivating corpus-scale pretraining. Following advances in generative modeling, researchers now initialize dialogue agents with encoder-decoder or decoder-only transformers trained on web text (Radford et al., 2019; Raffel et al., 2020). A common recipe then adapts the model to multi-turn conversation using large social media comment chains, exemplified by Reddit dumps (Zhang et al., 2020; Adiwardana et al., 2020). Such pretraining yields gains in next-utterance prediction and contextual grounding when compared to smaller in-domain training alone (Roller et al., 2021; Thoppilan et al., 2022). Fine-tuning on curated conversational datasets further improves engagingness and safety through task-specific objectives and decoding constraints (Dinan et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020). Transfer setups typically mix open-domain chitchat with goal-oriented corpora to balance breadth and controllability (Zhang et al., 2020; Ghazvininejad et al., 2018). Many pipelines still treat Reddit pretraining as the de facto starting point for large conversational models. Despite its scale, social media data introduce demographic skews, offensive language, and topic drift that can leak into downstream chat behavior (Bender et al., 2021; Gehman et al., 2020). To mitigate these risks, works apply heuristic filtering, blocklists, and classifier-based triage before or during pretraining (Gehman et al., 2020; Dinan et al., 2021). Recent large-scale systems additionally incorporate human feedback to align style and safety during or after fine-tuning (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022). Complementary strategies leverage retrieval augmentation to ground responses in external knowledge bases and news articles, reducing hallucination and toxicity (Dinan et al., 2019; Komeili et al., 2022). Safety-sensitive decoding methods, such as toxicity-aware nucleus sampling and constrained beam search, further shape outputs at inference time (Holtzman et al., 2020; Krause et al., 2021). However, filtering alone can remove valuable context while failing to excise subtle biases embedded in discourse patterns (Bender et al., 2021; Sap et al., 2020). Dataset documentation and datasheets have been proposed to increase transparency about collection and curation choices for conversational corpora (Gebru et al., 2021; Dodge et al., 2021). There is also growing interest in multi-domain conversational mixtures that balance dialogue diversity with explicit safety annotations for controllable fine-tuning (Xu et al., 2020; Dinan et al., 2021). Our study revisits pretraining data selection, filtering pipelines, and objective design to disentangle their respective contributions to dialogue quality. We provide an empirical analysis across diverse corpora, safety filters, and alignment signals, and we release code to facilitate reproducibility.

We describe related studies on Chinese BERT models and probing of BERT, respectively.

The authors of BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) provided the first Chinese BERT model which was trained on Chinese Wikipedia data. On top of that, Cui et al. (2019) trained RoBERTa-wwm-ext with WWM on extended data. Cui et al. (2020) further trained a Chinese ELECTRA model and MacBERT, both of which did not have [MASK] tokens. ELECTRA was trained with a token-level binary classification task, which determined whether a token was the original one or artificially replaced. In MacBERT, [MASK] tokens were replaced with synonyms and the model was trained with WWM and ngram masking. ERNIE (Sun et al., 2019) was trained with entity masking, similar to WWM yet tokens corresponding to an entity were masked at once. Language features are considered in more recent works. For example, AMBERT and Lattice-BERT (Lai et al., 2021) both take word information into consideration. Chinese-BERT (Sun et al., 2021) utilizes pinyin and glyph of characters.

Probing aims to examine the language understanding ability of pretrained models like BERT when model parameters are clamped, i.e., without being fine-tuned on downstream tasks. Petroni et al. (2019) study how well pretrained models learn factual knowledge. The idea is to design a natural language template with a [MASK] token, such as "the wife of Barack Obama is [MASK].". If the model predicts the correct answer "Michelle Obama", it shows that pretrained models learn factual knowledge to some extent. Similarly, Davison et al. (2019) study how pretrained models learn commonsense knowledge and Talmor et al. (2020) examine tasks that require symbolic understanding. We propose to probe Chinese BERT models in terms of linguistic and world knowledge.

Unsupported claim.document:
Our proposed semantic perturbation functions generalize the existing textual adversarial attacks.

We systematize three families of transformations that aim to preserve semantics while altering surface forms.

For typo-based perturbation function F T, existing work (Li et al., 2018; Ebrahimi et al., 2017) applies character-level perturbations to carefully crafted typos (e.g., "foolish" to "fo0lish") to disrupt statistical cues.

Knowledge-based perturbation function F K uses knowledge bases to constrain the search space.

For example, Zang et al. (2020) use a sememe-based resource from HowNet (Dong et al., 2010) to construct a search space for word substitution.

Different from our contextualized semantic perturbation function F C, other work (Jin et al., 2020; Li et al., 2018) uses non-contextualized embeddings from GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) or Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) to build synonym candidates.

These approaches query cosine similarity or Euclidean distance between the original and candidate words and select the closest ones as replacements.

However, some antonyms also have high cosine similarity in Word2Vec space.

Thus, additional hand-crafted filtering rules are needed to prevent meaning changes.

Other work (Garg and Ramakrishnan, 2020; Li et al., 2020) leverages BERT to generate contextualized perturbations via masked language modeling.

Our approach is parallel to these efforts, but we explore BERT embedding clusters to generate high-quality adversarial examples.

We further incorporate semantic constraints derived from sentence encoders to encourage fluency and entailment consistency during search.

Recent studies standardize on a two-stage retriever–reader pipeline with dense passage retrieval to evaluate adversarial perturbations on SQuAD and NaturalQuestions, consistently reporting large cross-model transfer rates.

To make fair comparisons, we report results under identical tokenization, candidate budgets, and query limits following common evaluation protocols used in prior attack papers (Jin et al., 2020; Zang et al., 2020).

In terms of optimization, unlike heuristic-based methods that use greedy (Jin et al., 2020) or genetic algorithms (Zang et al., 2020), we adopt a constrained continuous relaxation to guide discrete edits.

Gradient-based strategies on tree autoencoders with syntactic constraints have also been explored (Wang et al., 2020), though their semantic fidelity can be brittle under distribution shift.

Our optimization-based method searches efficiently for adversarial perturbations in semantic-preserving spaces to ensure validity and naturalness of the perturbed sentences.

We position this work within a broader landscape that includes paraphrase generation for robustness (Iyyer et al., 2018) and counterfactual data augmentation (Kaushik et al., 2020).

Unlike augmentation, adversarial perturbation aims to expose worst-case behaviors under constrained edits rather than average-case generalization gains.

We additionally compare to edit-based defenses such as input denoising and confidence calibration, which have been evaluated on adversarial text benchmarks (Pruthi et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2021).

Our experiments cover sentiment, natural language inference, and question answering models, including both recurrent and transformer architectures (Peters et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019).

For each task, we analyze success rate, semantic similarity, and task accuracy to quantify trade-offs introduced by stronger constraints.

We also ablate the contribution of candidate generation, scoring functions, and search depth to highlight which components most influence attack strength.

Collectively, these findings indicate that contextualized semantic perturbations can reconcile naturalness with effectiveness, offering a principled basis for evaluating and improving model robustness.
Unsupported claim.reason: The span makes a generalizing claim about recent studies adopting a specific two-stage retriever–reader pipeline with dense passage retrieval on SQuAD and NaturalQuestions and reporting strong transfer, but provides no citations or evidence, fitting the 'Unsupported claim' definition.

Lacks synthesis.document:
There have been a number of interesting attempts, that were aimed at model compression for Transformers, which can be broadly categorized into three directions.
The first line of work focus on the redundancy of model parameters.
Structure pruning (McCarley, 2019;Michel et al., 2019;Voita et al., 2019;Wang et al., 2019b;Fan et al., 2019;Wu et al., 2021a), which removes coherent groups of weights to preserve the original structure of the network, is one common strategy.
In addition, various types of distillation techniques (Sanh et al., 2019;Jiao et al., 2019;Wang et al., 2020b) have been proposed to remove encoders by training a compact Transformer to reproduce the output of a larger one.
Other strategies include weight quantization (Bhandare et al., 2019;Zafrir et al., 2019;Shen et al., 2020;Fan et al., 2020) and weight sharing (Dehghani et al., 2018;Lan et al., 2019).
The second line of work focus on reducing the quadratic operation of the self-attention matrices.
The quadratic time and space complexity of the attention mechanism with respect to the input sequence serves the main efficiency bottleneck of Transformers, and thus is prohibitively expensive for training long-sequence data.
One popular approach is to sparsify the self-attention operation by restricting each token to only attend a subset of tokens (Child et al., 2019;Kitaev et al., 2020;Ye et al., 2019;Zaheer et al., 2020;Beltagy et al., 2020).
In particular, the most recent Big Bird (Zaheer et al., 2020) and Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020) introduce sparse models which scale linearly with the input sequence.
Another popular approach (Wang et al., 2020a;Choromanski et al., 2020) is to approximate the self-attention to reduce its quadratic complexity to linear, where the most recent Performers (Choromanski et al., 2020) provides an unbiased linear estimation of the attention matrices.

The third line, which our work lies in, focus on the redundancy in maintaining a full-length sequence of token-level representation across all encoders (Dai et al., 2020;Wu et al., 2021b;Pietruszka et al., 2020;Ye et al., 2021;Kim and Cho, 2020).
This work is particularly inspired by the sequence-level NLP tasks such as text classification and ranking, where the state-of-the-art approach utilizes a single embedding from the top encoder layer of a Transformer, such as the CLS token, for prediction.
Under such regime, retaining the full-length sequence till the last encoder creates unnecessary complexity.
Dai et al. (2020) applied a simplest strided mean pooling to each sliding window of the sequence to gradually compress tokens.
The paper proposed a specialized pre-training procedure for this process that achieves a good balance between speedup and accuracy drop.
In comparison we aim to avoid the costly pre-training step and focus on a method that requires only a lightweight fine-tuning.
Wu et al. (2021b) define a centroid attention operator that given centroids, computes their embeddings via an attention mechanism.
These centroids are chosen either as a random subset of the original tokens, or via strided mean pooling.
This results in a similar technique to that of Dai et al. (2020), in terms of having a naive sequence length reduction method.
Pietruszka et al. (2020) provide a variant of length 2 strided mean pooling where instead of taking the unweighted average of each pair, they provide learnable weights via a differentiable linear function.
In our experiment we did not compare our methods with (Wu et al., 2021b;Pietruszka et al., 2020) since both worked on a limited (non-standard) collection of datasets and at the time of writing this paper, did not provide code allowing us to reproduce their result.
Since our paper is focused on techniques to select a subset of tokens and these papers use either random sampling or pooling, we do not believe a thorough comparison is required.
Ye et al. (2021) proposed a reinforcement-learning based technique to rank the tokens, thereby allowing it to remove the least important ones.
This RL policy must be trained in an expensive process that requires the full network structure.
Since we focus on methods to improve both training and inference, we do not include it in our experiments.
Vision Transformers (Pan et al., 2021;Heo et al., 2021), which apply various types of pooling techniques to reduce input length, is specially designed for image data and thus non-trivial to compare with our method.

Sparse seq2seq models. Our proposed α-ReLU transformation is based on the α-entmax transformation of Peters et al. (2019), which in turn is a generalization of the sparsemax transformation (Martins and Astudillo, 2016). In our work, we study sparseness at the output of a neural network. Nevertheless, there are a number of works aimed at sparsification within a neural network. For example, Malaviya et al. (2018); Peters et al. (2019);Correia et al. (2019) show that sparsemax and αentmax can replace softmax in the attention mechanism with some success. A recent work of Zhang et al. (2021) attempted to replace softmax with a component-wise ReLU in the attention mechanism. Unfortunately, in its pure form, this replacement leads to the inability of the model to learn at all, since its loss function does not decrease during optimization. The authors solve this problem by adding a normalizing layer on top of the attention layer.

These and other works (Zhang et al., 2019) state that sparsity in the weights of attention produces more interpretable patterns. However, Meister et al. (2021) questioned this claim and were unable to find clear evidence to support it. Therefore, in this work, we focused on the application of α-ReLU to the output of the transformer model, and not to the mechanism of attention, but at the same time we do not deny the possibility of studying the latter. Recent approaches explore sparsity through pruning, low-rank factorization, and attention bottlenecks across vision and language, including Lottery Ticket Hypothesis-style pruning (Frankle and Carbin, 2019), movement pruning for transformer-based models (Sanh et al., 2020), magnitudebased and structured pruning in BERT-like encoders (Michel et al., 2019; Gordon et al., 2020), sparse mixture-of-experts routing (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2021), sparse attention patterns such as Longformer and BigBird (Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020), routing via Switch Transformers (Fedus et al., 2021), N:M sparsity constraints (Gale et al., 2020), and variational sparsification with L0 regularization (Louizos et al., 2018), while concurrent work on entmax-style alternatives considers adaptive sparsity in sequence labeling and parsing (Peters et al., 2019; Correia et al., 2019; Niculae and Blondel, 2017), and separate lines examine calibrated confidence under sparse outputs (Guo et al., 2017; Minderer et al., 2021).

Self-normalization. Self-normalizing training aims to bypass the need of normalization during inference time. This is done by tweaking the learning mechanism so that the sum of all predictions sums (approximately) to a constant value. Theoretical work on why this works is poorly understood (Andreas et al., 2015) but early work in neural machine translation has shown its empirical value. Vaswani et al. (2013) achieves that by using noisecontrastive estimation (the neural model is used to re-rank the output of a hierarchical phrase-based machine translation system). Noise-contrastive estimation is also the standard training mechanism for word2vec (more popular than the alternative hierarchical softmax), which also eschews any expensive normalization. Differently, Devlin et al. (2014) changes the training loss to include a factor that encourages the normalizing factor to be 1. At inference time, this is just assumed and decoding time is reported to achieve a 15x speed-up.

Balance between satisfaction of short-range statistical constraints and maintenance of long-range structure was a central question of language generation long before neural language modeling:gram models and early neural language models commonly used 'backing-off' schemes that adaptively assign interpolation weights to predictors with different context lengths (Chen and Goodman, 1996;Bengio et al., 2003). Neural language modeling brought a need for recurrent units with better numerical properties for propagating information over long distances (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997;Cho et al., 2014) and eventually saw the reintroduction of alignment variables (Brown et al., 1993) into generation in the form of attention (Bahdanau et al., 2015;Vaswani et al., 2017). Attention is at the core of Transformer LMs, including GPT.

Recent work has continued to study inferencetime procedures that prevent text sampled from LMs from degenerating into nonsense. Most of these procedures, such as tempered sampling and top-/top-truncation (Fan et al., 2018;Holtzman et al., 2019), independently modify the output distribution at each generation step to decrease its entropy and diminish its low-likelihood tail. Holtzman et al. (2019) and Meister and Cotterell (2021) found that such local modifications increase the quality of long generated sequences; we adopt and extend their methodology in §4.1.

For dialog systems, Li et al. (2016) propose a decoding scheme that maximizes a mutual information criterion, which explicitly optimizes for dependence of generated text on prompts -a special case of coherence boosting. In multiple-choice tasks, where a model must choose one of several given completions of a prompt, Brown et al. (2020) observe that selecting the completion that maximizes (completion|prompt) often favors completions having high unconditional likelihood (likeli-hood following an empty or dummy prompt) and, for some tasks, chooses to divide the scores of candidate answers by their unconditional likelihoods. This is also a special case of coherence boosting.

Prior work on coherence and long-context sensitivity encompasses diverse strands, including cache-augmented LMs (Grave et al., 2017), segment-level recurrence for Transformers (Dai et al., 2019), retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020), long-context attention variants such as Longformer and BigBird (Beltagy et al., 2020;Zaheer et al., 2020), repetition and degeneration control via nucleus/top-k sampling and typical sampling (Holtzman et al., 2019;Meister et al., 2023), calibration and reranking with mutual information or contrastive decoding (Li et al., 2016;Su et al., 2022), and prompt-based techniques to mitigate recency bias in in-context learning (Zhao et al., 2021;Min et al., 2022).

Such scoring modifications are more thoroughly studied by Zhao et al. (2021); Holtzman et al. (2021). The latter attributes the problem to 'surface form competition': there are many variants of the correct completion that together may capture a large part of probability mass, but the form of the given answer choice alone is not the most likely. However, we show that other causes are at play: surface form competition is impossible when the completion is known to be a single token and the range of choices is the whole vocabulary ( §3), and it is not applicable to open-ended generation ( §4).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Introduction

Human values are of concern to most if not to all social sciences (Rokeach, 1973) and have also been integrated into computational frameworks of argumentation (Bench-Capon, 2003). In NLP, values have been analyzed for personality profiling (Maheshwari et al., 2017), but not yet for argument mining, as considered here. Addressing this gap requires clarifying which value constructs are operationalizable from argumentative text and how these constructs interact with claims and premises. We define value salience as the degree to which a text segment signals a preference over competing ends, and value alignment as the compatibility between an argument’s inferred ends and an external value schema. Building on these definitions, we ask whether values can be reliably identified at the component level and whether their lexical and rhetorical markers generalize across topics. To ground the inquiry, we consider value theories that provide organizing axes for ends, including terminal/instrumental distinctions and higher-order clusters. We then assess how these axes map to argument roles, defeasible rules, and audience-sensitive framing in practical settings such as policy debates.

Related Work

Schwartz’s theory of basic human values systematizes motivational goals along circumplex dimensions, enabling comparative analyses across cultures. Computationally, argument mining has matured from component identification to relation parsing and scheme classification, with resources such as UKP, IBM Debater, and ArgMining shared tasks catalyzing progress. Moral and ethical NLP has concurrently advanced value-adjacent constructs, including moral foundations detection, stance-conditioned framing, and normative reasoning from policy texts. In parallel, prior research has cataloged value lexica, persuasion strategies, and ethical taxonomies across disciplines without a unifying lens (Rokeach, 1973; Schwartz, 1992; Bench-Capon, 2003; Mullen and Malouf, 2006; Mohammad et al., 2016; Maheshwari et al., 2017; Gardenfors and Makinson, 1994; Floridi and Cowls, 2019), and resources such as Moral Foundations, the Schwartz Value Survey, and PECO have been used alongside methods like LIWC, VAD norms, and topic modeling in a range of datasets including Opinosis, ConvAI, IAC, and UKP, while modeling approaches have spanned lexicon-based tagging, supervised classification, distant supervision, and weakly supervised pattern induction. Prior work on argumentative style shows that hedging, modality, and discourse connectives modulate perceived persuasiveness, suggesting potential value cues at the pragmatic layer. Recent studies connect audience features to rhetorical success, indicating that value resonance may be partially predicted from socio-demographic proxies.

Motivation and Scope

Despite this progress, there is limited evidence on whether value constructs can be annotated consistently at the claim and premise levels across heterogeneous topics. Moreover, existing lexicons often conflate moral sentiments with instrumental preferences, obscuring the link to argument structure. We focus on text-only signals in public discourse to disentangle value salience from topic priors and sentiment polarity. Our objective is to bridge argument mining with operational value schemas, providing measurable targets that enable downstream tasks such as audience-aware retrieval and deliberation support. Finally, we outline desiderata for datasets that capture cross-topic generalization, annotator calibration, and hierarchical value labels suitable for modern sequence tagging architectures.

spans.span: Zero-shot methods for relation extraction have explored a wide array of formulations and resources, including slot filling with reading comprehension templates (Levy et al., 2017), natural language inference casts of relation labels (Obamuyide and Vlachos, 2018;Yin et al., 2019;Soares et al., 2019), semantic matching with description encoders (Broscheit, 2019;Chen and Li, 2021;Han et al., 2018), and concept-level generalization with knowledge-graph text corpora (Xiong et al., 2018;Baldini Soares et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2020). Parallel advances combine meta-learning with episodic training over relation descriptions (Geng et al., 2021;Bansal et al., 2020) and use large pretrained encoders to align entity mentions and label semantics (Wu et al., 2020;Gao et al., 2021;Ye et al., 2022). Recent benchmarks and resources provide open-domain settings for evaluating unseen relations (Levy et al., 2017;TACRED-ZS;FewRel;Wiki-ZSL).

Prompting for information extraction has likewise diversified across cloze-style prompts (Petroni et al., 2019;Jiang et al., 2020;Shin et al., 2020), instruction-tuned models (Sanh et al., 2022;Wei et al., 2022;Ouyang et al., 2022;Mishra et al., 2022), automatic prompt search and calibration (Gao et al., 2021;Zhao et al., 2021;Lester et al., 2021;Liu et al., 2023), and constrained decoding for structured outputs (Lu et al., 2022;Creswell et al., 2022;Zhong et al., 2021;Creswell and Shanahan, 2022). Complementary strands include pretrained relation matching heads (Baldini Soares et al., 2019), entity-centric prompting (Cui et al., 2021;Zhong and Chen, 2021), and retrieval-augmented prompting pipelines that integrate external evidence into generation (Lewis et al., 2020;Izacard and Grave, 2021;Shi et al., 2023;Borgeaud et al., 2022).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Zero-Shot Relation Extraction Zero-shot relation extraction was previously framed as a slotfilling task and solved by reading comprehension methods (Levy et al., 2017). However, their approach requires manual template design for each relation label, which cannot scale well to new relation types. On the other hand, RelationPrompt generates synthetic relation samples for any relation without relying on label-specific templates. Another approach to zero-shot relation extraction is the formulation into an entailment task (Obamuyide and Vlachos, 2018), which is not constrained to a fixed relation label space and instead determines if arbitrary pairs of sentences and relation labels are compatible, allowing for zero-shot inference. However, it is designed for sentence-level classification and cannot be easily applied to ZeroRTE.

Zero-shot methods for relation extraction have explored a wide array of formulations and resources, including slot filling with reading comprehension templates (Levy et al., 2017), natural language inference casts of relation labels (Obamuyide and Vlachos, 2018;Yin et al., 2019;Soares et al., 2019), semantic matching with description encoders (Broscheit, 2019;Chen and Li, 2021;Han et al., 2018), and concept-level generalization with knowledge-graph text corpora (Xiong et al., 2018;Baldini Soares et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2020). Parallel advances combine meta-learning with episodic training over relation descriptions (Geng et al., 2021;Bansal et al., 2020) and use large pretrained encoders to align entity mentions and label semantics (Wu et al., 2020;Gao et al., 2021;Ye et al., 2022). Recent benchmarks and resources provide open-domain settings for evaluating unseen relations (Levy et al., 2017;TACRED-ZS;FewRel;Wiki-ZSL).

Data Augmentation A popular method for improving model performance in supervised lowresource tasks is data augmentation. Simple heuristics such as token manipulation (Kobayashi, 2018) were initially developed, new methods in language modeling improved the quality of augmented samples (Xie et al., 2020;Wei and Zou, 2019). Although there are data augmentation methods that can be applied to structured tasks such as named entity recognition (Ding et al., 2020) and relation extraction (Papanikolaou and Pierleoni, 2020;Lee et al., 2021), they require existing training samples and cannot be easily adapted to zero-shot tasks.

Language Model Prompts Prompting-based methods have shown promise as a new paradigm for inference in natural language processing . Given language models that have large-scale and general language pre-training, welldesigned prompts are able to elicit the desired answer sequences for different tasks in few-shot or even zero-shot settings. Another advantage is the potential to adapt very large language models (Reynolds and McDonell, 2021) to new tasks without relatively expensive fine-tuning. However, such methods have not yet proven effective for more complex tasks such as triplet extraction.

Prompting for information extraction has likewise diversified across cloze-style prompts (Petroni et al., 2019;Jiang et al., 2020;Shin et al., 2020), instruction-tuned models (Sanh et al., 2022;Wei et al., 2022;Ouyang et al., 2022;Mishra et al., 2022), automatic prompt search and calibration (Gao et al., 2021;Zhao et al., 2021;Lester et al., 2021;Liu et al., 2023), and constrained decoding for structured outputs (Lu et al., 2022;Creswell et al., 2022;Zhong et al., 2021;Creswell and Shanahan, 2022). Complementary strands include pretrained relation matching heads (Baldini Soares et al., 2019), entity-centric prompting (Cui et al., 2021;Zhong and Chen, 2021), and retrieval-augmented prompting pipelines that integrate external evidence into generation (Lewis et al., 2020;Izacard and Grave, 2021;Shi et al., 2023;Borgeaud et al., 2022).

Knowledge Retrieval RelationPrompt also leverages the knowledge stored in language models (Roberts et al., 2020) to compose relation samples that are grounded in realistic contexts. To ensure that the generated samples are factually accurate, the language model requires strong knowledge retrieval capabilities (Petroni et al., 2019).

spans.span: Recent progress in long-document modeling, retrieval-augmented generation, and controllable text generation provides additional context for our setting, including hierarchical transformers for extended contexts (Beltagy et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020; Rae et al., 2021), sparse attention and memory mechanisms for scaling sequence length (Child et al., 2019; Tay et al., 2020; Ainslie et al., 2020), retrieval-augmented models for knowledge-intensive tasks (Guu et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020; Izacard and Grave, 2021; Borgeaud et al., 2022), and content planning or control signals for generation (Kiddon et al., 2016; Yao et al., 2019; Narayan et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022), as well as evaluation protocols for question generation and summarization (Nema and Khapra, 2018; Durmus et al., 2020; Honovich et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2020).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Document understanding is a critical and challenging task in information processing. There have been many related research works in this direction. Keyword detection (Liu et al., 2009;Tixier et al., 2016) & topic modeling (Blei et al., 2003) works aim is to describe the document by a few important words or topics for concise representation. The first step is to acquire a list of keyword candidates (e.g., n-grams or chunks) with heuristic methods (Hulth, 2003;Shang et al., 2018), then rank them in accordance with their importance to the document (Wu et al., 2005;Gollapalli and Caragea, 2014;Bougouin et al., 2013). Another task is compact and informative headline generation from a document (David and Zajic, 2003;Lopyrev, 2015). Text summarization is the process of generating natural language summaries from an input document retaining the most important information (Rush et al., 2015;See et al., 2017). Recently, an Outline Generation task was introduced by (Zhang et al., 2019) as a hierarchical structured prediction problem. Given a document, their aim is to first predict a sequence of section boundaries and then a sequence of section headings accordingly to come up with a Table of Contents for the same.

A related direction of work to ours is of aspect detection, which has been explored in the literature largely using user reviews for products. Early works focused on rule-based approaches using lexicons and dependency relations, and utilize manually defined rules to identify patterns and extract aspects (Qiu et al., 2011;Liu et al., 2016), which require domain-specific knowledge and human expertise. Supervised approaches formulate aspect extraction as a sequence labelling problem that can be solved by hidden Markov models (HMM) (Jin et al., 2009), conditional random fields (CRF) (Li et al., 2010;Mitchell et al., 2013;Yang and Cardie, 2012), and recurrent neural networks (RNN) (Wang et al., 2016;Liu et al., 2015). These approaches have shown better performance compared to the rule-based ones, but require large amounts of labelled data for training. Early unsupervised systems are dominated by Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)-based topic models (García-Pablos et al., 2018;Shi et al., 2018;Alvarez-López et al., 2016). Recently, deep learning based topic models (Srivastava and Sutton, 2017;Luo et al., 2019;He et al., 2017;Shi et al., 2021) have shown strong performance in extracting coherent aspects in an unsupervised manner. None of the prior works on aspect detection have worked with contracts or financial documents that are quite long (50-100 pages) in comparison to user reviews. Even if we break the document at paragraph level, it can still go over tens of lines. Hence, the importance of word frequency is much more in our case. We bridge the gap between directly using the unsupervised aspect detection frameworks for the financial documents by adding a TF-IDF based weighing parameter while training. Moreover, there are no gold standards for aspect detection for contract or finance domain, hence, we use unsupervised clustering based metrics for validating the output detection.

Further, it has been shown that question-answers play a critical role in scientific inquiry, informationseeking dialogue, and knowledge acquisition (Hintikka and Saarinen, 1979;Stede and Schlangen, 2004). In a dialogue system, question generation is used to obtain specific information from the user or make the conversation more pleasant (Shukla et al., 2019;Saeidi et al., 2018). Hence, we hypothesize that augmenting the default ToC with Questions that give a high level overview of the paragraphs can enhance the reading experience of the users. Question generation can also be seen as a summarization or seq2seq task. Various pre-trained language models like BART (Lewis et al., 2020), PEGASUS (Zhang et al., 2020), etc., have shown excellent results for these tasks. Researchers have worked on top of these language models & proposed various rewards for QGen to optimize these models. (Kumar et al., 2019) has employed BLEUbased rewards, (Zhang and Bansal, 2019) have used answerability rewards, whereas (Xie et al., 2020) has used a combination of fluency, relevance, and answerability rewards.

Previous question generation literature has focused on generating questions based on an entity, phrase, or sentence. In this work, we explore longform question generation, i.e., question-based long text. We explore deep reinforcement learning techniques for the same. as they have shown competitive results in various natural language generation tasks such as summarization (Pasunuru and Bansal, 2018), style transfer (Liu et al., 2021;Goyal et al., 2021), question generation (Hosking and Riedel, 2019;Xie et al., 2020) etc. Motivated by this we use BART as our base model. As there is a lack of labeled question datasets in financial domain, to overcome the domain shift problem, we train the model with additional rewards in a reinforcement learning setup to make more suitable for a general domain.

There are several commercial products for reading documents across devices, but all of them have a fixed document navigation, based on chapters and headings. To the best of our knowledge, there is no prior art looking into providing an end-to-end persona-based navigation. The mentioned technologies address only part of the required solutions. Following are the key contributions of our work:

1. We propose a novel DYNAMICTOC technology to enable persona-based non-linear navigation for efficient consumption of long documents.

2. We extend the unsupervised aspect detection to long domain-specific documents by combining TF-IDF with aspect detection process to make it more robust and show the improvements experimentally.

3. We propose a method to generate questions based on the content of the paragraph maximizing the information coverage, entity correctness & answerability of the question.

4. We showcase the viability of our pipeline and evaluate it using metric-based and a human survey-based evaluation.

3 Datasets SEC Filing: The SEC filing is a financial statement document submitted to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Public companies, certain insiders, and broker-dealers are required to make regular SEC filings. There are many types of documents available on the EDGAR website (Eg. 10-K, 10-Q, Form 4, etc.). For our work, we focused on the SEC 10-K documents available on the EDGAR website 1 . For a given company, the 10-k documents are available in HTML, XBRL and XML format. The complete submission text file for a 10-k document (XML) was used for parsing. We split the document content into different items ranging from item 1 to item 16. These 10-K documents range from 50 to 120 pages and contain multiple tables along with text paragraphs. ELI5: We use the ELI5 dataset (Fan et al., 2019) to train the question generation model. ELI5 or Explain Like I'm 5, is a question-answer dataset scraped from the subreddit r/explainlikeimfive/. The subreddit rules encourage people to ask a question about any topic and get an answer for it. To maintain the dataset's quality, we only select those question-answer pairs with more than two upvotes. Note that no dataset for such question generation task exists for contractual and financial documents. Hence, we resort to use the ELI5 dataset for supervised training and use that model for inferencing on documents from a different domain. To test the model's performance on the domainspecific dataset, we also scrape question-answer pairs from two different subreddits -r/AskLegal and r/AskEconomics. As the name suggests, they contain questions (and answers) from the legal and economics domain respectively. Table  includes the statistics of the three datasets.

Conversational question answering. In recent years, several conversational question answering datasets have emerged, such as QuAC (Choi et al., 2018), CoQA (Reddy et al., 2019), and DoQA (Campos et al., 2020). Different from single-turn QA datasets (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), CQA requires the model to understand the question in the context of conversational history. There have been many methods proposed to improve CQA performance (Ohsugi et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2021) and significant improvement has been made on CQA benchmarks. Recent advances in modeling have also been reported across pre-training and response selection, with approaches leveraging context-aware attention, hierarchical encoders, and span-based retrievers on prominent datasets and benchmarks (Qu et al., 2020;Yatskar, 2019;Lewis et al., 2020;Zhu et al., 2021;Huang et al., 2021;Gao et al., 2021;Chen et al., 2021;Reddy et al., 2019), along with multi-task learning and domain adaptation techniques that integrate external supervision signals and curriculum strategies (Zhang et al., 2021;Kumar and Talukdar, 2020;Liu et al., 2020;Talmor et al., 2019).

Besides text-based CQA tasks, there also exist CQA benchmarks that require other forms of modeling ability, such as combining textual evidence with background knowledge (Saeidi et al., 2018), utilizing structured knowledge base (Saha et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2018), as well as CQA in other modalities (Das et al., 2017). These extensions broaden the scope of conversational understanding and present different forms of context grounding. In turn, they emphasize the need for methods that can track dialogue states, disambiguate co-references, and manage long-term dependencies. They also introduce evaluation complexities that go beyond single utterance quality and hinge on multi-turn coherence.

Evaluation with predicted history. Only recently has it been noticed that the current method of evaluating CQA models is flawed. Mandya et al. (2020); Siblini et al. (2021) point out that using gold answers in history is not consistent with the real-world scenario and propose to use predicted history for evaluation. Building on this critique, subsequent studies explored how error propagation affects downstream reasoning and retrieval under imperfect histories. However, most automated metrics remain insensitive to pragmatic repair and contextual grounding that humans readily perform during conversation. To address this mismatch, we design a large-scale human study focusing on faithfulness under noisy histories and calibrate automatic proxies against these judgments. We further analyze the distribution of error types in predicted histories and introduce a question rewriting protocol that improves robustness without requiring oracle interventions. Our findings inform the construction of future CQA benchmarks and provide guidance for evaluation under realistic deployment constraints.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Introduction

Hallucination in neural language generation has recently received increasing attention from the NLP community, including machine translation (Raunak et al., 2021;Wang and Sennrich, 2020). While early work highlighted semantic drift and unsupported content in summarization (Maynez et al., 2020) and dialogue (Nie et al., 2021), subsequent analyses have emphasized the spectrum of phenomena from minor factual slips to fully fabricated entities (Ji et al., 2023). Definitions of hallucination vary across tasks, with some focusing on faithfulness to input (Kryściński et al., 2020) and others on external factual consistency (Manakul et al., 2023), which complicates both evaluation and mitigation.

Related Work

Measurement frameworks now include automatic factuality metrics, human evaluation protocols, and hybrid checkers. Automatic metrics such as QAGS (Wang et al., 2020), FactCC (Kryściński et al., 2020), and SummaC (Laban et al., 2022) aim to quantify input groundedness in summarization. For dialogue and open-ended generation, methods leverage question answering probes and entailment-based tests to assess consistency with provided context or retrieved evidence (Honovich et al., 2022;Rashkin et al., 2021). Human protocols standardize annotation of error types and severities, though inter-annotator agreement remains a challenge (Pagnoni et al., 2021).

Recent studies catalog a variety of mitigation strategies spanning constrained decoding and calibration (Kumar and Talukdar, 2021;Nie et al., 2021), post-hoc factuality ranking (Kryściński et al., 2020;Goyal and Durrett, 2021), retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020;Izacard and Grave, 2021), instruction tuning and preference optimization (Ouyang et al., 2022;Rafailov et al., 2023), and automatic verification with external knowledge bases or tool use (Thorne et al., 2018;Schick et al., 2023;Creswell et al., 2022). However, the interaction between these interventions and domain shift, prompt sensitivity, and input noise is not yet fully characterized by standardized stress-testing.

In machine translation, hallucinations often manifest as fluent yet semantically unrelated outputs or as overconfident insertions of non-source content (Raunak et al., 2021). Regularization with source-conditioned confidence and coverage penalties has been found to reduce such errors, though trade-offs with adequacy and fluency persist (Wang and Sennrich, 2020). Domain adaptation and terminology constraints offer complementary levers but may amplify brittleness when constraints are mis-specified (Song et al., 2021;Chen et al., 2020).

For knowledge-intensive tasks, retrieval augmentation lowers the rate of fabrications by grounding generation in evidence, yet susceptibility to retrieval drift and spurious matches can reintroduce inconsistencies (Lewis et al., 2020;Izacard and Grave, 2021). Adaptive retrieval policies and reranking improve evidence quality, but latency and memory constraints limit applicability in interactive settings. Recent tool-use approaches integrate verifiers or calculators, which help in narrow domains but struggle to generalize verification schemas across heterogeneous data sources (Schick et al., 2023;Creswell et al., 2022).

Our work situates within this landscape by targeting robustness to perturbations that commonly degrade grounding. We focus on evaluating factual consistency under controlled input corruptions that emulate realistic user and data pipeline noise. We further analyze failure modes that evade current factuality metrics and propose diagnostics that connect model calibration, retrieval quality, and generation dynamics under perturbation.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Introduction

Dense retrievers have emerged as a dominant paradigm for open-domain and web-scale search because they learn compact representations that enable efficient approximate nearest neighbor lookup while preserving semantic relevance. Despite steady progress, robustness to limited supervision and distribution shift remains a central concern for practical deployment in high-variance domains such as news, forums, and scientific literature. Recent work on pre-trained encoders and dual-encoder architectures has reported strong performance for large-scale passage retrieval, in particular DPR and its variants (Karpukhin et al., 2020;Xiong et al., 2021;Sachan et al., 2021;Izacard et al., 2021), momentum-contrast and late-interaction schemes (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020;Luan et al., 2021;Hofstätter et al., 2021;Santhanam et al., 2022), as well as multi-vector retrieval with ColBERTv2 and SPLADE-like sparse expansions (Formal et al., 2021;Chen et al., 2021;Lin and Ma, 2021;Luan et al., 2021). To alleviate data scarcity, augmentation has been widely explored in both vision and language settings.

Related Work

Classical augmentation techniques show broad gains in supervised learning (Shorten and Khoshgoftaar, 2019;Hedderich et al., 2021), where interpolation and perturbation are dominant methods. Mixup interpolates two different items, such as pixels of images, to augment the training data (Zhang et al., 2018;Verma et al., 2019), which has also been adopted for NLP classification and sequence labeling tasks (Chen et al., 2020a;Yin et al., 2021). However, little is known about the effectiveness of mixup when applied to retrieval objectives that rely on pairwise or contrastive losses rather than token-level supervision. Beyond interpolation, Wei and Zou (2019) and Ma (2019) proposed perturbation over words to simulate lexical variation, and Lee et al. (2021) proposed perturbation over word embeddings to encourage representation stability. Jeong et al. (2021) perturbed document embeddings to generate diverse summaries, indicating that representation-level noise can induce output diversity. In the context of retrieval, augmentation methods must preserve alignment between queries and relevant documents while enriching negatives to avoid trivial shortcuts.

Overview of Our Approach

We revisit perturbation at the representation level and study its effect on dense retrievers trained with in-batch negatives. Concretely, we perturb document representations via dropout during training to create stochastic views that act as implicit augmentations without altering text. This design keeps query text intact while inducing diversity on the document side, aiming to regularize the scoring function against spurious correlations. We analyze how dropout interacts with temperature-scaled contrastive losses and hard-negative mining, and we compare against token-level noise that can degrade encoder calibration. Our experiments span web QA and passage retrieval benchmarks, using consistent encoder backbones and index configurations to isolate the contribution of representation perturbation.

Contributions

We provide a systematic evaluation of representation perturbation via dropout for dense retrieval, including ablations on dropout placement, rate schedules, and coupling with hard negatives. We report improvements under low-resource and domain-shifted settings, and we quantify effects on recall@k, calibration, and embedding anisotropy. Finally, we release code and scripts to facilitate reproduction and further study of representation-space augmentation for retrieval.

Previously, most length-controllable approaches in abstractive summarization focused on stoping decoding at a particular time.
Ad-hoc (Rush et al., 2015) generated the eos token by assigning a score of -∞ to the tokens in vocabulary and generate a fixed number of words.
LenEmb and LenInit (Kikuchi et al., 2016) input length embeddings to decoder respectively.
LC (Liu et al., 2018) added the desired length into the first layer of CNN encoder.
Fan et al. (2018) predefined some special markers to denote different length ranges and prepended the input with such markers during training and testing.
Takase and Okazaki (2019) extended the sinusoidal positional encoding to take account of stepwise remaining length.
GOLC (Makino et al., 2019) optimized LenEmb and LC by formalizing loss with an overlength penalty.
Bian et al. (2019) took LenInit and LenEmb as an agent and adjusted the reward incorporating with desired length.
LenAtten (Yu et al., 2021) added a length attention unit to exploit proper length information based on the stepwise remaining length.

Other length-controllable approaches decided the content to be summarized by length-aware intermediate summaries.
LPAS (Saito et al., 2020) extracted a word sequence with desired length from source document and generated summary by nonlength-controllable model with document and extracted summary as input.
MLS (Sarkhel et al., 2020) generated a general summary and then input it to a length-controllable model.

Compared with previous methods, our approach can effectively control the length of generated summaries by pretrainig the length-controllable information selection model on length-balanced dataset.
Meanwhile, it can generate summaries with length approximate to the desired length in zero-shot controlling length problem.

Recently, the approaches fine-tune the pretrained transformer seq2seq models (Lewis et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Dou et al., 2021; Raffel et al., 2020; Liu and Lapata, 2019; Narayan et al., 2018; Rothe et al., 2021; Xiao et al., 2022) on summarization datasets, with evaluations frequently reported on CNN/DailyMail, XSum, and Gigaword using BART, PEGASUS, T5, ProphetNet, and Longformer-Encoder-Decoder.
They achieve outstanding performances on summarization tasks.
Our approach is applied on transformer seq2seq model, which is orthogonal to above pretrained transformer models and can be added to them.

spans.span: Prior work spans social media corpora, misinformation benchmarks, and multimodal verification without drawing consistent connections among them, including pandemic-focused Twitter collections (Banda et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2020; Lamsal, 2021; Ziems et al., 2020), climate and disaster datasets (Littman and Wrubel, 2019; Alam et al., 2018; Imran et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2017), annotated rumor and claim corpora (Qazvinian et al., 2011; Kwon et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2016; Zubiaga et al., 2016), and multimodal misinformation resources emphasizing images or memes (Kiela et al., 2020; Abdali et al., 2021; Khattar et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2019).

Related lines of work on cross-modal retrieval and grounding leverage image–text alignment and external references (Karpathy and Fei-Fei, 2015; Faghri et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019), while multimodal fact-checking systems integrate retrieval with reasoning or graph structures (Popat et al., 2018; Zhou and Zafarani, 2019; Gupta et al., 2013; Boididou et al., 2015).

Lacks synthesis.document:
There exist a number of large-scale Twitter datasets concentrated on topics such as COVID-19 (Banda et al., 2021) or Climate Change (Littman and Wrubel, 2019). However, it remains difficult to collect labeled misinformation. Researchers have collected COVID-19 misconceptions on social media via manual annotation (Hossain et al., 2020) or by linking to fact checking articles (Patwa et al., 2021). Not only are these datasets small (a few thousand samples), but they focus on false claims rather than multimodal inconsistency.

Prior work spans social media corpora, misinformation benchmarks, and multimodal verification without drawing consistent connections among them, including pandemic-focused Twitter collections (Banda et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2020; Lamsal, 2021; Ziems et al., 2020), climate and disaster datasets (Littman and Wrubel, 2019; Alam et al., 2018; Imran et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2017), annotated rumor and claim corpora (Qazvinian et al., 2011; Kwon et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2016; Zubiaga et al., 2016), and multimodal misinformation resources emphasizing images or memes (Kiela et al., 2020; Abdali et al., 2021; Khattar et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2019). In the news domain, Luo et al. (2021) automatically generate out-of-context images. Here, we curate social media posts that are topical and multimodal, and demonstrate an application to misinformation detection of human-generated fakes. There also exist general approaches for multimodal fact checking, e.g., Jaiswal et al. (2017) and Müller-Budack et al. (2020) that query an external knowledge base. Instead, we use a large pretrained model that does not require an external reference set.

We focus on out-of-context and semantically conflicting image–text pairs that arise in real social media conversations, emphasizing non-synthetic manipulations such as re-captioning and narrative drift. Our curation pipeline filters trending topics, verifies media provenance, and preserves conversational context to support evaluations that reflect practical constraints. We release metadata with privacy-preserving handles and provide reproducible splits for cross-topic generalization, enabling controlled comparisons across settings.

To situate our contribution within multimodal learning, we review complementary efforts on visual entailment and image–text contradiction that build upon pretrained vision–language models. Related lines of work on cross-modal retrieval and grounding leverage image–text alignment and external references (Karpathy and Fei-Fei, 2015; Faghri et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019), while multimodal fact-checking systems integrate retrieval with reasoning or graph structures (Popat et al., 2018; Zhou and Zafarani, 2019; Gupta et al., 2013; Boididou et al., 2015). In contrast, our approach evaluates instruction-tuned encoders under weakly supervised objectives that prioritize internal consistency signals over explicit retrieval. We further compare zero-shot and few-shot adaptation regimes and quantify robustness to topical domain shift.

Finally, we articulate evaluation desiderata for multimodal misinformation: balanced coverage across topics and media types, decoupling veracity from political stance, and scenario-driven stress tests for out-of-context use. We report metrics at both instance and thread levels to capture the role of conversational context, and we ablate the contribution of provenance cues, image–text alignment features, and pragmatic markers. Our released resource and baselines aim to close the gap between synthetic benchmarks and real-world moderation settings.

spans.span: Early studies take LDA (Blei et al., 2003) as the backbone and incorporate seeds into model learning. For example, Andrzejewski et al. (2009) consider must-link and cannot-link constraints among seeds as priors. SeededLDA (Jagarlamudi et al., 2012) encourages topics to contain more seeds and encourages documents to select topics related to the seeds they contain. Anchored CorEx (Gallagher et al., 2017) extracts maximally informative topics by jointly compressing the corpus and preserving seed relevant information. Subsequent work also explores user interaction, posterior regularization, and semi-supervision in related formulations (Ramage et al., 2009; Mei et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2014; Zhai et al., 2013).

The common strategy is to adapt distributions in LDA to generate real-valued data (e.g., Gaussian LDA (Das et al., 2015), LFTM (Nguyen et al., 2015), Spherical HDP (Batmanghelich et al., 2016), and CGTM (Xun et al., 2017b)). Some other studies think out of the LDA backbone. For example, TWE (Liu et al., 2015) uses topic structures to jointly learn topic embeddings and improve word embeddings. CLM (Xun et al., 2017a) collaboratively improves topic modeling and word embedding by coordinating global and local contexts. ETM (Dieng et al., 2020) models word-topic correlations via word embeddings to improve the expressiveness of topic models. More recently, Sia et al. (2020) show that directly clustering word embeddings (e.g., word2vec or BERT) also generates good topics; Thompson and Mimno (2020) further find that BERT and GPT-2 discover high quality topics, but RoBERTa does not.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Seed-Guided Topic Discovery. Seed-guided topic models aim to leverage user-provided seeds to discover underlying topics according to users' interests. Early studies take LDA (Blei et al., 2003) as the backbone and incorporate seeds into model learning. For example, Andrzejewski et al. (2009) consider must-link and cannot-link constraints among seeds as priors. SeededLDA (Jagarlamudi et al., 2012) encourages topics to contain more seeds and encourages documents to select topics related to the seeds they contain. Anchored CorEx (Gallagher et al., 2017) extracts maximally informative topics by jointly compressing the corpus and preserving seed relevant information. Subsequent work also explores user interaction, posterior regularization, and semi-supervision in related formulations (Ramage et al., 2009; Mei et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2014; Zhai et al., 2013). Recent studies start to utilize embedding techniques to learn better word semantics. For example, CatE (Meng et al., 2020) explicitly encourages distinction among retrieved topics via categoryname guided embedding learning. However, all these models require the provided seeds to be invocabulary, mainly because they focus on the input corpus only and are not equipped with general knowledge of PLMs.

Embedding-Based Topic Discovery. A number of studies extend LDA to involve word embedding. The common strategy is to adapt distributions in LDA to generate real-valued data (e.g., Gaussian LDA (Das et al., 2015), LFTM (Nguyen et al., 2015), Spherical HDP (Batmanghelich et al., 2016), and CGTM (Xun et al., 2017b)). Some other studies think out of the LDA backbone. For example, TWE (Liu et al., 2015) uses topic structures to jointly learn topic embeddings and improve word embeddings. CLM (Xun et al., 2017a) collaboratively improves topic modeling and word embedding by coordinating global and local contexts. ETM (Dieng et al., 2020) models word-topic correlations via word embeddings to improve the expressiveness of topic models. More recently, Sia et al. (2020) show that directly clustering word embeddings (e.g., word2vec or BERT) also generates good topics; Thompson and Mimno (2020) further find that BERT and GPT-2 discover high quality topics, but RoBERTa does not. These models are unsupervised and hard to be applied to seed-guided settings. In contrast, our SEETOPIC framework joint leverages PLMs, word embeddings, and seed information.

spans.span: Recent efforts further broaden this landscape with block-sparse Transformers (Child et al., 2019), routing-based sparsity in Switch Transformers (Fedus et al., 2021), linearized attention kernels such as Performer (Choromanski et al., 2021), kernelized low-rank projections in Linformer (Wang et al., 2020), and long-context pretraining strategies exemplified by LED (Beltagy et al., 2020) and UL2 (Tay et al., 2023).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Sparse attention mechanism The full attention mechanism has a quadratic memory cost. Prior research works have proposed different sparse attention mechanisms to reduce the memory cost. Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020) uses a dilated sliding window of blocks and global attention patterns. BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) employs sliding window and random blocks. Reformer (Kitaev et al., 2020) uses the locality-sensitive hashing. In addition to optimizing the encoder self-attention, Huang et al. (2021) proposes head-wise positional strides to reduce the cost of the encoder-decoder attention. Recent efforts further broaden this landscape with block-sparse Transformers (Child et al., 2019), routing-based sparsity in Switch Transformers (Fedus et al., 2021), linearized attention kernels such as Performer (Choromanski et al., 2021), kernelized low-rank projections in Linformer (Wang et al., 2020), and long-context pretraining strategies exemplified by LED (Beltagy et al., 2020) and UL2 (Tay et al., 2023). However, sparse attention diminishes the benefits of pretraining and sacrifices parts of the receptive field.

Extract-then-generate method The model first extracts salient text snippets from the input, followed by generating a concise overall summary. Most two-stage summarization approaches (Zhang et al., 2019;Lebanoff et al., 2019;Xu and Durrett, 2019;Bajaj et al., 2021) are trained separately, which suffer from information loss due to the cascaded errors. Some approaches attempt to reduce that loss by bridging the two stages. Chen and Bansal (2018) adopts reinforcement learning with a sentence-level policy gradient method. Bae et al. (2019) proposes summary-level policy gradient. In addition to the drawbacks explained in Section 2.3, our model is different as we jointly train an extractthen-generate model for summarization using latent variables.

Divide-and-conquer approach A common approach in long input summarization is divide-andconquer (Gidiotis and Tsoumakas, 2020;Grail et al., 2021). This approach breaks a long input into multiple parts, which are summarized separately and combined to produce a final complete summary. However, these models do not capture the contextual dependencies across parts and assumes a certain structure of the input (such as paper sections).

Hierarchical models Various hierarchical models have been proposed to handle the longer inputs. Cohan et al. (2018) models the document discourse structure with a hierarchical encoder and a discourse-aware decoder to generate the summary. HAT-Bart (Rohde et al., 2021) proposes a new Hierarchical Attention Transformer-based architecture that attempts to capture sentence and paragraphlevel information. HMNet (Zhu et al., 2020) builds a hierarchical structure that includes discourselevel information and speaker roles. However, these models focus mainly on model performance and not on reducing the memory and computational cost.

spans.span: Beyond ABSA, related problems have been studied under joint extraction and structured prediction paradigms, including table-filling for relation extraction (Miwa and Sasaki, 2014;Gupta et al., 2016), dependency-guided opinion mining (Klinger and Cimiano, 2013;Zhang and Liu, 2014), span-based sentiment-role labeling (He et al., 2019;Li et al., 2019a), and sequence-to-sequence triplet generation (Yan et al., 2021;Xu et al., 2021;Wu et al., 2020a;Mao et al., 2021).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Traditional sentiment analysis tasks are sentencelevel (Yang and Cardie, 2014;Severyn and Moschitti, 2015) or document-level (Dou, 2017;Lyu et al., 2020) oriented. In contrast, Aspect-based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) is an aspect or entity oriented fine-grained sentiment analysis task. The most three basic subtasks are Aspect Term Extraction (ATE) (Hu and Liu, 2004;Yin et al., 2016;Li et al., 2018b;Xu et al., 2018;Ma et al., 2019;Chen and Qian, 2020;, Aspect Sentiment Classification (ASC) (Wang et al., 2016b;Tang et al., 2016;Ma et al., 2017;Fan et al., 2018;Li et al., 2018a;Li et al., 2021) and Opinion Term Extraction (OTE) Cardie, 2012, 2013;Fan et al., 2019;Wu et al., 2020b). The studies solve these tasks separately and ignore the dependency between these subtasks. Therefore, some efforts devoted to couple the two subtasks and proposed effective models to jointly extract aspect-based pairs. This kind of work mainly has two tasks: Aspect and Opinion Term Co-Extraction (AOTE) (Wang et al., 2016aDai and Song,  2019; Wang and Pan, 2019;Wu et al., 2020a) and Aspect-Sentiment Pair Extraction (ASPE) (Ma et al., 2018;Li et al., 2019a,b;He et al., 2019).

Most recently, Peng et al. (2020) first proposed the ASTE task and developed a two-stage pipeline framework to couple together aspect extraction, aspect sentiment classification and opinion extraction. To further explore this task, (Mao et al., 2021;Chen et al., 2021a) transformed ASTE to a machine reading comprehension problem and utilized the shared BERT encoder to obatin the triplets after multiple stages decoding. Another line of research focuses on designing a new tagging scheme that makes the model can extract the triplets in an endto-end fashion Wu et al., 2020a;Xu et al., 2021;Yan et al., 2021). For instance,  proposed a positionaware tagging scheme, which solves the limitations related to existing works by enriching the expressiveness of labels. Wu et al. (2020a) proposed a grid tagging scheme, similar to table filling (Miwa and Sasaki, 2014;Gupta et al., 2016), to solve this task in an end-to-end manner. Yan et al. (2021) converted ASTE task into a generative formulation. However, these approaches generally ignore the relations between words and linguistic features which effectively promote the triplet extraction.

Beyond ABSA, related problems have been studied under joint extraction and structured prediction paradigms, including table-filling for relation extraction (Miwa and Sasaki, 2014;Gupta et al., 2016), dependency-guided opinion mining (Klinger and Cimiano, 2013;Zhang and Liu, 2014), span-based sentiment-role labeling (He et al., 2019;Li et al., 2019a), and sequence-to-sequence triplet generation (Yan et al., 2021;Xu et al., 2021;Wu et al., 2020a;Mao et al., 2021).

spans.span: Recent progress on multi-modal or cross-modal pre-training has also been reported across disparate threads of work, including joint speech-text representation learning with multimodal contrastive objectives (Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021; Baevski et al., 2022; Hsu et al., 2021), unified encoder-decoder formulations for conditional generation (Raffel et al., 2019; Lewis et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021b; Li et al., 2022), multi-task training recipes for speech recognition, synthesis, and translation (Watanabe et al., 2018; Kharitonov et al., 2021; Popov et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020), and benchmark-driven evaluations of representation quality over diverse speech tasks (Yang et al., 2021; Tsai et al., 2022; Conneau et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Large-scale pre-training models such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), T5 (Raffel et al., 2019), wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski et al., 2020), and HuBERT (Hsu et al., 2021) have drawn much attention in the NLP and speech communities, due to its strong capability of generalization and efficient usage of largescale data (Devlin et al., 2019;Yang et al., 2019;Lewis et al., 2020;Chen et al., 2021c;Baevski et al., 2020;Kharitonov et al., 2021;Chen et al., 2021a).
However, the research mentioned above effects gear towards single-modal learning, hence they can only be used in either text or speech modeling.
Although some speech-language pre-training work (Chung et al., 2021b;Kim et al., 2021; attempts to improve spoken language understanding tasks, these methods only focus on an encoder with task-specific layers for different tasks and do not pre-train a decoder for generation tasks such as speech synthesis or text generation.
Recent progress on multi-modal or cross-modal pre-training has also been reported across disparate threads of work, including joint speech-text representation learning with multimodal contrastive objectives (Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021; Baevski et al., 2022; Hsu et al., 2021), unified encoder-decoder formulations for conditional generation (Raffel et al., 2019; Lewis et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021b; Li et al., 2022), multi-task training recipes for speech recognition, synthesis, and translation (Watanabe et al., 2018; Kharitonov et al., 2021; Popov et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020), and benchmark-driven evaluations of representation quality over diverse speech tasks (Yang et al., 2021; Tsai et al., 2022; Conneau et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a).
The proposed SpeechT5 method is most related to T5 (Raffel et al., 2019).
The core idea of the T5 model, a unified framework for a variety of text-based language problems, is to treat every text processing problem as a "text-to-text" problem.
SpeechT5 is also related to Speech Chain (Tjandra et al., 2020), which leverages the ASR model and TTS model to build a closed-loop machine speech chain to train models on the concatenation of both labeled and unlabeled data, and SpeechNet (Chen et al., 2021b), which designs a universal modularized model to perform multiple speech processing tasks with multi-task learning.
The differences from the above models are that (1) SpeechT5 is a shared cross-modal encoder-decoder framework, whose input and output are speech or text through multiple pre/post-nets; (2) SpeechT5 attempts to pre-train and improve the universal model with large-scale unlabeled text and speech data.
Another related work is SUPERB (Yang et al., 2021), a benchmark to examine the capability of pre-trained models such as HuBERT (Hsu et al., 2021).
SUPERB focuses on investigating a simple framework to learn SUPERB tasks with a frozen and shared pre-trained encoder and lightweight prediction modules fine-tuned for each task.
In contrast, the goal of SpeechT5 is to learn all spoken language processing tasks by fine-tuning a unifiedmodal encoder-decoder model, which is pre-trained on unlabeled speech and text corpus.
To enable this goal, we consider a pre-training objective that aligns speech and text representations while preserving modality-specific information needed for generation.
We further incorporate task-agnostic pre/post-nets to flexibly adapt the shared backbone to different input and output modalities.
During fine-tuning, the same architecture is applied with minimal task-specific adjustments, avoiding extensive per-task heads.
This design facilitates transfer across ASR, TTS, speech translation, and spoken intent understanding with a single set of parameters.
We evaluate on diverse datasets to ensure robustness across domains and speaker conditions.
Our experiments compare against strong encoder-only and encoder-decoder baselines in both speech-only and text-only regimes.
We report results under both full-resource and limited-resource settings to assess data efficiency.
Finally, we analyze ablations to isolate the effect of cross-modal sharing and the contribution of each pre/post-net component.
