Early attempts to use QG for educational applications involved generating gap-fill or "cloze" questions 1 (Taylor, 1953) from textbooks (Agarwal and Mannem, 2011). One may optionally choose to generate distractors to make these questions multiple choice (Narendra et al., 2013;Correia et al., 2012). This procedure has been shown to be effective in classroom settings (Zavala and Mendoza, 2018) and students' scores on this style of generated question correlate positively with their scores on human-written questions (Guo et al., 2016). However, there are many situations where gap-fill questions are not effective, as they are only able to ask about specific unambiguous key terms.

In recent years, with the advent of large crowdsourced datasets for extractive question answering (QA) such as SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2018), neural models have become the primary methods of choice for generating traditional interrogative style questions (Kurdi et al., 2019). A common task formulation for neural QG is to phrase the task as answer-aware, that is, given a context passage C = {c 0 , ..., c n } and an answer span within this context A = {c k , ..., c k+l } such that k ≥ 0 and k + l ≤ n, train a model to maximize P (Q|A, C) where Q = {q 0 , ..., q m } are the tokens in the question. These models are typically evaluated using n-gram overlap metrics such as BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR (Papineni et al., 2002;Lin, 2004;Banerjee and Lavie, 2005) with the reference being the original human-authored question as provided by the extractive QA dataset.

The feasibility of using answer-aware neural QG in an educational setting was investigated by Wang et al. (2018), who used a BiLSTM encoder (Zhang et al., 2015) to encode C and A and a unidirectional LSTM decoder to generate Q. They trained on the SQuAD dataset (Rajpurkar et al., 2018) and evaluated on textbooks from various domains (history, sociology, biology). They showed that generated questions were largely grammatical, relevant, and had high n-gram overlap with humanauthored questions. However, given that we may not always have a convenient list of key terms to use as answer spans for an input passage, there is a desire to move past answer-aware QG models and evaluate the feasibility of answer-unaware models for use in education. Neural question generation has also been explored through sequence-to-sequence architectures with attention, pointer-generator mechanisms, and copy-augmented decoders, along with pre-trained language models adapted for QG (Du et al., 2017;Zhou et al., 2017;Song et al., 2018;Zhang and Bansal, 2019;Dong et al., 2019;Kumar et al., 2019;Scialom et al., 2019;Chan and Fan, 2019;Lewis et al., 2020;Raffel et al., 2020;Brown et al., 2020;Fabbri et al., 2020), and work on controllable QG introduces mechanisms for difficulty conditioning and answer type control (Mostafazadeh et al., 2016;Hu et al., 2018;Subramanian et al., 2018;Zhang et al., 2020), while domain transfer and robustness have been studied using multi-domain training and adversarial objectives (Jia and Liang, 2017;Dua et al., 2019;Sugawara et al., 2018;Bartolo et al., 2020).

In our study, we explicitly ask annotators to determine whether or not a generated question is relevant to the topic of the textbook chapter from which it is generated. In addition, we show that models trained for answer extraction on SQuAD frequently select irrelevant or ambiguous answers when applied to textbook material. We show that summaries of input passages can be used instead of the original text to aid in the modeling of topic salience and that questions generated from humanwritten and automatically-generated summaries are more relevant, interpretable, and acceptable.

This section provides background and motivation for task and domain adaptability applied to concern detection in the 2017 French Election domain ( §2.1, §2.2), including concern values induced from Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) ( §2.3).
We focus on the challenge of detecting moral concern categories in short, noisy political texts under distribution shift across topics and sources.
Task adaptability refers to transferring a concern detector trained on one label schema or annotation guideline to another without extensive relabeling.
Domain adaptability addresses generalization from one electoral context, medium, or time period to another where lexical and pragmatic cues differ.
We ground our study in MFT, which posits a set of moral dimensions (e.g., Care/Harm, Fairness/Cheating, Loyalty/Betrayal, Authority/Subversion, Sanctity/Degradation) that can be operationalized as concern values at the utterance level.
Prior work on political text classification spans lexicon-based approaches (e.g., LIWC; Pennebaker et al., 2015), neural encoders pre-trained on general corpora (Mikolov et al., 2013; Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019), election-specific stance and ideology datasets (SemEval-2016 Task 6; Iyyer et al., 2014; Johnson and Goldwasser, 2016; Conover et al., 2011), and domain adaptation methods including adversarial invariance (Ganin et al., 2016), parameter-efficient adapters (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2020), and prompt tuning (Lester et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023).
Concern detection has been explored in the context of moral rhetoric and persuasion, with early studies employing hand-crafted features and later work leveraging contextual representations.
However, most existing resources are centered on English-language debates or social media, limiting direct transfer to French political discourse.
The 2017 French Election provides a natural stress test for adaptability due to rapid agenda shifts, multilingual media ecosystems, and evolving party coalitions.
We curate a corpus that interleaves campaign speeches, televised debates, and Twitter posts, annotated with MFT-derived concern values.
To examine task adaptability, we consider mappings between fine-grained moral cues and coarser concern categories used by different annotator groups.
To examine domain adaptability, we analyze shifts across platforms and time segments within the campaign timeline.
Our methodology compares label-space alignment techniques with representation-level adaptation under controlled data budgets.
We report performance under zero-shot, few-shot, and continual adaptation regimes to assess robustness and data efficiency.
Finally, we discuss implications for building portable concern detectors that remain stable under policy salience changes and linguistic variability.
We release data splits, annotation guidelines, and code to facilitate reproducibility and further research.

Cross-lingual/Multilingual Machine Reading Comprehension Hsu et al. (2019) investigate cross-lingual transfer capability of multilingual BERT (mBERT) on MRC tasks and find that zeroshot learning based on PLM is feasible, even between distant languages, such as English and Chinese. Various approaches have been proposed on top of multilingual MRC based on PLMs. Cui et al. (2019) propose a method that combines multilingual BERT and back-translation for cross-lingual MRC. In order to effectively leverage translation Different from the above studies, we mainly consider the impact of syntactic divergences between the source and target language in zero-shot crosslingual transfer based on multilingual PLMs, and attempt to disassociate semantics from syntax and only transfer semantic to the target language.

Disentangled Representation Learning Recently, there has been a growing amount of work on learning disentangled latent representations in NLP tasks (Zhang et al., 2019;Hu et al., 2017;Yin et al., 2018). In this aspect, the most related work to our syntax-semantics decoupling method is the vMF-Gaussian Variational Autoencoder (VGVAE) model proposed by Chen et al. (2019). It is a generative model using two latent variables to represent semantics and syntax of the sentence, developed for monolingual setting and trained with paraphrases. It uses paraphrase reconstruction loss and a discriminative paraphrase loss to learn semantic representations and word order information for syntactic representations. Recent cross-lingual MRC efforts explore translation-based augmentation, multilingual pre-training, and alignment supervision across typologically diverse languages without a unified protocol (Artetxe et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020; Asai et al., 2021; Clark et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2020; Chi et al., 2021). We adapt this model to multilingual syntax-semantics disentanglement. We use bilingual sentence pairs to train our model with a cross-lingual reconstruction loss and semantic discrimination loss. To better disentangle semantics from complex and diverse syntax in multilingual PLMs, we introduce two additional syntax-related losses for incorporating POS tags and syntax trees.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Document-level neural machine translation is an important task and has been abundantly studied with multiple datasets as well as methods.

The mainstream research in this field is the model architecture improvement. Specifically, several recent attempts extend the Sent2Sent approach to the Doc2Sent-like one. Wang et al. (2017); Miculicich et al. (2018); Tan et al. (2019) and Voita et al. (2019) introduce additional encoders or query layers with attention models and feed the history contexts into decoders. Maruf and Haffari (2018) and Tu et al. (2018) propose to augment NMT models with a cache-like memory network, which generates the translation depending on the decoder history retrieved from the memory.

Besides, some works intend to resolve this problem in other ways. Jean and Cho (2019) propose a regularization term for encouraging to focus more on the additional context using a multi-level pair-wise ranking loss. Yu et al. (2020) utilize a noisy channel reranker with Bayes' rule. Garcia et al. (2019) investigate hierarchical context fusion with sentence- and document-level attention. Tiedemann and Scherrer (2017) study concatenation-based context modeling for discourse phenomena. Bawden et al. (2018) introduce contrastive test sets for evaluating pronoun resolution in context-aware MT. Voita et al. (2019) analyze context usage with targeted evaluation and context-aware transformers. Zhang et al. (2020) explore dynamic context selection to mitigate noise in document-level translation. Miculicich et al. (2018) present a context-aware encoder-decoder with hierarchical attention over previous sentences. Tu et al. (2018) leverage a recurrent memory to capture cross-sentence dependencies in translation. Wang et al. (2017) propose cache-based NMT for improved lexical consistency across sentences. Maruf et al. (2019) develop a global context representation using graph neural networks over document structures.

There are also some works sharing similar ideas with us. Tiedemann and Scherrer (2017) and Bawden et al. (2017) explore concatenating two consecutive sentences and generate two sentences directly. Obviously, we leverage greatly longer information and capture the full context. Junczys-Dowmunt (2019) cuts documents into long segments and feeds them into training like BERT (Devlin et al., 2019). There are at least three main differences. Firstly, they need to add specific boundary tokens between sentences while we directly translate the original documents without any additional processing. Secondly, we propose a multi-resolutional training paradigm that shows consistent improvements compared with regular training. Thirdly, for extremely long documents, they restrict the segment length to 1000 tokens or make a truncation while we preserve entire documents and achieve literal document-to-document training and inference.

Finally, our work is also related to a series of studies in long sequence generation like GPT (Radford, 2018), GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019), and Transformer-XL (Dai et al., 2019). We suggest that deep neural generation models have the potential to process long-range sequences effectively.

spans.span: Recent advances in syntactic control span a variety of mechanisms and datasets, including parse-template conditioning (Iyyer et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2020), structured decoders over constituency or dependency trees (Zhang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020), latent-variable controls for style and syntax (Bao et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2018), and evaluation suites such as PARANMT, PPDB, and ParaNMT-50M that benchmark form-preserving rewrites (Wieting and Gimpel, 2018; Dolan and Brockett, 2005; Gupta et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019).

Lacks synthesis.document:
We focus primarily on the task of syntactically controlled paraphrase generation, which has recently attracted increasing attention (Iyyer et al., 2018;Chen et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2020;Kumar et al., 2020;Li et al., 2020). According to the control element, previous works can be divided into two categories. The first strand of research uses sentential exemplar as syntactic control. The second line relies on explicit structures, such as templates or parse trees, to constrain generation. Prior encoder–decoder architectures often treat tree information as side features attached to token sequences. This can make it difficult to capture hierarchical dependencies that extend beyond local n-gram windows. To address this, structural attention and composition functions have been explored for syntax-aware generation. Nevertheless, capturing both vertical and horizontal relations in a unified model remains challenging. Recent advances in syntactic control span a variety of mechanisms and datasets, including parse-template conditioning (Iyyer et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2020), structured decoders over constituency or dependency trees (Zhang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020), latent-variable controls for style and syntax (Bao et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2018), and evaluation suites such as PARANMT, PPDB, and ParaNMT-50M that benchmark form-preserving rewrites (Wieting and Gimpel, 2018; Dolan and Brockett, 2005; Gupta et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019). Differing from previous approaches, we propose a novel tree-transformer to model parent-child and sibling relation for better capturing the tree structure of the parse tree. Our design disentangles vertical and horizontal message passing while maintaining global contextualization. We instantiate separate attention heads for upward, downward, and lateral flows in the tree. This encourages the model to propagate constraints across complementary structural axes. To learn the alignment relation between words and nodes, we also propose an attention regularization objective, which makes the decoder accurately select corresponding syntax nodes to guide the generation of words. The loss encourages sparse, topology-consistent alignments between surface tokens and latent structural anchors. We derive supervision from automatically constructed word-to-node heuristics. These heuristics rely on head rules and span overlaps computed from the gold parse. Additionally, we propose a syntactic template retriever that can help to retrieve compatible syntactic structures for any input sentences. The retriever is trained with a contrastive loss over paired sentences and templates. It encodes inputs with a lightweight bi-encoder and indexes templates for efficient search. Retrieved templates serve as soft priors for the tree-transformer decoder. We evaluate our approach on multiple paraphrase benchmarks with gold parses. Metrics include semantic similarity, syntactic conformity, and fluency. We also conduct ablations to quantify the contribution of structural heads and alignment regularization. Results indicate consistent gains over baselines that do not explicitly model sibling relations. Qualitative analysis shows improved control over clause reordering and attachment. Error cases highlight limitations in long-range reattachment under noisy parses.

spans.span: Recent work on multimodal pretraining and grounding spans a broad spectrum of objectives and data regimes, including contrastive image–text alignment (Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2021), region-level grounding with phrase localization (Plummer et al., 2015; Akbari et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020), compositional reasoning benchmarks (Hudson and Manning, 2019; Johnson et al., 2017; Bahdanau et al., 2019), and emergent communication for symbol use in referential games (Lazaridou et al., 2017; Havrylov and Titov, 2017; Mordatch and Abbeel, 2018; Chaabouni et al., 2020).

Lacks synthesis.document:
Symbol Grounding. Contemporary grounders extensively utilize batch learning (e.g. Shridhar and Hsu (2018)). Yet, ITL requires incremental learning because without it the teacher guidance cannot influence the learner's inferences about plans as and when the advice is given. Further, many grounders assume that the learner starts out with a complete and accurate conceptualisation of the domain using pre-defined visual features and a known vocabulary (Kennington et al., 2015;Kennington and Schlangen, 2017;Wang et al., 2017). In ITL, both of these assumptions are unrealistic; therefore in this paper we explore models for which these assumptions don't apply. Finally, in contrast to all prior grounders, we support incremental learning when the training exemplars feature REs that are linguistically complex: e.g., "two red circles that aren't to the right of both green squares".

Representation Learning. Models for jointly learning a representation for vision and language utilize either explicit alignment via bounding boxes or instance segmentation (Lu et al., 2019;Chen et al., 2020;Tan and Bansal, 2019;Kamath et al., 2021;Yu et al., 2021), or a large-volume of weakly labeled data in the form of image-caption pairs (Radford et al., 2021). These models rely on offline learning with large datasets. This work, on the other hand, explores how to incrementally extract knowledge in a few-shot manner, using sequentially observed evidence that consists of weakly-labelled annotations, including neologisms.

Grounded Language Acquisition. This task is commonly realized as grounded grammar induction from image-caption pairs (Shi et al., 2019;Zhao and Titov, 2020), or as (neural) semantic parsers learning from a reward signal (Williams, 1992) in visual question answering Yi et al., 2018) or in planning (Azaria et al., 2016;Wang et al., 2016Wang et al., , 2017Karamcheti et al., 2020). In these scenarios, the primary objective is to learn mappings from linguistic expressions to logical forms, which in turn get associated with certain visual percepts during the learning process. This paper does not tackle learning logical forms. Instead, we obtain them from an existing broad-coverage grammar and focus on exploiting the logical consequences of those logical forms during symbol grounding-i.e., our focus is to utilise the interpretation of logical forms, and in particular the truth functional meanings of close-class words like quantifiers and negation, to inform the learning of mappings from (open-class) symbols like red to their denotations, given the visual percepts.

Visual Questions Answering (VQA) is a task of answering free-form questions about an image (Antol et al., 2015). VQA has reached impressive performance in recent years (Fukui et al., 2016;, yet VQA models struggle with out-of distribution generalization for new types of questions, requiring multi-step reasoning, with analysis revealing that they often rely on shortcuts (Jiang and Bansal, 2019;Subramanian et al., , 2020. Grounded VQA models like (Yi et al., 2018) and Bogin et al. (2021) tackle these shortcomings by learning to ground parts of the question and then learning to compose those parts via the question's syntax to compute the answer. They thus estimate denotations of linguistic parts that are not denoted by the answer to the question. By doing so, these models achieve out-of-distribution generalization for novel questions. However, these models lack the ITL's requirement for incremental learning: model training relies on batch learning. Furthermore, while their performance is impressive, error analysis shows that it tends to make mistakes on sentences containing logical concepts like quantifiers and negation (e.g. Bogin et al. (2021) Figure  shows that the determiner most incorrectly denotes an arbitrary subset of entities). Our view is that there is little benefit in trying to learn to ground these concepts as they are domain independent and can be interpreted using formal semantics. In our experiments, we are testing the extent to which knowing and reasoning with the logical meanings of these symbols helps incremental grounding, and in particular estimating denotations of symbols within an RE that aren't designated by that RE.

Visual Reference Resolution. In previous experimental setups, it is often assumed that there is a unique referent in the visual scene for the given RE in the test phase (e.g., Kazemzadeh et al. (2014); Whitney et al. (2016)). We aim to cope with situations where the RE has multiple referents: identifying all the referents that satisfy an RE enables efficient planning, because it affords free choice when executing certain commands-e.g., "move a circle to the left." when there is more than one circle affords choosing a control policy so that resources are optimized.

In this section, we discuss various attempts on N-NER corpora. As shown in Table , existing N-NER corpora are mostly high-resource languages, i.e., English and German, while Vietnamese is the only Asian language that has an N-NER dataset.

Prior work on nested named entity recognition has largely centered on English and German benchmarks with a mix of classical sequence labeling and span-based formulations, including ACE-2004 and ACE-2005 (Doddington et al., 2004; Walker et al., 2006), GENIA for biomedical entities (Kim et al., 2003; Ohta et al., 2002), OntoNotes-style conversions for nested spans (Pradhan et al., 2013; Finkel and Manning, 2009), and fine-grained resources such as NNE (Ringland et al., 2019) and NoSta-D (Benikova et al., 2014), alongside multilingual efforts like WikiAnn (Pan et al., 2017) and cross-lingual transfer via mBERT and XLM-R (Devlin et al., 2019; Conneau et al., 2020).

In terms of the number of classes, it is also worthnoting that three out of six corpora has less than ten and only NNE (Ringland et al., 2019) has more than 100 classes. The details of these corpora are given as follows. ACE-2004 (Doddington et al., 2004) and ACE-2005 (Walker et al., 2006) are early examples of N-NER datasets. ACE-2005 (Walker et al., 2006) dataset comprises 30,966 mentions from 12,548 sentences with 7 coarse-grained entity types. In addition to N-NER annotations, ACE-2005 also contains labels for other tasks such as recognition of relation and event extraction. GENIA introduces an N-NER data for bioinformatics. This project provides a high-quality corpus annotated for biological entity names. The dataset composed of 2,000 abstracts, 92,681 mentions from 9,533 sentences with 32 entity types.

NNE (Ringland et al., 2019) is a recent large finegrained N-NER dataset composed of 114 classes. Unlike previous N-NER corpora, the NNE dataset annotates entities with more details. For example, "6 September 2019", a date named entity mention, in the NNE dataset, each element in this mention is annotated with finer detail, "6" is annotated with day tag, "September" with month tag, and "2019" with year tag. NoSta-D (Benikova et al., 2014) DAN+ (Plank et al., 2020) presents the first N-NER dataset for Danish. This work investigates the possibility of transfer-learning between languages for the N-NER task. Moreover, DAN+ is a multi-domain dataset; they also study the challenges of domain-shift in their dataset. The dataset contains 6,425 mentions, 130,095 tokens, 4 classes from 6,867 sentences, obtained from multiple domains such as news and social media (Reddit, Twitter, and Arto). NoSta-D, VLSP-2018, and DAN+ have a modest corpus size and a small number of entity types comparing to the NNE dataset. This shows that there is still a resource gap for non-English corpora. On the other hand, for Thai, there are only coarsegrained flatten-NER datasets which are publicly available.

Methodologically, nested structures have been addressed through hypergraph models (Lu and Roth, 2015), layered CRFs (Ju et al., 2018), region-based or span classification (Sohrab and Miwa, 2018; Wang et al., 2020), constituency-inspired parsers (Finkel and Manning, 2009), sequence-to-nugget decoders (Zhang et al., 2020), and transition systems (Wang and Lu, 2018), with pre-trained encoders such as BERT, SpanBERT, and SciBERT (Devlin et al., 2019; Joshi et al., 2020; Beltagy et al., 2019), as well as datasets spanning legal, news, and biomedical domains (GENIA; ACE-2005; LitBank; NoSta-D).

Prior approaches focused on framing DST as question answering (Ruan et al., 2020;Ma et al., 2020;Zhang et al., 2021). Many MultiWoZ cross-domain models leverage slot names/descriptions (Wu et al., 2019;Lin et al., 2021a).

Pretrained generative LLMs (Raffel et al., 2020;Brown et al., 2020) have enable framing NLP tasks as seq2seq problems. Some DST papers (Zhao et al., 2021a;Feng et al., 2021) look at settings with no train-test discrepancy. Many studies explore the efficacy of task-specific prompts (Jiang et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2021). Madotto et al. (2020) prime LMs with examples for dialogue tasks, but without finetuning. Wei et al. (2021) fine-tune language models to understand prompts for a different task. A broader line of work examines prompt-based and instruction-tuned approaches across diverse NLP tasks without restricting to dialogue state tracking, including pattern-exploiting training and automatic prompt search (Schick and Schütze, 2021; Gao et al., 2021), calibration and template engineering for zero-shot classification (Zhao et al., 2021b; Holtzman et al., 2021), chain-of-thought prompting and rationale-augmented decoding (Wei et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023), in-context learning with retrieval or demonstration selection (Rubin et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022), and instruction tuning with mixtures of datasets such as FLAN, T0, and Super-NaturalInstructions (Sanh et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022).

Despite these advances, DST in noisy, multi-domain settings remains challenging due to annotation inconsistencies and slot ontology drift. The literature has also examined leveraging semi-structured knowledge and schema linking to reduce manual engineering. Recent benchmarks highlight brittleness to paraphrase and domain shift, motivating approaches that better separate representation from ontology-specific constraints. We focus on settings with limited supervised data and heterogeneous slot formulations. Our study targets cross-domain generalization under realistic distribution shift and weak supervision. We compare generative and discriminative formulations while controlling for prompt design and calibration. We further analyze failure modes related to long-context dialogues and compositional slot dependencies. Finally, we discuss implications for robust deployment and evaluation protocols in evolving task ontologies.

Lacks synthesis.document:
Introduction Textual EL has matured with robust benchmarks and methods, yet entity-centric applications increasingly involve images and text together in the wild. There is vast prior research on textual entity linking. Multiple datasets have been proposed over the years including the manuallyannotated high-quality datasets like AIDA (Hoffart et al., 2011), automatically-annotated large-scale datasets like CWEB (Guo and Barbosa, 2018) and zero-shot datasets like Zeshel (Logeswaran et al., 2019). To evaluate the EL models' performance, it is usual to train on the AIDA-train dataset, and test on the datasets of AIDA-test, MSNBC (Cucerzan, 2007), AQUAINT (Milne and Witten, 2008), DBpedia Spotlight (Daiber et al., 2013), TAC-KBP EL (Ji et al., 2010), and WNED (Guo and Barbosa, 2018). Recent neural models span local-collective graph approaches (Ganea and Hofmann, 2017), bi-encoder and cross-encoder retrievers (Gillick et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020), span-based disambiguation with pre-trained transformers (Yamada et al., 2020), and end-to-end EL pipelines over Wikipedia/Wikidata (Kolitsas et al., 2018; Broscheit, 2019). Additional resources include Wikipedia hyperlinks (Spitkovsky et al., 2012), Wikidata descriptions (Vrandečić and Krötzsch, 2014), and cross-lingual corpora such as Mewsli-9 (Botha et al., 2020). However, as mentioned in (Cao et al., 2021), many methods have achieved high and similar results within recent three years. One possible explanation is that it may simply be near the ceiling of what can be achieved for these datasets, and it is difficult to conduct further research based on them. This observation motivates a closer look at settings where textual context alone is insufficient for disambiguation.

Background and Motivation Multimodal EL aims to ground mentions in text to a knowledge base while leveraging complementary visual cues to reduce ambiguity. In recent years, the growing trend towards multimodality requires to extend the research of EL from monomodality to multimodality. Moon et al. (2018), Zhang et al. (2020), Chen et al. (2021), and Peng (2021) propose three MEL datasets, which are built from Weibo, Wikipedia, and Richpedia information and use CNDBpedia, Wikidata, and Richpedia as the corresponding KBs, alongside related benchmarks such as XMEL (Zhang et al., 2022), WikiDiverse-MEL (Liu et al., 2023), and WebQSP-Vis (Huang et al., 2022). Methods range from visual-semantic alignment via multimodal transformers (Lu et al., 2019; Tan and Bansal, 2019), cross-modal contrastive pretraining (Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021), entity-aware visual grounding (Kim et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021), and fusion-based disambiguation with region features (Anderson et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019). Datasets for related tasks include entity-centric image-caption corpora (Biten et al., 2019; Tran et al., 2020), multimodal NER (Lu et al., 2018; Arshad et al., 2021), and multimodal relation extraction (Zheng et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021). However, using Wikipedia as the target dataset may lead to the data leakage problem as many language models are pretrained on it. Prior work has also noted that noisy social media images and informal text present new failure modes for canonical EL pipelines.

Problem Setting and Contributions We formulate multimodal entity linking as ranking KB candidates given a mention, its textual context, and associated images. We define a candidate generation step based on surface forms and cross-modal retrieval, followed by a re-ranking model that fuses text and vision. Our MEL dataset is also related to other named entity-related multimodal datasets, including entityaware image caption datasets (Biten et al., 2019;Tran et al., 2020;, multimodal NER datasets Lu et al., 2018), etc. However, the entities in these datasets are not linked to a unified KB. So our research of MEL can enhance the understanding of named entities, thereby enhancing the research in these areas. We present three contributions: a carefully curated and leakage-aware MEL benchmark, a strong fusion-based baseline with interpretable cross-modal signals, and an analysis of where vision most improves disambiguation. We further release standardized evaluation scripts to encourage reproducible comparison across future methods.

Related Work: Modeling Approaches Early multimodal EL used late fusion with separate text and image encoders and simple heuristics for entity priors. Recent works adopt unified transformers with cross-attention to align tokens and visual regions, enabling fine-grained grounding signals. Contrastive pretraining has proven useful for robust representations, while knowledge-aware adapters inject KB semantics without retraining full backbones. Our work builds on these insights by integrating candidate-aware prompts and visual-region gating into the re-ranker, tailored to mitigate leakage and ambiguity.

Related Work: Evaluation and Fairness Evaluation protocols for MEL vary widely in negative sampling, candidate set size, and use of in-KB versus NIL labels. Leakage-aware splits, rigorous ablations over vision availability, and cross-domain generalization remain under-specified in many benchmarks. We therefore articulate a transparent protocol, report per-entity-type breakdowns, and include analyses under missing or misleading images to provide a reliable basis for future research.

Lacks synthesis.document: Our contributions add to a large body of work on grounded representation learning. Much of this work augments language modeling objectives with images (Silberer and Lapata, 2012;Lazaridou et al., 2015;Kiela et al., 2017) and videos (Sun et al., 2019). In this work, we focus on representations that encode verb semantics. Prior work on verb learning has been conducted in the computer vision community, typically described as "humanobject interactions" (Regneri et al., 2013;Chao et al., 2018;Ji et al., 2019). In contrast, we focus on learning representations from trajectory data. We are not aware of any prior work that attempts to learn verb semantics from trajectory data. However, prior work in grounded language learning focuses on reasoning about objects through space and time in text (Aroca-Ouellette et al., 2021) and grounding to 3D objects with varying rotation (Thomas, 2019). Outside of NLP, models have been trained on trajectory data for applications like human motion path forecasting (Giuliari et al., 2021) and human activity recognition (Wang et al., 2018). Recent multimodal grounding approaches integrate contrastive objectives, masked modeling, and alignment losses across text, image, audio, and video, with large-scale datasets enabling pretraining at web scale (Radford et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Bain et al., 2021; Alayrac et al., 2022; Zellers et al., 2021; Dong et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2021; Lei et al., 2021), while compositional generalization and structured grounding have been explored via synthetic benchmarks and neuro-symbolic pipelines (Lake and Baroni, 2018; Johnson et al., 2017; Mao et al., 2019; Hudson and Manning, 2019; Bahdanau et al., 2019; Nye et al., 2021; Yi et al., 2020; Gupta et al., 2019). Our work lies at the intersection of grounded language learning and spatiotemporal machine learning, using representations of trajectory data to study verb semantics. We situate our method relative to prior grounded language research by emphasizing temporal reasoning and motion-centric cues. Specifically, we concentrate on the mapping between discrete linguistic predicates and continuous kinematic traces. This focus allows us to examine action granularity beyond categorical labels tied to static visual frames. We also explore whether trajectory-derived embeddings capture relational structure among verbs. To that end, we evaluate lexical and event similarity judgments using movement-based features. Finally, we discuss the implications of trajectory alignment for context-sensitive verb interpretation. We conclude by outlining how spatiotemporal priors can complement text-only distributional learning.

spans.span: Mishra et al., 21

Format.document: Semantic parsing via paraphrasing began with Berant and Liang (2014), who proposed completing the mapping through an intermediate natural-language reformulation. Subsequent work generated canonical paraphrase candidates from grammars and scored partial derivations against target formal languages (Wang et al., 2015; Marzoev et al., 2020). However, these methods largely predated and therefore did not exploit pretrained sequence models for generating paraphrases. Compositional generalization remains central because formal languages are inherently compositional. Approaches inject inductive bias via modular architectures (Dong and Lapata, 2018), symbolic-neural hybrids, and latent-variable or intermediate representations (Zheng and Lapata, 2020) alongside program-like learning signals (Lake, 2019). A complementary line performs data augmentation to expand combinatorial coverage before training (Andreas, 2019; Zhong et al., 2020; Akyürek et al., 2020). Pretrained encoders and decoders have also improved compositional parsing performance (Oren et al., 2020; Furrer et al., 2020). Prompt-based methods span tuning-free cloze prompting (Petroni et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2020) and few-shot in-context learning (Brown et al., 2020; Shin et al., 2021). Parameter-efficient prompt tuning reduces adaptation cost while preserving strong performance (Li and Liang, 2021; Schucher et al., 2021; Qin and Eisner, 2021; Liu et al., 2021b), and fixed-prompt LM tuning aligns with our setting. Related work also explores prompt decomposition during tuning-free prompting by Mishra et al., 21, with corroborating results on other NLP tasks. In parallel, zero-shot pretrained models show stronger out-of-distribution robustness than fine-tuned counterparts, motivating weight ensembling and model editing for robustness transfer (Wortsman et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2021).

Format.document: Discrete Prompts The release of GPT-3 Brown et al. 2020) has led to interest in prompting, a new way to leverage pretrained language models (PLM). Brown et al. (2020) proposes an intuitive in-context learning paradigm by concatenating a few input and output examples and feeding them to the language model and let the model autoregressively generate answers for new examples. Recent works (Petroni et al., 2019; Davison et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2020) design prompts to probe the factual and commonsense knowledge encoded within a PLM. Recent works (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b; Gao et al., 2021) demonstrate that even smaller PLMs have similar few-shot learning capacity. Le Scao and Rush (2021) analyzes the effect of prompting and concludes that a single prompt may be worth 100 training examples in fine-tuning. Instead of manually designing prompts (i.e., prompt engineering), some recent studies also explore automatic prompt generation. PETAL (Schick et al., 2020) augments Pattern Exploiting Training (PET, Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b) with automatically identified label words; Gao et al., 2021 uses re-ranking to find the best label words by fine-tuning a RoBERTa model on the candidates searched by RoBERTa, and using an external generation model for data augmentation of prompt templates; AutoPrompt (Shin et al., 2020) uses a gradient-based search to determine both prompts and label words. However, these methods require parameter updates with gradient descent, which is infeasible without access to the model weights (e.g., GPT-3). PET and its variants also require a large unlabeled set and need to be fine-tuned multiple times. AutoPrompt uses discretization techniques to approximately map a continuous vector back to tokens in the vocabulary (i.e., "vocablization"). These searched prompts and labels are often uninterpretable by humans, and, different from these prior studies, our proposed AMuLaP is a simple and interpretable method for few-shot prompting that can work well with and without access to model weights, while concurrently to our work others propose a method that exploits an external knowledge base to find label mapping.

spans.span: (Conneau et al., 2020)

Format.document: The state of NLP in South Asia remains uneven across languages and tasks. Initiatives aimed at language technology have tended to prioritize officially recognized and standardized languages. Prominent resources include the EMILLE corpus (McEnery et al., 2000), IndicNLP Suite (Kakwani et al., 2020), and iNLTK (Arora, 2020). Community-building has been catalyzed by workshops such as DravidianLangTech (Chakravarthi et al., 2021) and WILDRE (Jha et al., 2020). Nevertheless, as survey tables consistently show, only a minority of regional languages benefit from sustained NLP research or consumer-facing tools. Computational historical linguistics intersects with core NLP activities including corpus construction, POS tagging, morphological analysis, and dependency parsing. For high-resource languages like Hindi, large hand-annotated treebanks support state-of-the-art neural modeling. Recent transformer models and pretraining pipelines have delivered strong performance for Hindi across semantics and transfer (Jain et al., 2020; Khanuja et al., 2021). Parallel resources and systems further enable robust English–Hindi translation and transliteration (Saini and Sahula, 2018). Yet sizable gaps persist for what Joshi et al. term the “Left-Behinds,” especially among minority and endangered languages (Joshi et al., 2020). Linguists have compiled small treebanks for languages such as Palula and Toda that await digitization and conversion to Universal Dependencies (Liljegren and Haider, 2015; Emeneau, 1984). New UD releases have begun to appear for Kangri, Mandeali, Bhojpuri, and Magahi (Ojha and Zeman, 2020). Historical and comparative linguistics in South Asia traces back to grammatical traditions associated with Pāṇini and Hemacandra. Following the recognition of the Indo‑European family, systematic comparative studies took root in the region. Influential grammars survey the Dravidian family (Caldwell, 1856; Andronov, 2003; Krishnamurti, 2003) and the Indo‑Aryan family (Beames, 1872; Hoernlé, 1880; Bloch, 1934; Masica, 1993). Emeneau introduced the notion of a South Asian linguistic area that cuts across genealogical boundaries (Emeneau, 1956). Subsequent micro‑areal work sheds light on contact and convergence dynamics (Peterson, 2017; Liljegren et al., 2021; Toulmin, 2006). The Linguistic Survey of India remains the only subcontinent‑wide undertaking of its scope (Grierson, 1903–1928). No comparably comprehensive, centralized repository covering lexicon, typology, and sociolinguistics has emerged since. Early comparativists often drew data from prestige standards like Delhi Hindi, with localized lects documented in a piecemeal fashion. Major reference works include the Comparative Dictionary of the Indo‑Aryan Languages (Turner, 1962–1966) and the Dravidian Etymological Dictionary (Burrow and Emeneau, 1984). Documentation of Austroasiatic languages has grown, though secondary analyses sometimes overgeneralize from limited primary data (Anderson, 2008). In NLP, corpus development and annotation workflows remain the main bottlenecks for many under-resourced languages. Multilingual pretraining has helped transfer representations across related scripts and families, as shown in (Conneau et al., 2020). However, domain mismatch, orthographic variation, and data scarcity still hamper downstream robustness. Progress also depends on open licensing, ethical data governance, and sustained community partnerships. For cross-lingual modeling, tokenization and script normalization require careful adaptation to Brahmic orthographies. Shared tasks have begun to benchmark morphological inflection, segmentation, and parsing for smaller languages. Nevertheless, many benchmarks underrepresent colloquial registers, code-mixing, and non‑standard spellings. Resource catalogs that integrate metadata on scripts, dialects, and domains can guide investment and reuse. As demonstrated in Kakwani et al. (2020), cross‑lingual toolchains can reduce duplication of effort when extended thoughtfully. This survey synthesizes the current landscape, emphasizing opportunities where modest curation could yield large gains. We conclude by outlining evaluation practices and reproducible baselines tailored to South Asian languages.

Format.document: Previously, most length-controllable approaches in abstractive summarization focused on stopping decoding at a particular time. An early ad-hoc approach (Rush et al., 2015) generated the EOS token by assigning a score of −∞ to tokens in the vocabulary and produced a fixed number of words. LenEmb and LenInit introduced length embeddings into the decoder to guide generation (Kikuchi et al., 2016). LC incorporated the desired length into the first layer of a CNN encoder (Liu et al., 2018). Fan et al. (2018) predefined special markers to denote different length ranges and prepended inputs with such markers during training and testing. Takase and Okazaki (2019) extended sinusoidal positional encoding to account for stepwise remaining length. GOLC optimized LenEmb and LC by formalizing a loss with an overlength penalty (Makino et al., 2019). Bian et al. (2019) treated LenInit and LenEmb as an agent and adjusted the reward to incorporate the desired length. LenAtten added a length attention unit to exploit length information based on the stepwise remaining length (Yu et al., 2021). Other length-controllable approaches determined content via length-aware intermediate summaries. LPAS extracted a word sequence with the desired length from the source document and generated a summary using a non–length-controllable model conditioned on the document and the extracted sequence (Saito et al., 2020). MLS first produced a general summary and then fed it to a length-controllable model (Sarkhel et al., 2020). Compared with previous methods, our approach controls the length of generated summaries by pretraining a length-aware information selection model on a length-balanced dataset. It can also generate summaries with length close to the target in zero-shot length control. This design avoids brittle length tokens while maintaining content fidelity across varying budgets. In addition, the model exposes an interpretable knob that can be adjusted without retraining. We further analyze how content selection interacts with compression under strict constraints. Empirically, we show consistent improvements across news and scientific domains. Our ablations confirm that learning to select yields better controllability than learning to stop. Recently, many studies fine-tune pretrained transformer seq2seq models on summarization datasets (Lewis et al., 2020; Zhang et al. 2020. These baselines achieve strong ROUGE improvements with minimal task-specific engineering. Our approach is implemented atop a transformer seq2seq model and can be combined with pretrained checkpoints without modification. We emphasize that our mechanism is orthogonal to architectural changes such as pointer networks or coverage penalties. By decoupling selection from realization, the method generalizes across compression ratios. Prior work on budgeted summarization explores token-level knapsack objectives and reinforcement learning. However, such methods often require delicate reward shaping and can be unstable. Curriculum strategies that gradually tighten length constraints have also been proposed. In contrast, we enforce the target budget directly via an auxiliary selection head. Length-conditioned planning is further supported by content salience predictors derived from extractive signals. We hypothesize that explicit selection encourages the decoder to avoid verbosity. To probe this claim, we measure off-target overflow and underflow relative to the requested budget. We also analyze sensitivity to mis-specified length prompts at inference time. The results indicate robust adherence up to moderate distribution shifts in desired lengths. Moreover, human raters prefer our outputs when budgets are extreme, suggesting better prioritization. Our contributions are threefold: a simple selection module for precise length control, a training recipe for balanced supervision, and a comprehensive evaluation under strict budgets. We release code and data splits to facilitate reproducibility and further research.

spans.span: Dai et al. (2021

Format.document:
Multimodal sentiment analysis has gained increasing attention from the community recently and some process has been made. In general, there are three findings presented by previous work.

Performing the cross-modal alignment is helpful for multimodal feature fusion. considered that the holistic features mainly contain global information, which may fail to capture local information. Therefore, they applied the force-alignment to align the visual and acoustic features with the words and further obtained the word-level features. To effectively fuse them, they proposed the GME-LSTM(A) model, which consists of two modules, the gated multimodal embedding and the LSTM with the temporal attention. However, obtaining the word-level features needs to perform the force-alignment, which is time-consuming. To address it, proposed the MulT model, which uses the crossmodal attention to align different modal features implicitly. Instead of performing the alignment in the time dimension, some works focusing on semantic alignment. Hazarika et al. (2020) considered that the semantic gaps between heterogeneous data could hurt the model performance and proposed the MISA model, which maps the different modal data into a shared space before multimodal feature fusion. first utilized the cross-modal prediction task to distinguish the shared and private semantics of non-textual modalities compared to the textual modality and then fuse them. The above works show that performing the cross-modal alignment is helpful for multimodal feature fusion.

Training the MSA models in an end-to-end manner is more effective. Most of the previous studies adopt a two-phase pipeline, first extracting unimodal features and then fusing them. Dai et al. (2021 considered that it may lead to suboptimal performance since the extracted unimodal features are fixed and cannot be further improved benefiting from the downstream supervisory signals. Therefore, they proposed the multimodal endto-end sparse model, which can optimize the unimodal feature extraction and multimodal feature fusion jointly. The experimental results on the multimodal emotion detection task show that training the models in an end-to-end manner can obtain better results than the pipeline models.

Leveraging the unimodal sentiment labels to learn more informative unimodal representations is useful for multimodal feature fusion. Yu et al. (2020) considered that introducing the unimodal sentiment labels can help the model capture the unimodal sentiment information and model the difference between modalities. Motivated by it, they built the CH-SIMS dataset, which contains not only the multimodal sentiment labels but also unimodal sentiment labels. And based on it, they proposed a multi-task learning framework to leverage two types of sentiment labels simultaneously. However, this method needs unimodal labels, which is absent for most of the existing datasets. To address it, Yu et al. (2021) proposed the Self-MM model, which first generates the unimodal labels by utilizing the relationship between the unimodal and multimodal labels and then uses the multi-task learning to train the model. These two works both address the usefulness of introducing unimodal labels.

However, even though lots of models are proposed and obtain promising results on the benchmark datasets, there are few works considering the noisy inputs when the MSA models are deployed in the real world. presented the Gated Multimodal Embedding to filter out the noises from the acoustic and visual data. Pham et al. (2019) considered that visual and acoustic data may be absent and proposed the MCTN model to handle it. and Mittal et al. (2020) also mainly focused on dealing with the noises introduced by the visual and acoustic data, and their models are based on the word-level features, which are obtained by aligning the audios with the gold texts. There is only one work (Dumpala et al., 2018) considering that the texts are output by the ASR models, which may be erroneous. But this work does not study how do the ASR errors affect the MSA models and does not evaluate the SOTA MSA models on the datasets. Besides, the proposed model needs the gold texts when training, which is time-consuming and labor-consuming.

Comparing to the above works, we evaluate the SOTA MSA models on the real-world datasets and observe that the performance of models decreases sharply because of the erroneous ASR texts. Through in-depth analysis of the ASR outputs, we find the sentiment word substitution error in the ASR texts could hurt the MSA models directly. To address it, we propose the sentiment word aware multimodal refinement model, which only uses the ASR texts in the training and testing phrases. We further discuss ethical considerations around annotation noise and deployment in sensitive applications. Overall, our analysis highlights the need for robustness-aware architectures and evaluation protocols in multimodal sentiment research.

Format.document: In this paper, we study sequence-to-sequence generation with an encoder–decoder architecture grounded in self-attention. We adopt the Transformer to instantiate both encoder and decoder components (Vaswani et al., 2017 and follow a standard maximum-likelihood objective. To simplify exposition, we focus on a minimal configuration that isolates self-attention while omitting positional encodings and deep stacking. The encoder maps the input sequence X into contextual representations H using multihead self-attention and feed‑forward sublayers (Gehring et al., 2017; Devlin et al., 2019). The decoder conditions on H to generate outputs autoregressively with causal self-attention, cross-attention to the source, and a softmax prediction layer. At time step i, previously generated word embeddings are packed into key and value matrices by a projection function M, yielding K_{i−1} and V_{i−1}. A self-attention block produces a target-side representation s_i that summarizes the partial hypothesis and its dependencies. We then compute a context vector c_i using cross-attention over the encoder states, parameterized by key and value transformations of H. The resulting distribution P_g(y_i | y_{<i}, X) is computed by an MLP followed by normalization, and the most probable token is selected. To avoid the noises caused by global features, methods (Malinowski et al., 2018) introduce various image attention mechanisms into VQA. Instead of directly using visual features from CNN-based feature extractors, to improve the performance of the model, BUTD (Anderson et al., 2018) adopts Faster R-CNN (Ren et al., 2015) to obtain candidate regional features, while Pythia (Jiang et al., 2018) integrates the regional feature with grid-level features. Meanwhile, Lu et al. (2016) and Nam et al. (2017) put more attention on learning better question representations. To merge information from different modalities sufficiently, MFB (Yu et al., 2017) and MUTAN (Ben-Younes et al., 2017) explore higher-order fusion methods. Further, BAN (Kim et al., 2018) and DCN (Nguyen and Okatani, 2018) propose dense co-attention models which directly establish interaction between modalities with word-level and regional features. Moreover, with the proposal of the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), MCAN and DFAF (Gao et al., 2019) adopt self-attention mechanisms to fully excavate the fine-grained information contained in text and image. Meanwhile, to fully cover the holistic scene in an image, MuREL (Cadène et al., 2019) and ReGAT (Li et al., 2019) explicitly incorporate relations between regions into the interaction process. Selvaraju et al. (2020) also introduce sub-questions into their work; the distinctness between us is that it constructs a Sub-VQA dataset for a subset of reasoning questions in the VQA dataset to evaluate consistency of VQA models, while we adopt sub-questions to achieve task dividing. Beyond architectural advances, large-scale pretraining on image–text pairs has become a de facto prerequisite for strong VQA performance (Lu et al., 2019; Tan and Bansal, 2019; Li et al., 2020). Such pretraining encourages models to align visual regions and linguistic phrases, which is later specialized via fine-tuning on VQA benchmarks (Goyal et al., 2017; Antol et al., 2015). However, a growing body of work documents that shortcut reasoning and language priors can still dominate predictions, resulting in inconsistent behavior under distribution shift (Agrawal et al., 2018; Cadene et al., 2019). Recent benchmarks therefore emphasize counterfactual evaluation, compositional generalization, and consistency across related question sets (Hudson and Manning, 2019; Kervadec et al., 2021). In parallel, research has examined the role of region proposals versus dense grids, reporting complementary benefits when both are available to the fusion module (Jiang et al., 2018; Anderson et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2020). Despite these advances, modeling multi-step reasoning over scenes with coreference and temporal cues remains challenging for current architectures (Zellers et al., 2019; Le et al., 2020). Visual Dialogue. Different from VQA, visual dialogue (VD) is a continuous conversation grounded in images and prior turns (Das et al., 2017). Several VD tasks—Visual Dialog, GuessWhich (Chattopadhyay et al., 2017), GuessWhat?! (de Vries et al., 2017), and MMD (Saha et al., 2018)—have been proposed. GuessWhat?!, as a goal-directed dialogue task, requires both players to continuously clarify the reference object through dialogue. The Oracle provides the Questioner with relevant information about the target object by constantly answering yes or no questions, and the Guesser generates the final answer based on the historical dialogue. Following this setting, our Co-VQA framework consists of three components in which the Questioner raises sub-questions, the Oracle answers them one by one, and finally the Answerer obtains the answer to the original question. Prior work in VD has highlighted the importance of leveraging co-reference resolution across turns and grounding follow-up questions in visual context (Kottur et al., 2018; Niu et al., 2019). Under this perspective, we position our approach at the intersection of compositional reasoning and dialogue-aware grounding, building on recent developments in self-attention architectures in (Vaswani et al., 2017. Format.document: Studying persuasiveness in argumentation is an active field of research. Beyond planning content, structure, and style, researchers also consider audience-based features to model persuasiveness. Among these, Durmus and Cardie (2018) and El Baff et al. (2020) analyze how factors such as religion and political background affect outcomes. Al Khatib et al. (2020) further show that user-based features reflecting beliefs, characteristics, and personality can improve prediction of argument success. Moral foundations offer a conceptual model for understanding everyday judgments (Haidt and Joseph, 2004). Liberals emphasize care and fairness, whereas conservatives weigh all foundations more evenly, with a tilt toward loyalty, authority, and purity (Graham et al., 2009). Empirical studies corroborate the theory across behaviors and decisions (Feinberg and Willer, 2015; Fulgoni et al., 2016; Johnson and Goldwasser, 2018). For computational analysis, Kobbe et al. (2020) annotate moral foundations in arguments and link them to quality. We use their corpus to evaluate a moral classifier and to study belief-aware generation. Argument generation has been explored for multiple tasks, including counter-argument generation (Hua et al., 2019; Alshomary et al., 2021b). Other work opposes a given claim (Bilu et al., 2015; Hidey and McKeown, 2019), produces topic-controlled claims (Schiller et al., 2020), or reconstructs implicit conclusions (Alshomary et al., 2020; Syed et al., 2021). However, few approaches aim to tailor argumentative text to a specific audience. Belief-based claim generation addresses this gap by seeking claims aligned with audience stances Alshomary et al. 2021a. Project Debater provides a large-scale system for mining, retrieving, and generating arguments (Slonim et al., 2021). Its hybrid pipeline combines retrieval, mining, clustering, and rephrasing, yielding competitive quality in manual assessments (Slonim et al., 2021). We build on this system to generate morally framed claims and isolate the effect of moral framing on audiences.

Format.document: The game of Mafia is particularly well-suited for the goal of determining whether the deceptive participants in a conversation can be identified from the contents of their utterances. As a social deduction game, Mafia elicits strategic lying and nuanced truth-telling under time pressure. This environment provides repeated, high-stakes interactions that approximate real-world deception while remaining ethically tractable. Unlike laboratory lie-detection protocols that isolate single statements, Mafia sessions produce long, interactive dialogues rich in pragmatic cues. These dialogues combine persuasion, accusation, and coalition formation, offering a natural testbed for computational models. In this paper we introduce a corpus of transcribed Mafia games annotated for speaker role and deception episodes. We study whether lexical, semantic, and discourse features are sufficient to identify deceptive speech without access to prosody or facial signals. Our approach treats deception detection as a supervised classification problem over utterance-level segments. We compare traditional bag-of-words baselines with pretrained transformer encoders adapted to conversational structure. To control for topical confounds, we design adversarial splits that prevent trivial memorization of player-specific idiolects. We further analyze feature importance and error patterns to understand when models succeed and fail. We position our work within the broader literature on deception in text and dialogue. Prior studies have examined stylistic markers such as function word rates, hedging, negation, and sentiment polarity. Other work explores discourse phenomena including contradiction, stance shifts, and turn-taking asymmetries in deceptive exchanges. Prosodic analyses of deception in laboratory dialogues report complementary cues, as in Levitan et al. 2018, though our focus is strictly lexical. Games and gamified protocols have also been proposed to simulate motivated reasoning and strategic communication. Compared with interview-style datasets, Mafia conversations offer contested claims, public evidence, and adversarial questioning at scale. From a methodological perspective, our study contributes a new multimodal alignment of utterances, timestamps, and player states. We release clear annotation guidelines that distinguish performative role-playing from intentional concealment of private information. We also quantify the extent to which deception correlates with role, pressure, and network centrality across sessions. Our baseline features include n-grams, dependency fragments, discourse markers, and conversation-level aggregation statistics. For neural models, we fine-tune a dialogue-aware encoder with segment embeddings, speaker tags, and relative turn indices. We evaluate accuracy, macro F1, and area under the precision–recall curve across multiple cross-validation folds. Robustness is assessed via counterfactual data augmentation that flips role labels while preserving lexical content where possible. We conduct ablation studies to measure the contribution of context window size, speaker history, and training-set balance. Human subject experiments provide upper bounds by asking annotators to identify deceptive utterances using text only. Qualitative analysis surfaces recurrent strategies such as vague quantification, evidential distancing, and selective agreement. Finally, we discuss ethical considerations, dataset licensing, and guidelines for responsible deployment in applied settings.

Format.document: Text attribute transfer has a vast literature with deep learning methods becoming popular (Jin et al., 2020a). The problem typically involves rewriting a sentence to alter a salient attribute while preserving the underlying content. Approaches are commonly divided into supervised and unsupervised families. Supervised methods repurpose sequence to sequence models used in machine translation to achieve the goals (Rao and Tetreault, 2018). However, collecting parallel corpora for every attribute pair is costly and often impractical. As a result, unsupervised methods that rely on weak or pseudo parallel signals have become prominent. Disentanglement based architectures were among the first to dominate unsupervised attribute transfer. In these models, content and attributes are separated in a latent representation to enable targeted manipulation. A popular tactic is to train an encoder while adversarially discouraging attribute information in the shared content space (Fu et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2018a; John et al., 2019). Yet the literature has paid comparatively little attention to defining and preserving content beyond surface heuristics. Cycle consistency encourages that a transformed sentence, when mapped back, reconstructs the source, thereby serving as a weak content proxy (Prabhumoye et al., 2018; Logeswaran et al., 2018; Dai et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2020; Yi et al., 2020). Despite its utility, cycle enforcement can be computationally heavy or require reinforcement learning to handle discrete text. Moreover, over reliance on reconstruction may inadvertently penalize legitimate paraphrases that improve fluency or coherence. Recent work has thus explored alternatives that directly model content similarity with learned objectives. Transformer based models, pretrained at scale, have accelerated this shift Dai et al., 2019; Krishna et al., 2020. However, many transformer systems still lack explicit mechanisms to preserve semantic relations that must remain invariant under style edits. For example, named entities, quantities, and event roles should persist unless the target attribute logically demands change. Several studies measure this persistence using content word overlap or entailment scores, but these proxies are imperfect (Logeswaran et al., 2018; Yi et al., 2020). Contrastive learning provides a principled alternative by pulling matched content pairs together while pushing mismatched pairs apart in representation space. When combined with attribute conditioning, such objectives can reduce leakage between style and content factors (Huang et al., 2020). Our framework formalizes content preservation as a set of constraints over entities, sentiment independent facts, and syntactic scaffolds. We then implement lightweight, differentiable losses that approximate these constraints without requiring full cycle reconstruction. Unlike prior disentanglement pipelines that depend on fragile adversarial games, our approach integrates smoothly with pretrained encoders (Subramanian et al., 2018). We also analyze failure modes where attribute control conflicts with content fidelity and propose calibration strategies for decoding. Empirically, we evaluate on sentiment, formality, and toxicity transfer using standardized splits and automatic metrics. Human evaluations further assess meaning preservation, grammaticality, and attribute strength to complement automatic scores. The results indicate consistent gains in content faithfulness with competitive style control across diverse domains. We conclude by outlining open questions on controllability, evaluation, and fairness that future work should address.

Format.document:
Given a set of entities E and a set of relations R, a knowledge graph K ⊆ E × R × E is a collection of subject-predicate-object (s, p, o) triples. Link prediction is the task of predicting missing triples in K by answering queries of the form of (s, p, ?) and (?, p, o). This is typically accomplished using knowledge graph embedding (KGE) models.

Conventional KGEs assign an embedding vector for each entity and relation in the KG. They model the plausibility of (s, p, o) triples via model specific scoring functions f (e s , e p , e o ) using the subject (e s ), predicate (e p ) and object (e o ) specific embeddings. Once trained, these embeddings are used for downstream tasks such as question answering.

Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) is the task of answering a natural language question using a KG as source of knowledge. The questions can be either simple factual questions that require a single fact retrieval (e.g. What language is spoken in India?), or they can be complex questions that require reasoning over multiple facts in the KG (e.g. What is the predominant religion where the leader is Ovadia Yosef?). KGEs can be utilized to perform KGQA when the background KGs are incomplete.

In the next few sections we will go into more detail about existing work on KGEs and KGQA.

Early translational models represent relations as translations in the embedding space and encourage s + p ≈ o under a chosen norm. Bilinear models instead parameterize relations as matrices and compute interactions via multiplicative forms that capture symmetry and antisymmetry. More recent neural models compose entity and relation features through non-linear transformations that can adapt to diverse relational patterns. Training commonly relies on margin or logistic losses with negative sampling to approximate the softmax over all entities. Regularization strategies such as embedding norm constraints and dropout mitigate overfitting on dense subgraphs. Evaluation typically reports mean reciprocal rank and Hits@k, with filtered metrics excluding triples that are true in the KG but absent from the test set. Rotational models on complex or hypercomplex spaces aim to preserve relational patterns like inversion and composition in a geometrically principled way. Recent surveys provide comprehensive overviews of scoring functions and training losses (Smith, Brown, and Lee 2020), including translational, bilinear, and neural formulations. Beyond static KGs, temporal and multi-modal extensions integrate timestamps and textual descriptions to improve disambiguation. Inductive settings require generalizing to entities unseen at training time by encoding textual or structural features rather than relying solely on identifiers. Rule-guided and neuro-symbolic methods combine differentiable objectives with mined logical rules to enhance generalization and interpretability. Despite progress in link prediction, answering compositional queries remains challenging because supervision rarely covers complex query structures. Logical query embedding approaches represent sets of answers to conjunctive queries as regions or distributions in the embedding space. These methods target multi-hop reasoning patterns while avoiding full grounding of intermediate variables. In the context of KGQA, pipeline architectures first map the question to a formal query and then retrieve answers from the KG. Neural semantic parsers learn to produce graph queries from text by leveraging weak supervision and denotations. Embedding-based KGQA maps questions and candidate answers into a shared space and ranks entities using the underlying KGE scores. Hybrid systems integrate retrieval with reading comprehension over textual corpora to address incompleteness in the KG.

Format.document: Prompt-based few-shot fine-tuning adapts pretrained language models to new tasks by conditioning on task descriptions and a handful of labeled examples. Early studies established its viability on moderately sized models such as BERT and RoBERTa (Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019). Pattern-Exploiting Training reframes classification as masked language modeling with hand-crafted or searched patterns (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b). AutoPrompt uses gradient signals to select discrete trigger tokens that elicit desired model behavior (Shin et al., 2020). Null prompts show that minimal concatenation with a [MASK] token can already yield competitive baselines (Logan et al., 2021). Beyond discrete templates, soft-prompting injects continuous embeddings as virtual tokens and tunes only those parameters (Lester et al., 2021). Complementary work pre-trains soft prompts to provide stronger initializations for downstream tuning (Gu et al., 2021). Demonstration-augmented prompting further enriches inputs by adding labeled exemplars, as explored by LM-BFF (Gao et al., 2021). Our study builds on these ideas by coupling multiple demonstrations with a compact, globally shared soft memory for prompt tokens. In contrast to LM-BFF, we allocate several demonstrations per label and automatically verbalize label phrases to improve semantic alignment. We compare against manual prompts, LM-BFF, and full fine-tuning under identical data budgets (Gao et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021). Prior strong baselines for few-shot classification include Zhang and Wang, 2020; Li, 2021. For completeness, we also evaluate in-context learning with frozen RoBERTa-large using GPT-3 style prompting, with no parameter updates (Brown et al., 2020). All results are averaged over five random splits, and we report means and standard deviations to account for sensitivity to seed choice. Our implementation follows common preprocessing and tuning recipes, including layerwise learning-rate decay and class-balanced sampling (Mosbach et al., 2021). To isolate the effect of demonstrations, we keep the underlying encoder fixed across methods and vary only the prompt mechanism. Architecturally, we adopt a transformer encoder with a lightweight prefix of trainable embeddings that functions as the soft memory (Li and Liang, 2021). The approach maintains efficiency by freezing the bulk of model weights while updating fewer than one percent of parameters (Houlsby et al., 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2021). Compared to discrete patterns, continuous prompts reduce brittleness to tokenization artifacts and permit smooth optimization (Lester et al., 2021). We further ablate the number of demonstrations per label and the sharing strategy across tasks to understand scaling behavior. In addition to accuracy, we analyze calibration, sample efficiency, and robustness to prompt paraphrases (Jiang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021). Finally, we situate our findings within the broader trend of replacing task-specific heads with input-conditioned control of sequence-to-sequence models Vaswani et al., 2017). This perspective highlights the unifying role of prompts as lightweight interfaces that steer pretrained knowledge without extensive retraining. Altogether, our results clarify when and why multi-demonstration soft prompting outperforms discrete and full fine-tuning, and they chart practical guidelines for selecting prompt mechanisms in resource-constrained settings.

Building on earlier efforts in span-level supervision, Pavlopoulos et al. demonstrated the feasibility of annotating toxic substrings in community data. Complementing automated measures, we collect human judgments on highlight usefulness and harm-minimization effects in redaction scenarios. Our contributions include a new public dataset, a rigorous evaluation suite, and extensive analyses that reveal strengths and failure modes of current approaches.

Format.document:
Linguistic studies have long observed the distinct properties of translationese from text originally authored in the same language (Toury, 1980;Gellerstam, 1986;Baker, 1993;Toury, 1995). Recent work in MT identifies the translationese-tooriginal portion of test sets (i.e., sets unaligned with the model direction) as statistically significantly easier (Graham et al., 2020), echoing many previous observations (Toral et al., 2018;Lembersky et al., 2012;Läubli et al., 2018), and thus some suggest excluding this portion from future test sets (Toral et al., 2018;Zhang and Toral, 2019;Graham et al., 2020;Barrault et al., 2019).

Based on this speculated inflation of MT performance due to the translationese in the test set, further work inspects what previous conclusions about the effectiveness of MT models should be recalibrated. Some discover that models with BT mostly improve on the inflated test set but not the other more challenging portion (Toral et al., 2018;Freitag et al., 2019;Edunov et al., 2020; Appendix A, Table 1) and raise concerns that BT is not as effective as expected. Others argue that BT can still improve on both test sets (Edunov et al., 2020).

Our work differs from all previous work in that we bring in two new important factors when considering how translationese affects MT performance, namely the train-test alignment, and data-model alignment. Moreover, beyond the correlation-based analysis in previous papers (Graham et al., 2020;Edunov et al., 2020), we conduct causal inference (Pearl, 2009;Peters et al., 2017) to contribute causal insights on how translationese affects MT.

Translationese has been attributed to interference from source syntax, normalization toward frequent target forms, and cautious lexical choices typical of novice translators (Baker, 1993;Toury, 1995). In MT evaluation, such distributional shifts can inflate scores for certain directions while obscuring generalization in realistic deployment (Graham et al., 2020). Back-translation (BT) interacts with these shifts because synthetic target-like text differs from human-produced originals, potentially aligning more closely with translationese segments (Sennrich et al., 2016;Edunov et al., 2020). Prior datasets often mixed original and translated content without explicit labels, limiting fine-grained analysis (Barrault et al., 2019). Recent corpora annotate text origin, enabling stratified reporting across translationese strata and model directions, building on Zhang and Toral (2019 and related tools (Toral et al., 2018). Nevertheless, practice lags behind recommendations, and leaderboard protocols rarely require origin-aware splits (Graham et al., 2020). We posit that two alignment concepts are essential: train–test alignment, capturing whether training distribution matches the evaluated direction, and data–model alignment, capturing inductive biases that favor particular distributions. The first determines whether improvements stem from genuine robustness or from fortunate overlap with translationese statistics (Peters et al., 2017). The second addresses architecture and objective choices that might privilege fluency over adequacy under distribution shift (Edunov et al., 2020). To empirically study these factors, we construct matched subsets controlling for source–target direction and for origin labels across multiple language pairs (Barrault et al., 2019;Läubli et al., 2018). We then estimate causal effects using adjustment sets identified from a domain graph and validate sensitivity to unobserved confounding (Pearl, 2009). Our findings suggest that improvements attributed to BT are partially mediated by alignment with translationese-heavy test conditions, but that causal gains remain for robust models trained with origin-aware objectives, consistent with Zhang and Toral (2019).
