Format.document: Dense retrieval has emerged as a dominant paradigm for open-domain question answering and web search. Unlike sparse term matching, dense retrievers encode queries and passages into a shared vector space for nearest neighbor search. Early work demonstrated that dual-encoders trained with in-batch negatives can rival BM25 on large benchmarks (Karpukhin et al., 2020). Subsequent studies proposed improved negative mining and post-training schemes to further strengthen representations (Xiong et al., 2021; Thakur et al., 2021). Despite these advances, data augmentation and regularization for retrieval remain underexplored compared to classification and generation. Mixup and related interpolation-based schemes have shown consistent gains in vision and some NLP tasks (Zhang et al., 2018; Verma et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020a). However, applying input-level interpolation to retrieval is nontrivial because meaning is not preserved under convex combinations in embedding space. Prior NLP augmentation often operates by token perturbations such as synonym replacement and random deletion (Wei and Zou, 2019; Ma, 2019). For dense retrieval, token-level noise can corrupt lexical cues without ensuring retrieval-aware invariances. In contrast, dropout provides a simple and scalable way to induce representation-level perturbations during training and inference (Srivastava et al., 2014; Gal and Ghahramani, 2016). Following Karpukhin et al., we revisit negative sampling under stochastic encoders to examine robustness. Our central hypothesis is that structured stochasticity can help models generalize across domains and retrieval tasks. We therefore study dropout-driven perturbations as implicit data augmentation for dual-encoders. We complement this strategy with standard retrieval training using hard negatives mined by BM25 and strong dense models (Nguyen et al., 2016; Xiong et al., 2021). We also compare with adversarial feature perturbations that explicitly craft gradient-aligned noise (Miyato et al., 2017). Beyond augmentation, we situate our work within research on calibration and ensembling for retrieval. Monte Carlo dropout provides a cheap approximation to Bayesian ensembling with minimal changes to training pipelines (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016). Prior evidence suggests that such stochastic ensembling can improve both accuracy and uncertainty estimates in neural ranking. For re-rankers, cross-encoders often provide stronger supervision signals than dual-encoders, enabling distillation into lightweight retrievers (Nogueira and Cho, 2019; Hofstätter et al., 2021). We assess whether dropout perturbations remain beneficial when training with teacher signals from cross-encoders. Closely related are late-interaction models that constrain how token embeddings combine at query time (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020). Another line of work explores query expansion and synthetic data generation to improve coverage on tail intents (Nogueira et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2021). Several competitive baselines report gains from better negatives and large-scale continual pretraining (Xiong et al., 2021; Luan et al., 2021, though their benefits may depend on the mining strategy. Nevertheless, the community lacks a systematic analysis of representation-level perturbations across diverse retrieval settings. We therefore evaluate on a heterogeneous suite of tasks that include passage retrieval, entity linking, and scientific citation search (Thakur et al., 2021). Our experiments control for index size, training data volume, and evaluation protocol to facilitate fair comparisons. We further ablate dropout schedules, masking rates, and inference-time sampling strategies to isolate key factors. We find that dropout-based perturbations yield consistent improvements on in-domain development sets and demonstrate robustness to distribution shifts on BEIR. The approach complements hard-negative mining and is compatible with mixed-precision and large-batch training on modern accelerators. Compared to interpolation-based mixup, our method preserves input semantics while promoting smoother score landscapes for gradient-based learning. Finally, we discuss limitations, including computational overhead from sampling and potential interactions with batch normalization, and we outline directions for principled retrieval-specific augmentation.

Format.document: Large pre-trained Seq2Seq Transformer models have transformed neural text generation across summarization, translation, and data-to-text. They are typically trained with denoising or reconstruction objectives that scale well with data. T5 treats every NLP problem as text-to-text and leverages span denoising to learn robust representations (Raffel et al., 2020). BART combines bidirectional and autoregressive training through denoising autoencoding to yield strong generative performance (Lewis et al., 2020). PEGASUS optimizes a gap-sentence objective tailored to extractive-like summarization signals (Zhang et al., 2020). Despite their accuracy, these models are computationally intensive at training and inference time. Model compression methods aim to mitigate these costs without severely degrading quality. Knowledge distillation transfers behavior from a large teacher to a compact student using soft targets or intermediate representations (Hinton et al., 2015;Romero et al., 2014). Early work showed that students trained on teacher logits can match or surpass baselines in classification tasks (Ba and Caruana, 2014). Later studies extended distillation to attention maps, hidden states, and gradients to better shape student learning (Zagoruyko and Komodakis, 2017;Czarnecki et al., 2017). Distillation for pre-trained Transformers has produced efficient encoders for natural language understanding, including DistilBERT, TinyBERT, MobileBERT, and MiniLM Sanh et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020) and subsequent variants (Sun et al., 2020;Wang et al., 2020). However, compression of Seq2Seq generators presents unique challenges because sequence-level behavior matters. A key idea is sequence-level distillation, which replaces gold outputs with teacher-generated hypotheses to align the student with the teacher's decoding distribution (Kim and Rush, 2016). This approach consistently improves training stability and decoding efficiency in neural machine translation (Gu et al., 2017;Denkowski and Neubig, 2017;Kasai et al., 2020). Recent work on summarization adopted similar pseudo-labeling strategies and compared them to direct KD on token distributions (Shleifer and Rush, 2020). Nonetheless, open questions remain about how to combine token-level and sequence-level signals effectively. Shrink-and-fine-tune methods prune layers and then re-optimize the teacher to recover lost capacity (Shleifer and Rush, 2020). Other lines of work study progressive module replacement to gradually morph a teacher into a student while preserving outputs (Xu et al., 2020). Self-training and self-distillation explore using the model's own predictions to improve generalization without changing capacity (Furlanello et al., 2018;Xie et al., 2020). For generative models, these techniques must address exposure bias and search errors that propagate into pseudo labels. Beam-search generated targets can be biased toward brevity and high-probability modes, which may underrepresent diversity. Temperature scaling and sequence reweighting have been proposed to smooth targets and emphasize informative examples. Another promising direction is to distill from multiple teachers trained with heterogeneous objectives to improve robustness. Research on task-specific compression indicates that students benefit from aligning with evaluation losses, such as ROUGE-aware objectives for summarization. While much prior work targets encoders, there is a growing need to design distillation protocols that respect autoregressive dependencies. Cross-attention supervision can guide students to attend to salient source tokens that teachers rely on. Consistency regularization across augmentations offers a complementary signal in low-resource regimes Sanh et al., 2019). Beyond accuracy, latency and memory footprint are critical metrics for deployment on edge devices. Quantization and pruning can be combined with distillation to yield additional speedups without drastic quality loss. In multilingual settings, distilled students can inherit cross-lingual generalization from a shared teacher. Nevertheless, rigorous evaluation across domains and input lengths is necessary to avoid overstating gains. Our study investigates how to structure pseudo-labeling to better preserve teacher coverage while reducing search cost. We compare against strong baselines and analyze errors by source length, extractiveness, and novelty. Results demonstrate that a carefully tuned sequence-level distillation pipeline achieves favorable trade-offs in accuracy and efficiency. We release code and scripts to facilitate reproducible research on generative model compression.

Format.document: We now introduce the task of entity set expansion (ESE), existing paradigms and evaluation methods. Entity set expansion aims to grow a small seed set of exemplars into a more complete list of entities belonging to the same semantic class. Classical approaches leverage distributional similarity in large corpora, assuming that co-occurrence contexts encode category membership (Hearst, 1992; Pantel and Pennacchiotti, 2006). Pattern-based bootstrapping expands seeds by harvesting lexico-syntactic patterns and iteratively extracting candidates (Etzioni et al., 2005; Kozareva et al., 2008). More recent neural methods learn embedding spaces or encoders that map entities and contexts into comparable representations for retrieval (Shi et al., 2018; Shen et al., 2020). Weak supervision and distant supervision have been explored to reduce annotation costs, especially when constructing seed sets from heterogeneous sources (Ratner et al., 2017; Safranchik et al., 2020). Bootstrapping reliability is often improved by enforcing diversity and precision constraints during iteration (Nguyen et al., 2020 while calibrating confidence scores to prevent semantic drift. In parallel, search-enhanced expansion leverages query logs and web tables to rank candidates with click-through and co-table signals (Dalvi et al., 2012; Lehmberg et al., 2016). Interactive ESE systems integrate human-in-the-loop feedback, balancing exploration of novel candidates with exploitation of high-confidence expansions (Yang et al., 2017; Strohmann and Schütze, 2019). Evaluation protocols typically report precision at k, mean average precision, and area under the precision–recall curve on held-out gold lists assembled from knowledge bases or expert annotations (Jin et al., 2013; Rong et al., 2016). However, metrics alone can be misleading when seed sets are biased or when categories have long tails that favor recall-heavy methods. To address this, several works propose stratified test splits and stress tests that vary seed quality, domain shift, and candidate universe size (Gao et al., 2021; Zeng et al., 2022). Recent pre-trained language models have further improved expansion quality by contextualizing entity mentions and enabling zero-shot generalization across domains (Petroni et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2020). Nevertheless, these models require careful negative sampling and calibration to avoid overfitting to surface forms and spurious correlations. In what follows, we situate our approach within these paradigms, specify a robust evaluation suite, and highlight open challenges for reproducible ESE research.

Format.document: We also compare our method with previous SOTA work, where all referred systems exploit the pre-trained BERT model. As shown, compared to Chen et al. (2020), our method performs better when using very limited training data. Besides, our method can match their performance in a semi-supervised setting that uses an additional 10K unlabeled training instances. Moreover, our final model, without utilizing much external knowledge (e.g., document-level or manually designed features), can achieve very competitive performance on the full training set in comparison to most of the previous systems. Furthermore, it should be noted that achieving the absolute SOTA results of our model on the full training data is not the primary motivation of our work. This section reviews prior approaches to low-resource fine-tuning and semi-supervised learning for language understanding. Early transformer-based baselines leveraged supervised objectives with large labeled corpora, prominently BERT (Devlin et al., 2019). Subsequent research explored knowledge distillation and data augmentation to improve label efficiency (Xie et al., 2020; Clark et al., 2020). In addition, consistency regularization and pseudo-labeling have proved effective in scenarios with scarce annotations (Sohn et al., 2020; Arazo et al., 2020). Domain adaptation techniques aim to bridge distributional shifts between source and target tasks while retaining generalization (Ben-David et al., 2010; Ganin et al., 2016). Recent parameter-efficient tuning methods reduce compute while maintaining accuracy, which aligns with our goal of practical deployment (Houlsby et al., 2019; Lester et al., 2021). From a retrieval perspective, stronger pre-training of encoders can enhance sample efficiency and robustness (Gao et al., 2021). Several studies report similar findings (Sohn et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2020), and we refer readers to (Li et al., 2021 for a comprehensive survey. Beyond classification, sequence labeling under limited data has benefited from span-level contrastive learning (Gunel et al., 2021). Data valuation methods further indicate that careful selection of a small subset can rival training on full datasets (Ghorbani and Zou, 2019; Paul et al., 2021). Our comparison emphasizes fairness by fixing backbones, tokenization, and optimization hyperparameters across methods. We also control for randomness by averaging over multiple seeds and reporting mean and standard deviation. In tasks with extreme imbalance, cost-sensitive losses often outperform naive oversampling (Cui et al., 2019). We thus evaluate under both balanced and imbalanced splits to assess robustness to label skew. Another line of work studies the impact of pre-training objectives such as masked language modeling versus replaced token detection (Devlin et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2020). While these objectives yield strong representations, they can still overfit in low-signal regimes without appropriate regularization. Our method differs by explicitly modeling uncertainty at both the instance and feature levels, which reduces confirmation bias during self-labeling. We also compare against stronger semi-supervised baselines that integrate confidence-aware thresholds and temperature scaling (Sohn et al., 2020; Rizve et al., 2021). On full-data settings, performance gaps narrow, suggesting diminishing returns for aggressive regularization (Kornblith et al., 2019). Overall, the empirical evidence supports our claim that careful calibration and parameter-efficient adaptation yield robust gains with minimal external knowledge.

Format.document: In this section, we summarize existing works on syntactically and lexically CPG. Syntactic CPG generates a paraphrase constrained by a prespecified sentence of a certain syntactic structure, namely an exemplar. However, the exemplar is only available during inference, resulting in a key challenge: obtaining manual exemplars for existing paraphrasing training datasets is prohibitively expensive. To address this, some previous works construct syntactic features from target sentences during training, such as POS tags, constituent trees, and masked templates, as illustrated in Table X. For instance, SCPN (Iyyer et al., 2018) makes the first attempt to introduce a linearized constituent tree (LCT) of the target sentence into paraphrasing, where the LCT is predicted based on predefined parse templates. Similarly, GuiG (Li et al., 2020) proposes two models to expand a partial template LCT and to generate paraphrases, respectively. Different from using LCT, SGCP (Kumar et al., 2020) introduces a graph encoder to encode the constituent tree of the exemplar as the condition. Besides, masked templates replace several words of the exemplar with a special token to form a controllable template. For example, BCPG (Liu et al., 2020b) follows BERT (Devlin et al., 2019 to randomly mask exemplar words, and ParafraGPT (Bui, 2019) makes the first attempt to integrate keywords with a copy mechanism. Despite these advances, existing works typically focus on a single conditioning signal under either lexical or syntactic CPG. In comparison, GCPG jointly includes lexical and syntactic CPG, flexibly combining conditions in a unified framework. Lexically controlled paraphrase generation usually specifies desired keywords, synonyms, or constraints such as inclusion or exclusion lists (Mao et al., 2020). Keyword-guided seq2seq models enforce coverage via copy mechanisms or constrained decoding (Hokamp and Liu, 2017; Post and Vilar, 2018). Exemplar-based paradigms condition on a retrieved prototype sentence to steer structure while preserving meaning (Guu et al., 2018; Weston et al., 2018). In paraphrase tasks, structural control aims to disentangle syntax from semantics so that models can reuse target-side structural priors (Zhang and Bowman, 2019). Recent transformer backbones have further reduced the cost of control via prompting and soft constraints (Lewis et al., 2020; Raffel et al., 2020). Nevertheless, aligning heterogeneous controls remains challenging because lexically feasible tokens may conflict with syntactic realizations when fluency is enforced by beam search (Stahlberg and Byrne, 2019). To mitigate this, several studies formulate control as a multi-source problem with learned fusion between exemplar encoders and lexical planners (Bawden et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020). Other work applies constrained decoding using finite-state controllers or differentiable relaxations to satisfy hard lexical constraints while respecting parse templates (Anderson et al., 2017; Miao et al., 2019). Beyond architecture, training data scarcity for paired exemplars has prompted weak supervision, back-translation, and retrieval-augmented pretraining (Edunov et al., 2018; Lewis et al., 2020). Evaluation remains difficult because BLEU and ROUGE under-reward structural control, leading to the adoption of parse-accuracy, tree-edit distance, and targeted acceptability judgments (Sulem et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). For fairness, researchers also examine paraphrase faithfulness with entailment and semantic similarity metrics to detect meaning drift under strong control (Wieting et al., 2019; Maynez et al., 2020). In practical deployments, controllable paraphrasing supports data augmentation, privacy-preserving text transformation, and controllable simplification (Kumar et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2022). Our study situates GCPG within this line by unifying structural templates, lexical keys, and exemplar graphs under a single training objective that preserves semantic equivalence. We next detail the problem formulation, modeling choices, and evaluation protocols used to assess controllability and faithfulness across diverse benchmarks.

Format.document: Large-scale pre-trained language models (PLMs) have achieved great success in recent years. Despite their power, the inference is time-consuming, which hinders their deployment in low-latency scenarios. To accelerate PLM inference, there are currently two streams of work: (1) compressing a cumbersome PLM through knowledge distillation (Sanh et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020), model pruning (Gordon et al., 2020; Michel et al., 2019), quantization (Shen et al., 2020), module replacing (Xu et al., 2020a), etc. (2) Selectively activating parts of the model conditioned on the input, such as Universal Transformer (Dehghani et al., 2019), FastBERT (Liu et al., 2020a), DeeBERT, PABEE, LeeBERT (Zhu, 2021), CascadeBERT (Li et al., 2021a), ElasticBERT (Liu et al., 2021a) and other similar methods (Elbayad et al., 2020; Schwartz et al., 2020; Liao et al., 2021; Xin et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2021). Different from these methods, our proposed HASHEE requires no internal classifiers (which imply extra parameters) and supervision, and therefore can be widely used in a variety of tasks and model architectures. Adaptive computation aims to allocate variable compute per example so that easy inputs exit early while hard inputs receive deeper processing. Early-exit methods typically attach auxiliary classifiers to intermediate layers and stop when a confidence criterion is satisfied (Teerapittayanon et al., 2016; Xin et al., 2021). However, auxiliary heads introduce training complexity, hyperparameters, and potential distribution shifts between pretraining and fine-tuning. Routing-based sparsification instead activates a subset of experts or channels conditioned on the input representation (Lepikhin et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2021). These methods can be effective but often require architectural changes, specialized training, or careful balancing of load across experts. Our approach is motivated by the observation that hidden representations in PLMs exhibit monotonic certainty increases across depth on many tasks. HASHEE computes a lightweight halting score from hashed token representations to approximate entropy dynamics without dedicated classifiers. The score is unsupervised, computationally cheap, and applicable to both encoder and encoder–decoder architectures. We evaluate HASHEE on text classification, natural language inference, and extractive question answering to assess generality. We compare against strong early-exit baselines including DeeBERT, PABEE, and CascadeBERT implemented under a shared protocol. We also examine uncertainty calibration, selective risk, and Pareto efficiency when trading accuracy for latency. We ground our design in the progressive refinement view of Transformer layers (Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, and Uszkoreit, 2017 which posits hierarchical feature composition. Concretely, HASHEE measures the stability of subword projections across consecutive layers and halts when changes fall below a task-agnostic threshold. Stable representations indicate that subsequent layers are likely to yield diminishing returns for the current example. We validate this proxy by correlating layerwise stability with correctness and margin on held-out validation sets. We further provide a simple latency model that captures per-layer compute, memory traffic, and device overheads. Experiments span A100 GPUs and edge-class CPUs under batch-one constraints to reflect interactive serving scenarios. We measure accuracy, expected executed layers, and realized speedup, and we report energy proxies via on-chip power sensors when available. Results show that HASHEE matches or surpasses internal-classifier baselines at comparable or lower average depth on GLUE benchmarks. On SQuAD-style question answering, the method preserves F1 while reducing median layers by up to 40 percent without task-specific tuning. Ablation studies isolate the contributions of hashing granularity, windowed stability estimation, and threshold scheduling. Sensitivity analyses explore robustness to domain shift, adversarial perturbations, and input length variations. Related work also investigates confidence-based stopping rules that rely on softmax entropy or margin at intermediate layers (Zhou et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2021). Unlike those methods, HASHEE leverages representation dynamics rather than classifier logits, which avoids training additional heads. The approach is complementary to compression and distillation and can be stacked with quantization or pruning for further gains. We release code, configurations, and inference scripts to facilitate reproducibility and fair comparisons in future research.

Format.document:
Semantic parsing seeks to map natural language to executable representations grounded in a schema or environment. Foundational work established grammar-based approaches and learning from denotations (Zelle and Mooney, 1996; Zettlemoyer and Collins, 2005; Pasupat and Liang, 2015). Recent neural models leverage sequence-to-sequence architectures and structured decoders to handle compositionality (Dong and Lapata, 2018; Yin and Neubig, 2017). This line of research emphasizes correctness of programs under a predefined grammar and type system (Krishnamurthy et al., 2017). Related advances in program synthesis similarly target mapping specifications to programs with formal semantics (Gulwani, 2011; Desai et al., 2016). A complementary thread uses weak supervision via answer supervision rather than full logical forms (Clarke et al., 2010; Berant et al., 2013). Despite progress, reliance on a fixed domain or API can limit generalization to open settings (Gupta et al., 2020). Our framing instead studies agents that communicate in free-form language to coordinate problem solving without assuming a hand designed DSL.

Multi-hop question answering evaluates the ability to integrate information across multiple sources. Benchmarks such as HotpotQA, QAngaroo, and StrategyQA operationalize multi-step reasoning across documents or facts (Yang et al., 2018; Welbl et al., 2018; Geva et al., 2021). However, numerous studies have revealed annotation artifacts and single-hop shortcuts that confound evaluation (Min et al., 2019a; Chen and Durrett, 2019). As a result, systems may achieve high scores without demonstrating robust compositional reasoning (Gardner et al., 2020; Trivedi et al., 2020). Dataset construction techniques such as adversarial filtering and perturbation aim to reduce these shortcuts (Nie et al., 2019; Bartolo et al., 2020). Modeling innovations include retrieval-augmented readers and graph-based reasoning over evidence chains (Clark and Gardner, 2018; Tu et al., 2020). Yet many approaches still struggle when intermediate steps are implicit, ambiguous, or require collaboration among distinct agents (Khot et al., 2021).

Question decomposition has emerged as a practical strategy to enforce intermediate structure in multi-hop QA. Pipelined methods decompose a question into sub-questions executed by a single model or toolset (Talmor and Berant, 2018; Perez et al., 2020). Other works learn latent decompositions using supervision only from final answers (Min et al., 2019b; Perez et al., 2020). While effective, these systems are often tailored to specific datasets and supervision regimes (Furrer et al., 2020). Moreover, evaluations rarely capture the dynamics of multi-agent collaboration that arise in realistic problem solving (Schick et al., 2023). Our study broadens this scope by involving multiple specialized agents that must exchange information through language to complete tasks. We further encourage models to learn decompositions through interaction rather than pre-specified schemes or gold step annotations.

Synthetic reasoning benchmarks offer controlled settings to probe systematic generalization. Classic datasets emphasize compositional rules and out-of-distribution splits that stress test neural models (Lake and Baroni, 2018; Keysers et al., 2020). More recent proposals introduce rich vocabularies, noise, and longer reasoning chains to close the gap with naturalistic tasks (Sinha et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021). Nevertheless, many synthetic setups lack interactive elements that reflect conversational coordination among agents (Hermann et al., 2017). We build on these insights to design environments where agents must request, provide, and verify partial information before committing to an answer. This design better isolates reasoning from spurious lexical correlations and shallow retrieval cues (Sagawa et al., 2020). It also facilitates transparent error analysis by tracing messages and intermediate commitments produced during collaboration.

Informed by the above literature, we structure our challenge around three dataset types and four cooperating agents. The agents include a retriever, a reader, a planner, and a verifier, each with distinct capabilities and partial observability. Interactions are governed by lightweight protocols that allow flexible turn taking while remaining agnostic to any particular ontology. To situate our work, we also draw methodological parallels with Lake and Baroni (2018 and subsequent analyses of systematicity in pretrained models (Nye et al., 2021). Unlike single-agent decomposers, our setting requires negotiation of subgoals and verification of evidence across turns. We provide evaluation protocols that measure both final accuracy and intermediate collaboration quality, including faithfulness of rationales and message utility. Together, these design choices aim to catalyze research on robust, interactive, and compositional reasoning beyond narrow dataset-specific heuristics.

The game of Mafia is particularly well-suited for the goal of determining whether the deceptive participants in a conversation can be identified from the contents of their utterances.
As an adversarial social deduction setting, Mafia provides repeated rounds of claims, counterclaims, and votes, offering rich linguistic signals tied to incentives under imperfect information.
Prior studies on deception in dialogue have charted varied operationalizations of lying signals in conversational dynamics (Hancock et al., 2007; Almela et al., 2012). Lexical cues such as uncertainty markers, negations, and hedging have been associated with deceptive intent in constrained tasks (Ott et al., 2011; Pérez-Rosas et al., 2015). Turn-taking irregularities and response latency have also been linked to strategic concealment in multi-party talk (Jiang and Sedoc, 2020). Feature-learning with contextual embeddings has expanded the scope of detectable cues in open-domain settings (Kleinberg et al., 2018).
While these findings motivate text-based inference, games like Mafia differ from dyadic or monologic deception by featuring strategic coalition dynamics and public commitments across rounds.
Research on computational social deduction has begun to exploit these properties using interaction graphs and role-conditioned language modeling (Deduct et al., 2021; Gamage and Hruschka, 2022).
Datasets curated from online play transcripts enable benchmarking of deception detection under shifting stakes and partial observability (Feng et al., 2021).
Work on persuasion in deliberative forums highlights the importance of stance shifts and narrative framing, both of which appear in Mafia accusations and defenses (Tan et al., 2016; Durmus and Cardie, 2019).
Complementary threads examine rumor veracity and misinformation cascades, emphasizing how group-level belief formation shapes the success of deceptive claims (Vosoughi et al., 2018; Shu et al., 2020).
In contrast to misinformation diffusion, Mafia imposes immediate feedback through voting, which sharpens the coupling between utterances and downstream accountability signals.
Approaches that integrate temporal argument structure with speaker roles have shown gains in multi-party analyses, suggesting value for role-aware modeling in Mafia (Niculae et al., 2017; Rosenthal and McKeown, 2015).
We build on this line by formalizing round-structured commitments and contradictions as latent states that condition surface text features.
Our contribution is threefold: we introduce a corpus with explicit role annotations across rounds, propose a sequence-labeling architecture that fuses dialogue acts with contradiction arcs, and release evaluation protocols for out-of-round generalization.
We hypothesize that role-conditioned contradiction density, rhetorical stance shifts, and commitment volatility are predictive of deception in this domain.
Finally, we discuss ethical considerations around surveillance misuse and propose protocols for consent, data minimization, and responsible deployment.

Coherence.document: Lexically Constrained Translation Existing translation methods impose lexical constraints during either inference or training. At training time, constrained MT models include code-switching data augmentation (Dinu et al., 2019;Song et al., 2019; and training with auxiliary tasks such as token or span-level mask-prediction (Ailem et al., 2021;Lee et al., 2021). At inference time, autoregressive constrained decoding algorithms include utilizing placeholder tag (Luong et al., 2015;Crego et al., 2016), grid beam search (Hokamp and Liu, 2017;Post and Vilar, 2018) and alignment-enhanced decoding (Alkhouli et al., 2018;Song et al., 2020;Chen et al., 2021). For the purpose of efficiency, recent studies also focus on non-autoregressive constrained translation. Susanto et al. (2020) proposes to modify the inference procedure of Levenshtein Transformer (Gu et al., 2019) where they disallow the deletion of constraint words during iterative editing. Xu and Carpuat (2021) further develops this idea and introduces a reposition operation that can reorder the constraint tokens. Our work absorbs the idea of both lines of work. Based on NAT methods, we brings alignment information by terminologies to help learn the contextual information for lexical constraints, especially the rare ones. Recent efforts expand constrained decoding to phrase-level constraints and subword-aware handling in morphologically rich languages (Hasler et al., 2018;Song et al., 2020;Susanto et al., 2020). Concurrently, work on interactive post-editing integrates user-provided terms with constrained search to reduce editing effort (Knowles and Koehn, 2016;Marie and Fujita, 2018). Studies on document-level MT emphasize entity and terminology consistency with cache-based or memory-augmented models (Tu et al., 2018;Miculicich et al., 2018). Investigations into constraint extraction from noisy terminology lists address capitalization, inflection, and polysemy resolution (Dinu et al., 2019;Song et al., 2019). Non-Autoregressive Translation Although enjoy the speed advantage, NAT models suffer from performance degradation due to the multi-modality problem, i.e., generating text when multiple translations are plausible. Gu et al. (2018) applies sequence-level knowledge distillation (KD) (Kim and Rush, 2016) that uses an AT's output as an NAT's new target, which reduces word diversity and reordering complexity in reference, resulting in fewer modes (Zhou et al., 2020;Xu et al., 2021). Various algorithms have also been proposed to alleviate this problem, including incorporating latent variables (Kaiser et al., 2018;Shu et al., 2020), iterative refinement (Ghazvininejad et al., 2019;Stern et al., 2019;Gu et al., 2019;Guo et al., 2020), advanced training objective Du et al., 2021) and gradually learning targetside word inter-dependency by curriculum learning (Qian et al., 2021). Our work extends the family of editing-based iterative NAT models for its flexibility to impose lexical constraints (Susanto et al., 2020;Xu and Carpuat, 2021).

Detection of adversarial examples is a wellexplored field in the image domain. Earlier works have tackled in various ways such as input transformation (Xu et al., 2018), statistical analysis (Grosse et al., 2017), or training a separate binary classifier (Metzen et al., 2017). However, Carlini and Wagner (2017) has shown that an adversary with par- tial knowledge of the detector can easily nullify it. Meanwhile, early works in novelty detection have shown that a generative model can detect anomaly samples (Bishop, 1994). Following this line of research,  have proposed a method to detect out-of-distribution samples by using features of a neural network for maximum likelihood estimation. Kim et al. (2018) explore temperature scaling for confidence calibration in classifiers. Liang et al. (2018) introduce a simple input preprocessing with perturbations to separate in- and out-of-distribution examples. Hendrycks et al. (2019) study baseline confidence scores for OOD detection in deep networks.

In the NLP domain, few efforts have been made in detecting word-level adversarial examples. Zhou et al. (2019, DISP) utilize a detector trained on adversarial samples for a joint detect-defense system. FGWS (Mozes et al., 2021) outperforms DISP in detection by building on the observation that attacked samples are composed of rare words. FGWS experiements on 2 proposed attack methods. Le et al. (2021) tackle a particular attack method called UniTrigger (Wallace et al., 2019), which pre-pends or appends an identical phrase in all sentences. While the performance is impressive, applying this method to other attacks requires significant adjustment due to the distinct characteristics of UniTrigger. Meanwhile, Pruthi et al. (2019) analyze character-level noise by simulating human typos in text classification. Li et al. (2020) evaluate robustness under synonym substitution attacks in sentiment analysis. Ebrahimi et al. (2018) present HotFlip, which uses gradient-based character edits to fool neural models.

Beyond detection, a parallel line of work focuses on certifiable robustness and defenses. Jia et al. (2019) propose certified robustness guarantees against word substitutions in text classification by interval bound propagation. Huang et al. (2019) study randomized smoothing for discrete text perturbations to yield probabilistic robustness certificates. Ye et al. (2020) investigate adversarial training tailored to token replacement budgets and show improved stability under lexically constrained attacks. These developments inform detector design by clarifying which perturbations remain plausible under constrained adversaries.

Another related area is confidence estimation in NLP models. Hendrycks and Gimpel (2017) show that softmax probabilities can act as simple confidence baselines, though they are poorly calibrated. Guo et al. (2017) introduce temperature scaling for post-hoc calibration, and Desai and Durrett (2020) assess calibration in modern transformers across tasks. Calibration-aware detection leverages the mismatch between confidence and likelihood under adversarial shifts to flag suspicious inputs.

We also note connections to out-of-distribution detection for text. Hendrycks et al. (2020) curate large-scale benchmarks for detecting dataset shift in language understanding. Lee et al. (2018) propose a Mahalanobis distance-based method using classifier features to separate in-domain and OOD text. Ren et al. (2019) adapt likelihood ratios for language models to reduce the bias toward background statistics. These methods inspire feature choices and scoring rules for our detector.

Our work contributes by unifying rarity-aware lexical cues with calibrated feature densities from intermediate layers. We design a scoring pipeline that aggregates token rarity, sentence-level embedding distances, and calibration-adjusted confidence margins. The resulting detector is attack-agnostic and requires no knowledge of the adversary, while remaining efficient at inference time. We evaluate across multiple datasets and attack settings to assess generality and robustness. Finally, we release code and standardized splits to facilitate reproducibility and future comparison.

Coherence.document: A Brief History of NLU Datasets. As a core module of ToD systems, NLU has been researched since the early 1990s, when the Airline Travel Information System (ATIS) project was started (Hemphill et al., 1990), consisting of spoken queries on flightrelated information. Over the next two decades, very few NLU resources were released. The lack of ToD NLU resources ended in 2013, with the beginning of the 'dialogue state tracking (DST) era' (Williams et al., 2013;Henderson et al., 2014;Kim et al., 2016). Instead of just classifying each turn of the user, DST deals with keeping track of the user's goal over the entire dialogue history, i.e., all the previous user and system turns. Several datasets where released during the DST challenges, all of them comprising simple intent sets (usually tagged as dialogue acts). To adapt to the increasing data requirements of deep learning models, increasingly larger dialogue datasets have been released in recent years (Budzianowski et al., 2018;Wei et al., 2018;Rastogi et al., 2019;Peskov et al., 2019). However, the design of ToD datasets comes with some profound differences to datasets for e.g. machine translation or speech recognition, which affect current ToD datasets. The domain-specific nature of ToD datasets made the data tied to its ontologies, not allowing data reusability across different domains. The domain-specific ontologies required a lot of expertise for annotation, therefore many annotation mistakes were made (Eric et al., 2019). These constraints motivated initiatives that attempt to abstract slot-value spaces, unify schema representations, and reduce annotation costs through programmatic supervision. Schema-Guided Dialogue (Rastogi et al., 2019) proposed a unified ontology interface that generalizes to unseen services by representing slots and intents via natural language descriptions. MultiWOZ (Budzianowski et al., 2018) scaled multi-domain coverage but also exposed the fragility of annotation pipelines and the need for rigorous validation protocols. Recent updates to MultiWOZ introduced refined slot ontologies, turn-level corrections, and clearer delexicalization rules to foster consistency across domains. The emphasis on generalization further spurred work on transferable representations that minimize ontology coupling while preserving task fidelity. The shift from turn-level intent tagging toward belief-state tracking and policy learning created pressure for richer supervision signals, including slot carryover, coreference, and correction phenomena. Benchmarking practices increasingly distinguish between in-domain and cross-domain generalization, as well as between seen and unseen schema elements at test time. Signal sparsity in end-to-end ToD datasets prompted the integration of weak labels from templates, synthetic dialogues, and self-training on unlabeled logs. Data-centric techniques such as active learning and error-driven relabeling were introduced to focus annotation budgets on the most impactful examples. Robustness concerns have also led to the inclusion of adversarial paraphrases and noise-injected utterances to emulate real-world ASR and typing errors. Recent work on broader conversational AI resources further diversified data characteristics, highlighting cross-domain task orientation (Budzianowski et al., 2018), schema-guided interactions (Rastogi et al., 2019), and mixed-initiative behaviors (Peskov et al., 2019). Multimodal task dialogue introduced visual grounding demands and alignment protocols (Wei et al., 2018). End-to-end dialogue collections reported scalability properties under weak supervision (Eric et al., 2019). Crowdsourced paraphrase banks examined lexical variety and robustness (Zhang et al., 2020). At the same time, dataset curation has increasingly emphasized provenance tracking, annotator training, and inter-annotator agreement as first-class artifacts. The emergence of instruction-tuned LLMs has revived interest in unifying NLU and DST signals under a single prompting interface. New benchmarks link semantic parsing, belief updates, and tool invocation logs to evaluate compositional generalization. Cross-lingual ToD datasets now explore ontology projection and slot canonicalization across languages with different morphological properties. Privacy-preserving data release has motivated federated collection protocols and selective redaction of personally identifiable information. Finally, our work synthesizes these lines by proposing evaluation settings that explicitly separate schema generalization, robustness to paraphrase, and tolerance to noisy supervision.

Coherence.document:
There have been a number of interesting attempts, that were aimed at model compression for Transformers, which can be broadly categorized into three directions. The first line of work focus on the redundancy of model parameters. Structure pruning (McCarley, 2019;Michel et al., 2019;Voita et al., 2019;Wang et al., 2019b;Fan et al., 2019;Wu et al., 2021a), which removes coherent groups of weights to preserve the original structure of the network, is one common strategy. In addition, various types of distillation techniques (Sanh et al., 2019;Jiao et al., 2019;Wang et al., 2020b) have been proposed to remove encoders by training a compact Transformer to reproduce the output of a larger one. Sanh et al. (2019) trained a smaller BERT variant with task-specific supervision, and Jiao et al. (2019) compressed multi-layer representations into a compact student for sequence labeling and QA. Wang et al. (2020b) explored multi-teacher aggregation for cross-task transfer, while convolutional student networks have also been considered for latency-critical settings (Sun et al., 2020). Other strategies include weight quantization (Bhandare et al., 2019;Zafrir et al., 2019;Shen et al., 2020;Fan et al., 2020) and weight sharing (Dehghani et al., 2018;Lan et al., 2019). The second line of work focus on reducing the quadratic operation of the self-attention matrices. The quadratic time and space complexity of the attention mechanism with respect to the input sequence serves the main efficiency bottleneck of Transformers, and thus is prohibitively expensive for training long-sequence data. One popular approach is to sparsify the self-attention operation by restricting each token to only attend a subset of tokens (Child et al., 2019;Kitaev et al., 2020;Ye et al., 2019;Zaheer et al., 2020;Beltagy et al., 2020). In particular, the most recent Big Bird (Zaheer et al., 2020) and Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020) introduce sparse models which scale linearly with the input sequence. Another popular approach (Wang et al., 2020a;Choromanski et al., 2020) is to approximate the self-attention to reduce its quadratic complexity to linear, where the most recent Performers (Choromanski et al., 2020) provides an unbiased linear estimation of the attention matrices.

The third line, which our work lies in, focus on the redundancy in maintaining a full-length sequence of token-level representation across all encoders (Dai et al., 2020;Wu et al., 2021b;Pietruszka et al., 2020;Ye et al., 2021;Kim and Cho, 2020). This work is particularly inspired by the sequence-level NLP tasks such as text classification and ranking, where the state-of-the-art approach utilizes a single embedding from the top encoder layer of a Transformer, such as the CLS token, for prediction. Under such regime, retaining the full-length sequence till the last encoder creates unnecessary complexity. Dai et al. (2020) applied a simplest strided mean pooling to each sliding window of the sequence to gradually compress tokens. The paper proposed a specialized pre-training procedure for this process that achieves a good balance between speedup and accuracy drop. Dai et al. (2020) used masked language modeling objectives adapted to pooled sequences to better preserve semantics during compression, and reported stable gains on GLUE. Wu et al. (2021b) benchmarked centroid schemes on document classification with balanced accuracy and throughput, and domain-matched pretraining corpora were shown to further stabilize convergence for compressed models (Gururangan et al., 2020). Ye et al. (2021) studied policy gradients with reward shaping to mitigate sparsity in token selection. In comparison we aim to avoid the costly pre-training step and focus on a method that requires only a lightweight fine-tuning. Wu et al. (2021b) define a centroid attention operator that given centroids, computes their embeddings via an attention mechanism. These centroids are chosen either as a random subset of the original tokens, or via strided mean pooling. This results in a similar technique to that of Dai et al. (2020), in terms of having a naive sequence length reduction method. Pietruszka et al. (2020) provide a variant of length 2 strided mean pooling where instead of taking the unweighted average of each pair, they provide learnable weights via a differentiable linear function. In our experiment we did not compare our methods with (Wu et al., 2021b;Pietruszka et al., 2020) since both worked on a limited (non-standard) collection of datasets and at the time of writing this paper, did not provide code allowing us to reproduce their result. Since our paper is focused on techniques to select a subset of tokens and these papers use either random sampling or pooling, we do not believe a thorough comparison is required. Ye et al. (2021) proposed a reinforcement-learning based technique to rank the tokens, thereby allowing it to remove the least important ones. This RL policy must be trained in an expensive process that requires the full network structure. Since we focus on methods to improve both training and inference, we do not include it in our experiments. Vision Transformers (Pan et al., 2021;Heo et al., 2021), which apply various types of pooling techniques to reduce input length, is specially designed for image data and thus non-trivial to compare with our method. We developed an attention based mechanism to progressively eliminate tokens in the intermediate encoders in the fine-tuning, while maintaining the classification accuracy.

Coherence.document:
Our approach is closely related to the existing works on cross-lingual NER, knowledge distillation and siamese network.

Cross-Lingual NER aims to extract entities from a target language but assumes only source language is annotated. The existing models can be categorized to: a) Shared feature space based models, b) Translation based models, c) Knowledge distillation based models.

Shared feature space based models generally train a language-independent encoder using source and target language data (Tsai et al., 2016). Recently, the pre-trained multilingual language models mBERT is effective to address the challenge (Devlin et al., 2019). Moreover, some research introduces new components on top of the mBERT by directly transferring the model learned from labeled source language to that of target languages (Keung et al., 2019). The performance is still weak due to the lack of annotations of target languages. Translation based models generally generate pesudo labeled target data to alleviate target data scarcity. For example, (Wu et al., 2020b;Zhang et al., 2021) gain a improvement by translating the labeled source language to the target language word-by-word. Our model achieves considerable improvement by learning entity similarity in target language data without translation.

Knowledge distillation based models includes a teacher model and a student model (Wu et al., 2020c). The teacher model is trained on labeled source language. The student model learns from the soft label predicted by teacher model on unlabeled target language data. Therefore, the student model can capture the extra knowledge about target languages. In our work, the student model not only learns the recognizer teacher knowledge, but also learns the entity similarity knowledge inspired by multi-task learning.

Siamese Network is originally introduced by (Bromley et al., 1994) to treat signature verification as a matching problem. It has been successfully applied to transfer learning such as one-shot image recognition (Koch et al., 2015), text similarity (Neculoiu et al., 2016). However, there is a dilemma to adapt siamese network to token-level recognition tasks such as NER. Siamese network assumes the input is a pair, and the output is a similarity score. To handle this issue, we reconstruct the data to pair format. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to learn the entity similarity by siamese network.

Benchmarks targeting pragmatic inference and world knowledge reveal gaps between surface-form competence and deeper understanding (Zhou et al., 2020;Talmor et al., 2020). Coherence.document:
PLMs are at the core of many success stories in natural language processing (NLP). However, it remains unclear to what extent PLMs understand the syntactic and semantic properties of the human language. A series of probing tasks have been conducted on PLMs and have found them lacking or falling short on some language properties. Among the many findings of these probing tasks, PLMs have been found to be insensitive to the order of sentences when generating representations (Pham et al., 2020;Gupta et al., 2021;Sinha et al., 2021a), struggle to comprehend number-related representations (Wallace et al., 2019;Lin et al., 2020;Nogueira et al., 2021), and display a lack of semantic content understanding (Ravichander et al., 2020;Elazar et al., 2021).

In addition to the above faulty behaviours, Ettinger (2020) and Kassner and Schütze (2020) show that PLMs fail to comprehend negation, which is an important property of language in many natural language understanding (NLU) tasks. Ettinger (2020) check the ability of PLMs to understand of the meaning of negation in given contexts. In their work, they check whether models are sensitive in their completions of sentences that either include negation or not. Under normal circumstances, the completions are expected to vary in truth depending on the presence or absence of negation in given sentences. Their results show that PLMs are insensitive to the impacts of negations when completing sentences. Kassner and Schütze (2020) construct the negated LAMA dataset by inserting negation elements (e.g., "not") in the LAMA cloze questions (Petroni et al., 2019). They use negated and original question pairs to query PLMs and establish that models are equally prone to make the same predictions for both the original and negated questions. In a well-informed setting, it is expected that PLMs should make different predictions for the original and negated questions. This shows that PLMs struggle to comprehend negation.

In light of the highlighted faulty behaviours of PLMs, especially their struggle to comprehend negation, Hosseini et al. (2021) propose a remedy to alleviate the problem. In their remedy, they augment the language modelling objective with an unlikelihood objective (Welleck et al., 2019) based on negated sentences from the training corpus. They use a syntactic augmentation method to generate negated sentences. In this method, the dependency parse of the sentences, POS tags and morphological information of each word are taken as input and the negation of sentences is done using sets of dependency tree regular expression patterns, such as Semgrex (Chambers et al., 2007). During training, they replace objects in negated sentences with [MASK] tokens and use unlikelihood training to make the masked-out tokens unlikely under the PLM distribution. To ensure that negated sentences are factually false, they use the corresponding positive sentences as context for the unlikelihood prediction task.

Previous studies, e.g., Kassner and Schütze (2020), have mostly limited the scope of the logical negation property only to the negation expressions (e.g., "no" and "not"). However, the core spirit of the property is opposite-meaning, which is not only limited to negation. Welleck et al. (2019) consider negating sentences using dependency tree regular expression patterns. This widens the scope of negation, as it is not only limited to negation expressions "no" and "not". However, their approach relies on other components, such as Semgrex, and dependency and POS parsers which could impact the quality of the data, hence impact the models' performance. In this work, we consider other perturbation methods to generate the opposite-meaning sentences to investigate whether PLMs satisfy the logical negation property, and we propose a remedy called intermediate-training on meaning-matching (IM 2 ) that hardly employs additional linguistic components.

Linguistic studies have long observed the distinct properties of translationese from text originally authored in the same language (Toury, 1980;Gellerstam, 1986;Baker, 1993;Toury, 1995). Recent work in MT identifies that the translationese-tooriginal portion of the test sets (i.e., test sets unaligned with the model direction) being statistically significantly easier (Graham et al., 2020), echoing with many previous observations (Toral et al., 2018;Lembersky et al., 2012;Läubli et al., 2018) and thus some suggest to exclude this portion from future test sets (Toral et al., 2018;Zhang and Toral, 2019;Graham et al., 2020;Barrault et al., 2019).

Based on this speculated inflation of MT performance due to the translationese in the test set, further work inspects what previous conclusions about the effectiveness of MT models should be recalibrated. Some discover that models with BT mostly improve on the inflated test set but not the other more challenging portion (Toral et al., 2018;Freitag et al., 2019;Edunov et al., 2020, Appendix A Table ) and raises concerns that BT is not as effective as expected. Others argue that BT can still improve on both test sets (Edunov et al., 2020).

Recent investigations of robustness in multilingual evaluation provide related context. Smith et al. (2021) examine calibration drift across language families and report uneven gains tied to tokenization granularity. Koehn and Knowles (2017) document a wide range of pitfalls in neural MT evaluation, with emphasis on domain and sentence length effects. Concurrently, data-centric approaches emphasize distributional matching between training and evaluation corpora (Sagawa et al., 2020; Koh et al., 2021). Liu et al. (2022) study memorization under dataset shifts in pretraining regimes. Findings on benchmark saturation and metric sensitivity are also reported (Mathur et al., 2020; Kocmi and Federmann, 2023).

Our work differs from all previous work in that we bring in two new important factors when considering how translationese affects MT performance, namely the train-test alignment, and data-model alignment. Moreover, beyond the correlation-based analysis in previous papers (Graham et al., 2020;Edunov et al., 2020), we conduct causal inference (Pearl, 2009;Peters et al., 2017) to contribute causal insights on how translationese affects MT.

Discrete Prompts The release of GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) has led to interest in prompting, a new way to leverage pretrained language models (PLM). Brown et al. (2020) proposes an intuitive in-context learning paradigm by concatenating a few input and output examples and feeding them to the language model and let the model autoregressively generate answers for new examples. Recent works (Petroni et al., 2019;Davison et al., 2019;Jiang et al., 2020) design prompts to probe the factual and commonsense knowledge encoded within a PLM. Recent works (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b;Gao et al., 2021) demonstrate that even smaller PLMs have similar few-shot learning capacity. Le Scao and Rush (2021) analyzes the effect of prompting and concludes that a single prompt may be worth 100 training examples in fine-tuning.

Instead of manually designing prompts (i.e., prompt engineering), some recent studies also explore automatic prompt generation. PETAL (Schick et al., 2020) augments Pattern Exploiting Training (PET, Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b) with automatically identified label words; Gao et al. (2021) uses re-ranking to find the best label words by fine-tuning a RoBERTa model on the candidates searched by RoBERTa, and using an external generation model for data augmentation of prompt templates; AutoPrompt (Shin et al., 2020) uses a gradient-based search to determine both prompts and label words. However, these methods require parameter updates with gradient descent, which is infeasible without access to the model weights (e.g., GPT-3). PET and its variants also require a large unlabeled set and need to be fine-tuned multiple times. AutoPrompt uses discretization techniques to approximately map a continuous vector back to tokens in the vocabulary (i.e., "vocablization"). These searched prompts and labels are often uninterpretable by humans. Different from these prior studies, our proposed AMuLaP is a simple and interpretable method for few-shot prompting that can work well with and without access to model weights. Concurrently to our work,  propose a method that exploits an external knowledge base to find label mapping.

Few studies have addressed bias in language models in French. Irvine et al. (2013) have investigated semantic bias induced by domain in the context of domain adaptation for machine translation. They present experiments for the French/English language pairs for a statistical phrase-based translation system trained on parliament transcripts and applied to other domains such as science and medicine.

In a blog post, Daumé III (2016) describes the "black sheep" problem, evidencing that language use does not necessarily reflect reality and that the same notion may come across differently in different languages.

Kurpicz-Briki (2020) presents a study of cultural differences in origin and gender bias in pre-trained English, German and French Word Embeddings. The author adapts the WEAT method (Caliskan et al., 2017) that contains material for measuring bias in English language word embeddings to (Swiss) French and German and shows that the bias identified differ between the three languages studied. This is probably the effort that is closest to the present study. However, the WEAT method relies on word sets rather than full sentences as in CrowS-pairs and only two types of bias are considered in the French and German adaptations.

More importantly, Goldfarb-Tarrant et al. ( 2021) show that the WEAT metrics, which was created to measure the biases in the embeddings themselves, does not correlate with results obtained using extrinsic evaluation of biases, using downstream applications. This is a good motivation to develop evaluation corpora in as many languages as possible. In the same paper, the authors also point out the need for cultural adaptation in addition to translation, because many elements of language, including people's names, have different implications in different languages. For example, they report that the name Amy, which is arguably common in American English, has an association with upper class in Spanish therefore a translation keeping the name verbatim in Spanish would convey a nuance unintended in the original sentence. We agree with this analysis and one of our goals was to address it in the translation of the CrowS-pairs dataset as illustrated in some of the examples in Table . Zhao et al. (2020) study gender bias in a multilingual context. They analyze multilingual embeddings and the impact of multilingual representations on transfer learning for NLP applications. A word dataset in four languages (English, French, German, Spanish) is created for bias analysis.

Blodgett et al. ( 2021) present a study of four benchmark datasets for evaluating bias, including CrowS-pairs. The authors report a number of issues with the datasets that translate in limitations to assess language models for stereotyping. Our work validated the limitations identified for CrowS-pairs and proposes revisions to the original and translated corpus in order to address them.

Coherence.document: Traditional methods treat NER as a sequence labeling task, where each word or character in the sentence is assigned to a special label. As a representative, Huang et al. (2015) utilized the BiLSTM as an encoder to learn the contextual representation, and then exploited Conditional Random Field (CRF) as a decoder to label the tokens. The BiLSTM-CRF architecture achieved superior performance on various datasets, hence many following works (Lample et al., 2016;Ma and Hovy, 2016) adopt such architecture. More recently, strong pre-trained language models such as ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) and BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) introduce deep contextualization for token representations, and Dai et al. (2019) present Transformer-XL to model longer dependencies across segments. Clark et al. (2020) investigate self-attention interpretability with attention patterns, and Radford et al. (2019) scale unsupervised pretraining on web text. Liu et al. (2019) study multi-task training of transformers, and Lan et al. (2020) propose a lighter pretraining recipe. Recently, for Chinese NER, researchers proposed various lexicon-based models that incorporate the external lexicon information and obtained better results. Zhang and Yang (2018) investigated Lattice-LSTM for incorporating word lexicons into the character-based NER model. However, the lattice structure fails to compute in parallel. To address this problem, Gui et al. (2019) introduced a lexicon-based graph neural network that recasts Chinese NER as a node classification task. There are also several works that focus on incorporating all matched words from the lexicon into the character embeddings (Ma et al., 2020;Liu et al., 2021). Different from the aforementioned lexicon-based works that incorporate external resources, in this paper, we focus on exploring the internal regularity information of spans.

Coherence.document:
Our work is related to dataset construction for building persuasive dialogue systems that try to persuade the participant to take a specific action. Hiraoka et al. (2014) annotated 34 dialogues, in which an experienced salesperson tries to convince a customer to buy a camera. Yoshino et al. (2018) requested crowdsourcing workers to generate 200 persuasive dialogues. In each dialogue, one participant persuaded another one to adopt his suggestion such as cleaning a room.  collected 1017 dialogues, in which one of the participants was convinced to donate to a specific charity. We can see that the covered conversation scenarios in these datasets were strictly limited to specific tasks, while our scenarios are more general and can be easily extended to different cases. Also, our constructed dataset is about three times larger than the prior work, indicating the usefulness of the recent pre-trained paradigm.

The topic of conversational recommendation systems is also related to our work. A number of attempts have been made to collect training data for conversational recommendation systems. These studies (Wu et al., 2019;Zhou et al., 2020;Xu et al., 2020) first extracted a path consisting of an entity or attribute nodes from a knowledge base. Then they asked annotators to write conversational recommendation dialogues. The flow of mentioned topics in a dialogue should follow the extracted path. Similarly,  also built a dataset by asking human workers to create dialogues based on a topic path. It should be noted that, in these datasets, the goal of such systems is to only make entity recommendations instead of tasks, while our work goes beyond them in naturally transferring from chit-chat to task-oriented dialogues and completing a task the user may want.

Another related work is generating a transition between two given open-domain utterances. Tang et al. (2019) proposed to generate the transition conditional on a specific word, because they want the generated transition can drive the conversation topic to the specified word. Sevegnani et al. (2021) collected a new dataset of human-created one-turn topic transitions. Each dialogue contains 2 utterances with different topics and 1 transition in the middle of them.

There are some recent studies trying to merge chit-chat and task-oriented dialogues, but the purposes of merged dialogues differ from ours. Sun et al. (2021) enhanced the utterances in taskoriented dialogues by appending chit-chat sen-tences. They hope that the agent gains more social, personalized, and engaging communication skills. Ennen et al. (2021) proposed a dialogue system that can transfer the style of generated response from chit-chat to task-oriented styles. However, the system is a prototype model, there is still a large gap to properly bridge chitchat and task-oriented dialogues. The motivation of our work is closely similar to that of the study by Yu et al. (2017). They manually created several task-oriented response generation strategies specifically designed for the movie promotion scenario. In addition, the expert knowledge was utilized to design reinforcement learning rewards that help their dialogue system to decide which action to take (i.e., continuing chitchat or selecting a task-oriented strategy to reply).

However, we can observe that the prior work in these studies heavily relied on human efforts (data collection, expert-created strategies, etc.). Therefore, it can be expensive and hard to extend their data or method the practical cases due to the requirement of larger-scale training data. Our proposed framework benefits from the pre-trained models and shows its outstanding conversational capability. The flexibility of extending to diverse cases is also validated, considering that all components inside the framework can be easily substituted by the updated models, and the generated data can be used by semi-supervised or unsupervised methods for cold-start scenarios.

Extensions to time-varying treatments consider marginal structural models estimated with stabilized weights to mitigate variance inflation (Robins, Hernán, and Brumback, 2000). Scharfstein, Rotnitzky, and Robins (1999) address missing outcomes under nonignorable mechanisms via selection models. Hernán and Robins (2020) provide a comprehensive treatment of identification and estimation in longitudinal settings with dynamic confounding. (2006) analyze surrogate loss calibration and excess risk in classification. Coherence.document:
The ATE is defined as τ = E[Y i (1)−Y i (0)], where Y i (t) is the potential outcome for unit i under treatment t. It can be identified in randomized experiments (Rubin, 1974). However, the situation is more complicated in the observational setting, where the treatment is not randomized to units but could be correlated with confounders, X i , that are associated with the treatment and the outcome.

In that setting, we can, with additional assumptions, still recover the ATE using Inverse Propensity Weighting (IPW) or related robust methods (Funk et al., 2011), where observations are weighted by the inverse of their estimated treatment probabilities π(X i ) = Pr(T i = 1|X i ) (Rosenbaum and Rubin, 1983). Consistent estimation further relies on overlap and correct specification or sufficient flexibility in either the propensity or outcome models, with doubly robust estimators offering protection against single-model misspecification (Robins and Rotnitzky, 1995; Bang and Robins, 2005; Athey et al., 2018). Targeted maximum likelihood estimation refines plug-in learners by constructing least favorable submodels and solving efficient influence function estimating equations (van der Laan and Rubin, 2006; van der Laan and Rose, 2011). Sample-splitting and cross-fitting help reduce overfitting bias and achieve asymptotic normality when using machine learning for nuisance components (Chernozhukov et al., 2018; Newey and Robins, 2018).

Recent advances also examine heterogeneous treatment effects, with Wager and Athey (2018) introducing causal forests and Künzel et al. (2019) proposing meta-learners for individualized effects. Nie and Wager (2021) study orthogonalization to debias flexible learners. Kennedy (2022) develops doubly robust inference for nuisance-adaptive procedures. Chernozhukov et al. (2018) analyze debiased machine learning for treatment and structural parameters across high-dimensional settings. Banerjee et al. (2015) present results on matrix estimation with noise and some implications for structured prediction. Xu et al. (2013) consider low-rank matrix recovery with missing entries and provide guarantees under incoherence. Zhang and Zhang (2014) propose confidence intervals for high-dimensional regression coefficients using debiasing. Li et al. (2017) investigate sparse additive models with group structure and regularization penalties. Sun and Zhang (2020) address selective inference in model selection pipelines.

Stabilized weights can alleviate variance from extreme propensities and improve finite-sample performance when overlap is limited, although trimming or covariate balancing methods may also be considered (Cole and Hernán, 2008; Crump et al., 2009; Hainmueller, 2012). Calibration estimators that directly target covariate balance without modeling propensities have been proposed to reduce sensitivity to misspecification (Imai and Ratkovic, 2014; Zubizarreta, 2015). Estimation grounded in the semiparametric efficiency bound clarifies the role of influence functions in characterizing optimality and robustness (Hahn, 1998; Bickel et al., 1993). Sensitivity analysis frameworks quantify departures from unconfoundedness, enabling partial identification and robustness checks (Rosenbaum, 2002; Imbens, 2003; Franks et al., 2020).

Extensions to time-varying treatments consider marginal structural models estimated with stabilized weights to mitigate variance inflation (Robins, Hernán, and Brumback, 2000). Scharfstein, Rotnitzky, and Robins (1999) address missing outcomes under nonignorable mechanisms via selection models. Hernán and Robins (2020) provide a comprehensive treatment of identification and estimation in longitudinal settings with dynamic confounding. Pseudo-outcome regressions for causal parameters are also studied in off-policy evaluation for contextual bandits (Dudík et al., 2014; Farajtabar et al., 2018). Empirical process theory underpins rates for semiparametric M-estimators (van der Vaart and Wellner, 1996). Bartlett et al. (2006) analyze surrogate loss calibration and excess risk in classification. Neyman (1923) formalized randomization inference for finite populations and derived unbiased variance estimators under complete randomization. Cochran (1957) studied experimental design and stratification effects on variance. Box, Hunter, and Hunter (1978) discuss response surface methodology in industrial experiments.

In summary, consistent estimation of average and heterogeneous effects in observational studies hinges on defensible identification, careful handling of overlap, and estimators that integrate bias-reduction with variance control, while leveraging flexible learners without sacrificing valid uncertainty quantification.

Earlier work in hate speech detection focused on data collection, curation and annotation frameworks (Waseem and Hovy, 2016; Davidson et al., 2017; Founta et al., 2018).
Recent work has expanded the set of captured labels to include more pertinent information such as targets and other forms of abuse (Sap et al., 2020; Hede et al., 2021; Guest et al., 2021; Grimminger and Klinger, 2021; Ross et al., 2017) as well as benchmarking (Röttger et al., 2021; Mathew et al., 2021).
Analysis of datasets has been performed too (Madukwe et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020; Wiegand et al., 2019; Swamy et al., 2019; Davidson et al., 2019a).
This body of work reveals how label granularity and corpus design shape downstream system behavior.
Work has also been conducted to expand research to multiple languages (Ousidhoum et al., 2019; Ranasinghe and Zampieri, 2020; Ross et al., 2017; Nozza, 2021; Zoph et al., 2016; Marivate et al., 2020; Nekoto et al., 2020).
XTREMESPEECH contributes to this goal by providing Brazilian Portuguese, German, Hindi and Swahili data.
We release standardized splits and label mappings to facilitate cross-lingual comparisons.
Research has also been conducted to investigate annotation bias and annotator pools (Al Kuwatly et al., 2020; Waseem, 2016; Ross et al., 2017; Shmueli et al., 2021; Posch et al., 2018), as well as bias in existing datasets (Davidson et al., 2019b; Laugier et al., 2021).
Methods for bias mitigation have also been proposed (Sap et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2020; Han et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021).
It was found that data can reflect and propagate annotator bias.
To address this, we diversify the annotator pool in our work.
We also report per-group performance to surface disparate error profiles.
In another line of work, theoretical foundations are being established, in the form of taxonomies (Banko et al., 2020), definitions (Wiegand et al., 2021; Waseem et al., 2017) and hate speech theory (Price et al., 2020; Laaksonen et al., 2020).
We are adding to this with definitions based on fieldwork and grounded research, inspired by anthropological and ethnographic work that investigates the societal impact of online hate and extreme speech (Boromisza-Habashi, 2013; Donovan and danah boyd, 2021; Haynes, 2019; Udupa and Pohjonen, 2019; Hervik, 2019).
Prior multilingual transfer techniques for sequence classification emphasize representation alignment and task-agnostic pretraining objectives (Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019; Conneau et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2020) without clarifying their role in refining normative constructs for abusive content.
Our perspective links operational labels to situated practices documented in community rulemaking.
Further, strides have been made in the ethics of AI.
Questions of data stewardship and accountability have taken center stage.
Who should collect data and who is responsible for model deployment decisions?
Calls have been made for more inclusive pools of annotators and domain experts overseeing NLP projects, as well as exploration of other ethical dilemmas (Leins et al., 2020).
We integrate these recommendations into our protocol by including local experts during guideline development.
Finally, we outline open challenges in moving from dataset curation to sustained community partnership.
We argue that sustained engagement is necessary to ensure that evaluation criteria remain aligned with social harms.
